Hu Cang and Yuan Wang ask whether quantum spacetime itself would blur gravitational waves as they cross the universe. Microscopic curvature fluctuations, if real, should leave a mark on long traveling waves. The authors build a gauge invariant framework, free of coordinate artifacts, for that cumulative effect.

Working from the Riemann tensor's two point function, they use the extreme slowness of cosmic expansion versus wave frequency. Phase diffusion emerges as the unique leading imprint, not fading or mode mixing. A clear, falsifiable target helps future detectors test quantum gravity ideas with real data. A phase drift is a faint mark, but faint marks are what the next wave of gear is built to catch in flight.
arxiv-2512-02882:
Youkang Wang and five co-authors spend a language model's test time budget where it counts most. Test time policy optimization lets a model adapt to shifted tasks using feedback from its own trial answers. Common methods estimate rewards by majority vote over a fixed number of rollouts, wasting compute.

OptPO allocates rollouts adaptively, giving more trials where the reward is still uncertain. That principled budgeting trims substantial redundancy, the authors argue. Smarter allocation could make self improving inference cheaper, helping deployed models adapt without retraining or human labels. Trials cost time and coin, so a plan that spends them where doubt is thick is a plan that pays for its own keep.
arxiv-2512-02982:
Xiang Xu and six co-authors model moving 3D worlds from LiDAR sequences while tracking where the model is unsure. Dynamic scene modeling underpins 4D worlds for autonomous driving and embodied AI. Existing generative frameworks treat every region alike, ignoring how uncertainty varies across a real scene.

Uniform generation leaves artifacts in complex or ambiguous regions, hurting realism and temporal stability. U4D makes generation uncertainty aware, spending care where the scene is hardest. Worlds that know their own weak spots are safer to train and test driving systems inside. Marks of doubt on the map warn the car where to slow. A plain map with no doubt marks can not serve that use at all in fog or glare.
arxiv-2512-03082:
Large language models can favor their own past choices. Nan Zhuang and five co-authors study that flaw, called choice-supportive bias, in this 2025 work. When a model judges options, it may back the one it picked before, which can skew fair decisions.

Most past fixes target bias about social groups, not this kind of thinking bias. The authors build a method based on how reasons depend on each other. Their aim is to make model judgments more even and fair. Fair judging matters as these models help with hiring, grading, and other key choices. For model evaluators, the work shows that bias can hide in choices, not just in data about people.
arxiv-2512-03482:
Special wave functions on exotic surfaces hide number patterns. Jiaqi Hou studies Kakeya-Nikodym norms of Maass forms in this 2025 work. The setting is a compact arithmetic complex hyperbolic surface, with a Hecke-Maass form of large spectral parameter.

Hou applies the amplification method to bound the norm. The result gains a power saving over the trivial bound. Such bounds show how evenly wave functions spread. They connect analysis, geometry, and number theory in the study of quantum chaos on arithmetic spaces. Amplification boosts a chosen form's signal, a standard trick with delicate tuning.
arxiv-2512-03582:
Propaganda works through stories, not just slogans. This 2025 study proposes fine-grained narrative classification in biased news articles. Narratives organize persuasive techniques into coherent stories that assign blame and build identification with a camp.

The authors also explore article-bias classification as a precursor task. Sorting narratives at a fine grain could help analysts track how biased outlets frame events. Such tools may support media literacy and research on polarization. They must be used with care to avoid labeling disputes. Bias classification first helps sort articles before the harder narrative labels are applied, giving the pipeline a staged path to fine detail.
arxiv-2512-03782: Marco Adamo Seveso develops an explicit p-adic integration theory in this short 2025 number theory note. The setting is the Igusa towers built over Siegel modular varieties, families of spaces that organise modular forms of higher genus. P-adic integration assigns sizes to sets in the p-adic world, where distance is measured by divisibility by a prime. Seveso states that the theory he builds has applications to explicit reciprocity laws, a central theme in modern number theory.
arxiv-2512-04882:
Rahul Barthwal, Firas Dhaouadi, and Christian Rohde build approximation systems that tame dispersive wave equations by rewriting them as hyperbolic ones. Dispersive equations, where waves of different lengths travel at different speeds, resist standard solvers. Their 2025 arXiv paper constructs a first-order, strictly hyperbolic stand-in for purely dispersive problems with nonlinear fluxes. A unique symmetrizer, valid for any smooth flux, gives local well-posedness of smooth solutions.

Under stronger flux conditions, the hyperbolic system gains a strictly convex entropy that mirrors the original equation's energy. For equations that also diffuse, the team uses a viscoelastic damped system that respects the same entropy. That pairing yields global well-posedness for the mixed approximation. Relative entropy methods then prove the approximations converge to the true solutions. Reliable stand-ins open dispersive flows, from water waves to plasmas, to mature hyperbolic solvers.
arxiv-2512-04982:
Mostafa Behtouei, Carlos Salgado Lopez, and Giancarlo Gatti build a new mathematical frame for laser-plasma wakefield acceleration, a method that surfs electrons on waves in ionized gas to speed them up. Inside a narrow discharge tube, an intense laser pulse and the plasma answer each other in tangled ways, and the usual descriptions can be hard to steer or simplify. The authors recast the whole system with operators, the workhorse objects of quantum-style mathematics.

Four operators carry the story: one for the laser's crosswise modes, one for the plasma's nonlinear reply, one for its ringing, and one for the push of the light itself. In the gentle regime the modes stay separate and stable; stronger action mixes them, which is where energy passes into the wake. The frame also plugs into neural operator methods, pointing toward fast simplified models for planning and controlling future accelerator experiments.
arxiv-2512-05282:
Armand Ley studies what entropic regularization selects in optimal transport on a line. Optimal transport asks for the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. Adding an entropy penalty smooths the problem and makes it computable. But as the penalty shrinks, which optimal plan the smoothed solutions approach is subtle, when the cost is plain distance and the optimal plan is not unique. Outside discrete settings and unique-plan cases, existence and characterization were largely open.

Ley proposes a natural candidate for the limiting object and proves convergence to it when the two distributions share no common mass. For arbitrary distributions, he shows every limit point of the smoothed minimizers obeys a structural condition called weak multiplicativity. The candidate rests on a decomposition theorem for transport plans he flags as independently interesting, and the paper complements earlier work by Di Marino and Louet.
arxiv-2512-05482:
Mai Tsujimoto hunts the rare objects that self-driving systems need to see and least often do. Detectors trained on point clouds stumble on uncommon categories — construction vehicles, motorcycles, barriers — because labelled examples are scarce. Tsujimoto's cross-modal framework uses a vision-language model to mine driving scenes for exactly those rarities. It turns image understanding into training data for the three-dimensional detector.

The pipeline blends object detection, semantic feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and outlier detection from two matching methods. Concept-based filtering keeps the catch meaningful and easy to check. Because it labels concepts on its own, the burden collapses to the valuable samples. On a standard driving dataset, detectors trained with the mined data beat those trained on the same amount of random data. The biggest gains land on hard cases like trailers and bicycles. It is a data-picking strategy for safety-critical perception.
arxiv-2512-06682:
Boyang Xu and four co authors build a decision framework that runs machines and schedules their upkeep from the same live signals. Factories watch their equipment with many sensors, but folding all those streams into one good call on when to run hard and when to service is hard. The true wear state of a machine is never seen directly; sensors give a noisy window on it.

Their model treats the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, the standard frame for acting under hidden state. From the live degradation signals it derives joint policies for production capacity and preventive maintenance, with limits that keep wear in bounds. They test it on bearing wear data and on a NASA data set of aircraft turbofan engines. The framework improved performance in both cases, showing a systematic way to let real time wear data steer operations and maintenance together.
arxiv-2512-06982:
Yu Yu, Qian Xie, Nairen Cao, and Li Jin address a design chore in reinforcement learning: building the encoder that turns many kinds of input into one useful picture of the world. An agent may juggle sensor readings, signals over time, camera views, and written instructions at once. Hand-designing a module for each source, plus a module that fuses them, is slow. Automated architecture search exists, but standard versions ignore handy clues from the modules' own outputs.

The team hands the search to a large language model acting as a design agent. The model uses its prior knowledge plus signals about how well each candidate part represents its source. In a mixed traffic control task, the pipeline found better encoders than traditional search while testing fewer candidates. It also beat an earlier language-model framework called GENIUS, suggesting guided search can save costly trials.
arxiv-2512-07082:
Yuan-Ting Zhong and co-authors build TRACE, a detector for the moment a data stream changes its character. Streaming optimization, where decisions must track live data, breaks when the underlying pattern drifts, and the drift times are rarely known in advance. Older detectors assume tidy settings: fixed intervals between drifts or full sight of the environment. TRACE instead learns what drift looks like in general, then recognizes it in new streams.

Statistical features are first extracted from the stream by a principled tokenization, turning stretches of data into a sequence a model can read. An attention-based sequence learner then spots drift patterns across time scales. Plugged into a streaming optimizer, the detector lets the search adapt when the world shifts. Across diverse benchmarks, TRACE generalized to unseen data sets better than rivals and stayed robust under varied conditions.
arxiv-2512-07682:
Manika Bag wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on controlling how two phases separate. The Cahn-Hilliard equation describes that separation, here in a higher-order, sixth-order form. A Brinkman equation for fluid flow is coupled to it.

The coupled system includes a source term for mass exchange between phases. The flow equation carries a forcing term that is not divergence-free. That forcing serves as the distributed control the author can dial. Mobility and viscosity are held constant through the analysis. The nonlinearity takes the classic double-well shape, smoothed for the proofs. The goal is an optimal control that steers the mixture at least cost. The cost functional includes an absolute-value term that promotes sparse controls.  Bag derives the first-order conditions that any optimal control must obey. Both cases get full treatment.
arxiv-2512-07982: Eunice Sukarto, a mathematician working in homotopy theory, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. Her topic is the rational form of a classifying space for real special unitary groups, with a two element symmetry acting on it. It grows out of a motivic homotopy problem raised by Asok, Fasel, and Hopkins. Sukarto describes that homotopy type using equivariant Eilenberg MacLane spaces, standard building blocks in algebraic topology. That gives specialists a concrete way to compute with a space that had been hard to pin down.
arxiv-2512-08082:
Vala Vakilian, Zimeng Wang, Ankit Singh Rawat, and Christos Thrampoulidis, machine learning researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They test a simple hypothesis about natural language: for most text, only a short recent stretch of context is needed to predict what comes next. They call this short context dominance, and they measure it using large language models as statistical oracles.

Across long documents, most sequences needed only the last ninety six tokens or fewer to match full context predictions. The team then builds a practical proxy that flags the minority of sequences where distant context truly matters, without knowing the next token. A simple threshold on that proxy separates long context cases from short ones well. Finally, they design a decoding method that boosts tokens tied to distant context, reducing the bias short context creates. Across question answering tasks and model designs, that fix improved performance.
arxiv-2512-08182:
Yongda Wang and Shifeng Xiong, statisticians in China, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025 about empirical likelihood with massive data. Empirical likelihood is a flexible way to do inference without assuming a distribution, but with huge datasets it becomes painfully heavy. Their grouped method cuts that cost by treating blocks of data as units.

The method splits the observations into far fewer groups and gives every point in a group the same probability weight. Only the group weights must then be estimated, shrinking the optimization problem by orders of magnitude. The authors prove the grouped version keeps the same first order accuracy as the standard method for estimating equations and two sample mean problems. A distributed version spreads the work across servers. In tests, it matched the standard accuracy while running far faster, handling a billion data points in tens of seconds on one ordinary computer.
arxiv-2512-08582:
The CMS Collaboration, one of the two big detector teams at the Large Hadron Collider, posted a measurement paper on arXiv in December 2025. It measures how often proton collisions produce a Z boson together with a photon, using data the CMS detector gathered in 2022 at a record collision energy. Events were kept when they showed an electron or muon pair matching a Z boson, plus an isolated photon.

The measured rate matched the standard model prediction closely, well inside the uncertainties. Beyond a headline number, the result probes how force carriers interact with each other. Certain three way couplings among neutral bosons are forbidden in the simplest picture, and any sign of them would mean new physics. Using a modern effective theory framework, the team set the first constraints on those couplings from this channel. Precision measurements of clean processes remain sharp tools for cornering new physics.
arxiv-2512-08782:
Roopak Surendran presents a machine learning method to detect malicious smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain before they are deployed. Harmful contracts in the Solidity language can exploit flaws such as reentrancy or bad randomness to drain funds or block service. Finding them early can prevent those attacks.

The method analyzes the operation codes of the virtual machine that runs the contracts. Opcode counts are balanced with a synthetic oversampling method, then turned into binary features through an entropy based binning step. A classifier trained on those features detects almost all malicious contracts with a very low false positive rate. An explanation tool is added to show, for each flagged contract, which opcode features drove the decision. That transparency helps reviewers trust and audit the automated verdicts.
arxiv-2512-08882:
Mohamed Elmahallawy and Asma Jodeiri Akbarfam propose OrbitChain, a blockchain backed method for federated learning across satellite networks run by many vendors. Low Earth orbit satellites now produce huge data for tasks such as disaster detection, border monitoring, and climate study. Federated learning lets vendors train a joint model without sharing raw data, but slow links and trust problems remain.

Biased or falsified updates can enter through cyberattacks on satellite links, and intermittent connectivity slows convergence. OrbitChain offloads consensus to high altitude platforms with more compute power. It also records a transparent, auditable history for each model update from other orbits and vendors. Manipulated or incomplete contributions are blocked from the global aggregation step. Studies show lower overhead, better privacy and security, and improved model accuracy. The ledger finalizes many blocks with sub second latency, and convergence time falls sharply on real satellite data.
arxiv-2512-08982:
Jian Xu and coauthors present Consist Retinex, a one step method for enhancing low light images. Generative approaches can give high quality results, but they rely on repeated sampling and are hard to deploy when latency is strict. Consistency models allow one step restoration, yet direct use for Retinex enhancement is unstable.

Their system first uses a transformer decomposition network to obtain paired reflectance and illumination maps. Two conditional consistency models are then trained with a dual objective that joins trajectory consistency with alignment to ground truth components. A noise emphasized sampling rule concentrates supervision near the inference endpoint while keeping full noise coverage. Theory gives an endpoint error bound and explains why the two signals complement each other. Tests on paired and unpaired low light benchmarks show leading scores under one step inference, at lower cost.
arxiv-2512-09182:
Hunjae Lee studies failure modes of transformer models through the lens of graph neural network theory. Decoder only transformers dominate language models, yet they show surprising failures. The article argues that much of deep learning is about learnable mixing and propagation of information, so failures are best read as bottlenecks in that propagation.

Graph network theory already has a rich account of such bottlenecks and of theoretical failure modes. Lee makes the case that many issues known for graph networks also affect transformers. The causal nature of decoder only models adds its own geometry to information flow, producing predictable and potentially severe failure modes. Existing fixes in transformer research are often ad hoc and driven by intuition. The article unifies many of them under the graph based perspective, explaining why each works and what problem it truly solves. That framing can guide more targeted improvements to transformer design.
arxiv-2512-09882:
Justin W. Lin leads a large team in the first head to head test of AI agents against human professionals at live penetration testing. Ten cybersecurity professionals, six existing AI agents, and the authors' new agent scaffold, ARTEMIS, all attacked the same large university network of about eight thousand hosts. ARTEMIS is a multi agent system that can spawn sub agents and sorts found vulnerabilities automatically.

ARTEMIS placed second overall. It found nine valid vulnerabilities with a high valid submission rate, beating nine of the ten humans. Older scaffolds lagged behind most human participants. The agents shone at systematic enumeration, parallel attacks, and cost, with some variants running far cheaper per hour than professionals. But gaps remain: the agents produced more false positives than humans and struggled with tasks needing a graphical interface.
arxiv-2512-10182:
Tsuyoshi Kato, Daisuke Kishimoto, and Mitsunobu Tsutaya extend fixed point theory to infinite, noncompact spaces. Classical Lefschetz theory counts fixed points of maps on compact manifolds and obstructs vector fields. Many natural spaces, covering spaces and infinite complexes among them, are not compact. The authors work on complete Riemannian manifolds of bounded geometry with uniformly continuous maps. They define a uniform Lefschetz class for such a map. It vanishes exactly when the map can be deformed evenly to one with no fixed points at all, including at infinity.

A companion class obstructs nonvanishing vector fields; both vanish on their own on nonamenable spaces. For covering spaces of closed manifolds, a Lefschetz-Hopf style formula gives the class, and a Poincaré-Hopf theorem follows. The key new tool is a uniform bounded cohomology with the traits topology needs: homotopy invariance, excision, and Poincaré duality.
arxiv-2512-10582:
Tobias Rohe and co-authors argue that quantum circuits should be shaped by the problem they solve, not pulled from a generic shelf. Much quantum computing work reuses one-size-fits-all circuit layouts. And the authors test whether baking in geometric prior knowledge helps a hybrid quantum generative adversarial network that must produce graphs obeying geometric rules.

Their test bed is generating constrained complete graphs on four nodes, judged by how well outputs match the target distribution and respect rules such as the triangle and Ptolemaic inequalities. A portfolio of entanglement layouts and loss designs was compared. The circuit whose topology mirrored the triangle rule achieved the best geometric validity among quantum models and matched a classical GAN. Gate choices, variance control, and output scaling each shifted the balance between geometric consistency and statistical accuracy.
arxiv-2512-10782:
Alon Hever and co-authors hunt for undiscovered crystals by borrowing the shapes of neighbours. Their scheme adapts known structure types from compounds of nearby elements, reasoning that a stable arrangement for one element's compound often suits its neighbours in the table too. They show the search on the binary selenide and sulfide families, a key class of semiconductors.

The directed search predicts ten compounds missing from the inorganic crystal structure database. Comparing against wider searches that borrow structures from more distant elements shows the near-neighbour screen is relatively efficient, finding candidates without trawling the whole table. The authors propose the approach as a general heuristic rule: when prospecting for new stable compounds in other families, raid the neighbours' structures first. It is a simple scheme, aimed at guiding expensive stability checks toward promising ground.
arxiv-2512-11182:
Niranjana Shankarappa and colleagues use the Parker Solar Probe's full mission data to trace where small ion scale waves in the solar wind get their energy. These circularly polarised waves are common close to the Sun and mark where plasma instabilities and turbulence exchange energy. The team surveyed waves across many solar encounters and compared them with the measured shapes of proton distributions.

Left handed waves appeared often, and more frequently nearer the Sun, matching long storms of ion cyclotron waves running alongside the magnetic field. Energy spectra steepened during those storms, suggesting the waves carry energy tied to uneven proton temperatures. Right handed waves were rarer and matched fast magnetosonic waves, appearing when extra proton beams raised the heat flow along the field. A machine learning tool helped pin down the heat flow threshold at which those waves switch on.
arxiv-2512-11482:
Melih Catal, Pooja Rani, and Harald Gall apply differential privacy to code generating language models so they stop memorising their training data. Code models can reproduce training snippets verbatim, risking privacy breaches and intellectual property violations that keep them out of sensitive settings. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise during training to protect individual examples while preserving general patterns.

The authors first investigate what drives memorisation during fine tuning, then measure how privacy training changes it. Memorisation fell substantially across every snippet type tested, and the snippet types most prone to being memorised were also the ones privacy training protected best. Perplexity rose slightly, yet code generation ability was preserved and sometimes even improved. Training time and energy use barely changed. The study, presented as the first comprehensive evaluation of its kind, argues private code models are practical today.
arxiv-2512-11682:
Tim Cofala and co-authors report how TxAgent, an AI agent for drug choice help, fared in the CURE-Bench contest at NeurIPS 2025. Picking drugs is high stakes work shaped by patient traits, disease paths, and drug effects. TxAgent answers by repeated search and reasoning steps.

It uses a tuned Llama model that calls a shared tool set fed by the FDA drug API, OpenTargets, and Monarch. The contest grades not just final answers but the reasoning trace and the tool call order. The team shows that better tool search lifts the whole system. Their entry won the Excellence Award in Open Science, and the study maps where agent drug help still needs care.
arxiv-2512-11782:
Peiqing Yang and co-authors present MatAnyone 2, a system that cuts moving subjects out of video with fine edges. Video matting is held back by small, tame training sets. Adding segmentation data helps meaning but not hair thin borders.

Their Matting Quality Evaluator grades alpha mattes pixel by pixel with no ground truth, flagging good and bad zones. That grader guides training live and also curates new data by merging the strengths of top models. The result is VMReal, a set of 28,000 real clips with 2.4 million frames. A training trick that looks at far apart frames handles long videos. MatAnyone 2 topped prior methods on synthetic and real tests.
arxiv-2512-11982:
Nolan Koblischke and co-authors build a search engine that finds galaxies by meaning across more than 100 million images. Hunting rare objects by hand labeling is hopeless at that scale. Their pipeline lets vision language models write captions for unlabeled galaxy images.

Those captions train a model that aligns an astronomy foundation model with text, producing searchable embeddings. The search beat plain image similarity and set state of the art zero shot marks on rare object hunts, despite training on random images. A caption based re ranking step nearly doubles recall in the top 100 for the hardest targets. The hunt surfaced 36 new candidate stellar streams. The recipe suits any huge unlabeled science image archive.
arxiv-2512-12382:
Yaogan Mensah and Isiaka Aremua study spectral Barron spaces for vector valued functions in a 2025 math paper. Such spaces hold functions on a compact group whose Fourier transforms meet a summability rule. The values lie in a Banach space, so outputs can be vectors or more general objects, not just numbers.

The authors map the basic properties of these spaces and show how they embed into Sobolev spaces and bounded function spaces. Their main theorem gives an approximation rate: in a Hilbert space target, matrix coefficients of unitary representations approximate each function with error shrinking like n to the minus one half. A variant covers targets of Rademacher type 2.
arxiv-2512-12482:
Haipeng Li, Nanzhe Wang, Louis J Durlofsky, and Biondo L Biondi build a Bayesian method to monitor stored carbon dioxide underground in a 2025 paper. Watching buried CO2 plumes matters for storage safety. Full-waveform monitoring reads seismic data at high detail, but standard inversion gives no uncertainty and uses little prior knowledge, and sparse noisy data can make it unreliable.

Their framework mixes reservoir flow physics with a generative prior. Flow simulations on varied geology create sample plumes, and a variational autoencoder compresses them into a simple latent space. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo then infers plume changes from time lapse seismic data with uncertainty bounds. Tests stayed stable and accurate under very sparse, noisy setups.
arxiv-2512-12882:
V. A. Dzuba, V. V. Flambaum, and G. K. Vong compute a tiny effect in atoms called parity nonconservation, where a process that should be mirrored is not quite symmetric. They study rubidium and a strontium ion. Two electron jumps in each system are their focus.

Their results cover parts that depend on nuclear spin and parts that do not. They stress the possible effect of a hypothetical light particle, a Z prime boson. In light atoms, that new effect grows fast compared with the known one as nuclear charge falls. Light atoms may also allow cleaner theory, aiding searches for new physics.
arxiv-2512-13182:
Romana Mikusincova and co-authors report the first X-ray polarimetry of an eclipsing neutron star binary, AX J1745.6-2901. The source sits very close to the Galactic center and was caught by chance during a 150 kilosecond IXPE observation of a neighbor. Separating its signal from nearby glow was the main hurdle.

After careful handling of contamination, they found a polarization degree of 14.7 percent, plus or minus 4.0 percent, at an angle of 122 degrees, plus or minus 8 degrees. During eclipse, the degree rose to 34.2 percent, plus or minus 8.7 percent. That rise suggests the polarization comes from scattering, likely in disk winds.
arxiv-2512-13282:
Endri Taka and co-authors study GEMM performance, the matrix multiply operations at the heart of AI workloads, across generations of AMD Ryzen AI neural processing units. Getting the most from each chip generation takes careful tuning of tiling, data layout, and scheduling. Their paper's title frames the task as striking the right balance.

The work compares how matrix multiplication kernels perform as the hardware evolves from one generation to the next. Such studies guide compiler and kernel writers who must retune core routines for new silicon. Practical speed on these laptop class AI chips decides how fast local models run, making this optimization work directly relevant to on-device AI.
arxiv-2512-13582:
Roman Klopsch and co-authors study turbulent air flow over a Gaussian-shaped bump, in attached and separated forms. They focus on where slow, coherent structures in the flow come from. Their work blends time-resolved lab measures with linear physics models built on mean flow fields from the same data.

Spectral analysis finds coherent motion at low and medium rates in both flows, much stronger when the flow separates. In that case, a three-dimensional zero-frequency instability makes large, long structures past the bump. A standing-wave model matches the spanwise pattern seen in tests. The findings help explain gaps between simulations and lab results, and guide domain size choices.
arxiv-2512-13682:
J. M. S. Donnellan and co-authors test a deblending method for the PRIMA far-infrared space mission concept. PRIMAger would map the sky at 25 to 235 microns, where many galaxies blur together at the confusion limit. Their goal is to recover faint galaxy fluxes below that limit.

Their Bayesian method, XID+stepwise, uses hyperspectral imaging and passes flux constraints from short to long wavelengths in steps. With Euclid-like source positions, it recovers fluxes within 20% down to zero point two to zero point seven mJy at 45 to 84 microns. That is one point three to three point five times fainter than the confusion limit. IR-luminous galaxies near redshift 2 were detected in most channels, even well below the classical limit.
arxiv-2512-13782:
Gautham N. Sabhahit, Jorick S. Vink, and Andreas A. C. Sander compute wind mass-loss rates for very massive stars. Radiation-driven winds dominate how these stars evolve, what chemicals they return, and how they die. Past rates often extrapolated from O stars and likely understate true loss.

Their hydrodynamical atmosphere models span 40 to 135 solar masses at fixed luminosity, with solar-like metallicity. They confirm a predicted kink where wind optical depth crosses unity and spectra shift from O star to WNh type. The kink sits at an Eddington factor near 0.43, about 60 solar masses, matching Arches cluster transition stars. Above the kink, loss rates climb much more steeply as mass falls, with slope near 10.
arxiv-2512-14482:
Andre Pointner and nine co-authors built lab hardware for watching living cells with a diamond quantum sensor. Defects in diamond, called nitrogen-vacancy centers, detect tiny magnetic fields without fading under light, which suits long observations. Standard microscope incubators, however, do not fit the widefield setup these sensors need.

Their compact chamber is 3D-printed from a cell-safe material and holds temperature, carbon dioxide, and humidity steady right on the diamond surface. Colon cancer cells stayed alive and kept multiplying through ninety hours inside it. After that long cultivation, the team still imaged magnetic fields from cells tagged with magnetic labels.
arxiv-2512-14882:
Lindsey S. Wiser, Alexander Roth, Vivien Parmentier, and Michael R. Line compare two ways to model the air of planets outside our solar system. One way treats the air as a single column that varies only with height. The other runs a full three dimensional climate model that tracks winds around the planet.

The team matches the two model types on the same planets, with the same heat output, across a grid of heat levels, gravities, metal content, and spin rates. The dayside temperature layout splits into four layers, each shaping the light spectrum in its own way. At a heat level of 1400 K, the 3D models show a temperature inversion that the 1D models miss. The gaps shrink for hotter planets but can still exceed what the Webb telescope can measure, which could bias what observers infer.
arxiv-2512-14982:
Yaniv Leviathan and two coauthors report a disarmingly simple trick that makes language models answer better: say the prompt twice. Their tests skip the reasoning mode that lets models think step by step. In that plain mode, feeding the same input prompt a second time lifts performance.

The gain shows up across popular models from several makers, namely Gemini, GPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. It comes with no rise in the number of tokens the model generates, and no added delay for the user. The abstract states the finding in one sentence, and the study stands as a short, practical note for anyone who writes prompts.
arxiv-2512-15182:
Sarim Hashmi and four coauthors rethink deepfake detection around a humble question: can a sample be proven authentic, or could its authenticity be plausibly denied? Generative models now fake media so well that post hoc detection can be impossible in principle, leaving false positive rates unbounded. Attackers can also adapt to known detectors cheaply and slip past them.

Their resynthesis framework checks a sample by rebuilding it and comparing, with calibration that keeps false positives low and controlled. In the high precision, low recall setting against compute limited adversaries, it proved the most reliable way to verify authentic samples. It also held up under attack, while prior methods were easily evaded at the same compute budgets. The approach spans several media types and uses state of the art inversion techniques.
arxiv-2512-15982:
Brendan Sheehan and co authors explore overlapping dynamic nuclear polarization mechanisms in type 1b diamond in a 2025 paper. Dynamic nuclear polarization, or DNP, boosts NMR signals by passing polarization to nuclei, and unevenly spread P1 centers in these diamonds let several DNP mechanisms run in one crystal. Their overlap produces complex spectra that are hard to assign.

At some crystal orientations, rival mechanisms drive the effect with opposite signs at the same microwave frequency. The team compares plain and frequency modulated microwave excitation at room temperature. Shifting frequency can suppress one mechanism while enhancing another, and sometimes beats plain excitation on total signal. In powder samples, a signal sign change during buildup appears that single crystals never show.
arxiv-2512-16282:
Jinhao Zhang and four co-authors shrink language models more cleverly in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. Quantization stores a model's numbers in fewer bits to save memory and speed. Most post-training methods apply one uniform strategy to every layer, even though layers differ a lot in which algorithm suits them.

Their framework, CALM, tests several quantization algorithms on each layer separately. It scores them with centered kernel alignment, a similarity measure between representations, and picks the best strategy per layer. The winners combine into one hybrid model, with no fine-tuning needed. Across mainstream models including LLaMA and Qwen, CALM beat both uniform quantization and leading mixed-precision methods on perplexity and downstream tasks. The plug-and-play design makes it easy to adopt in existing pipelines.
arxiv-2512-16582:
Lintao Xiao and a large team build a giant atom from sound in an arXiv paper from 2025. A giant atom touches its environment at two separated points, so waves traveling between them create memory effects. The team coupled a superconducting transmon qubit to a lithium niobate phononic waveguide, a sound channel etched in a crystal.

The two contact points sit about 600 acoustic wavelengths apart, giving a propagation delay of 125 nanoseconds. The atom's relaxation became non-Markovian, with phonon backflow, and its decay rate swung fourfold across just 4 megahertz, a Purcell factor above 40. That frequency-dependent dissipation let the team prepare quantum superposition states with high purity. Phononic circuits, the authors argue, are a versatile new home for giant-atom physics and tunable quantum devices.
arxiv-2512-16682:
Nick von Selzam and Florian Marquardt ask whether hidden-variable models of quantum effects can be made to move in time. Bell nonlocality covers still snapshots of linked outcomes, but says nothing about how those links evolve as a system changes.

The authors define dynamic local hidden-variable models, where the hidden state itself evolves and yields the outcomes seen at each moment. They weigh what extra rules such models need, then give a simple counter-case. A firm no-go result backs their guess that such dynamics does not always exist. The upshot is a new kind of nonlocality read off from how measured stats change in time, common in interacting quantum systems.
arxiv-2512-16982:
Oscar J. C. Dias, David Sola Gil, and Jorge E. Santos study the stability of rotating BTZ black holes under scalar field perturbations with double-trace boundary conditions. BTZ holes are stable under standard wall rules, but double-trace rules let energy leak through the boundary.

Three findings stand out. Instability hits not only wavy non-axisymmetric modes, the one known sector, but also plain axisymmetric ones. The axisymmetric mode is the master one: any setup unstable to a wavy mode is already unstable to it. And zones exist where BTZ holes go unstable while global AdS3 stays stable, with full onset curves mapped. The energy influx through the boundary, not horizon effects, drives the growth.
arxiv-2512-17082:
Jonathan Junné, Raphael Winter, and Havva Yoldaş study the Landau equation when a gas holds several kinds of particles with different masses. Physicists use that equation to track how collisions spread particle speeds over time. The strength of each collision is set by a value called gamma, which runs from minus 3 to 1.

The team shows that when gamma stays at or above minus the square root of 8, a multi-species version of Fisher information always falls over time. Below that line they give a case where the same tool fails. They then build a new version, based on a spherical form, and use it to prove that good solutions exist for all time.
arxiv-2512-17182:
Kelong Cheng, Jingwei Sun, and Hong Zhang build a faster way to simulate fluids that cannot be squeezed, such as water in two dimensions. The governing rule is the Navier-Stokes equation, and good simulations need fine time steps to catch swirls and unsteady motion. Their scheme reaches third-order accuracy in time while solving just one Poisson-like equation per step.

Space is handled with a Fourier method and time with a BDF3 stencil, while the bending flow term is handled openly to keep each step cheap. The team then proves the spin of the flow, called vorticity, stays bounded for all time when steps are small. Those bounds yield the best possible error rates, and tests show the scheme allows larger steps than rivals.
arxiv-2512-17482:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures how precisely its detector gauges the energy of small radius jets, using top quark events in which one top decays through a charged lepton. The data come from proton collisions recorded in 2015 to 2018 at 13 TeV and in 2022 to 2023 at 13.6 TeV.

Instead of unfolding the data, the team forward folds the known W boson mass peak and reads the jet energy scale and resolution off the match. For jets of 20 to 200 GeV near the center of the detector, the scale is pinned down to about 0.93 to 1.7 percent for jets above 35 GeV, while the resolution carries an uncertainty of 14 to 28 percent. Such calibrations feed into nearly every ATLAS measurement that involves jets.
arxiv-2512-17582:
James Hancock, Matthew Craven, and Craig McNeile squeeze a wind farm puzzle onto a tiny quantum computer. Placing turbines on a grid so each steals as little wind from its neighbors as possible is a hard combinatorial problem. A naive quantum encoding spends one qubit per grid square, which caps the farm size at a handful of squares.

Two thriftier encodings pack more than one square's worth of choice into each qubit. The team tests both on three farm layouts, including one modeled on a real Welsh wind farm. A 9 by 9 grid, 81 candidate spots, now fits in just 20 qubits on a simulator. Both encodings held up well and scaled kindly, a step toward quantum help for real energy planning.
arxiv-2512-17782:
Arya Chavoshi and three co-authors fill in city heat maps where clouds blind the satellite. Surface temperature maps track the urban heat island effect, yet the hottest days often come with broken cloud decks that punch holes in the data. Older fillers borrow other days or other sensors, which stubborn cloud cover also ruins.

UrbanDIFF works from one image alone. A diffusion model imagines the missing patches, guided by maps of built-up land and elevation, and locked to agree with every clear pixel. Trained on NASA MODIS data from seven large United States metros, years 2002 to 2025, it held up even at 85 percent cloud cover, scoring 0.89 on image similarity. Heat planners gain maps that survive the weather.
arxiv-2512-17882:
Dominik Szczepaniak, Monika Harvey, and Fani Deligianni built a virtual reality game that trains attention and memory while watching the player. Eye tracking plus heart and skin signals feed a learning model that judges mental load moment by moment. The game then raises or lowers its difficulty to match the player.

The model was trained on data from 74 people and tested live with 54 more. Players often felt the tasks were too hard even while scoring their best. In the harder two task mode, the model pushed players to higher levels with no loss in scores or rise in frustration. Self judgment, it seems, can hold training back.
arxiv-2512-17982: M. E. Egwe studies a cohomological equation set on the discrete Heisenberg group, a step by step version of a classic group from quantum physics. The paper looks at discrete dynamical systems on that group, where a state moves by fixed steps. Egwe gives a condition under which the equation has a solution. Such equations matter because a solution lets a complicated orbit be rewritten in a simpler form, a standard step in the study of group dynamics.
arxiv-2512-18082:
Shreshth Rajan and Raymond Liu improve street scene labeling for self driving and guide tools. A system must tell road from sidewalk and people in shifting light and weather, in real time. Their method looks up help for scene regions only when the model is unsure, rather than for every region.

That gate raised the mean overlap score by 11.3 percent while cutting lookup costs by 87.5 percent. Help was fetched for just 12.5 percent of regions, against all of them in an always on rival. Picking when to ask for help, the work shows, can raise both accuracy and honesty about doubt.
arxiv-2512-18282:
Roberto Sanchez Peregrino widens the classic harmonic numbers, the sums of one over each whole number up to a limit. His version weights each term by a power of a free value, which bends the old sums into a family. Work in that wider family can both recover old results and expose new ones.

He extends a known identity of Gould so the classic sums can be swapped for their weighted kin. Fresh links tie the new numbers to Fibonacci numbers, Laguerre polynomials, and other named sequences. The paper leans on plain, step by step methods rather than heavy machinery, a show of how far basic tools can reach in the study of number patterns.
arxiv-2512-18482:
Petr Jizba and Tereza Lehečková work in Weyl conformal gravity, an alternative theory of gravity built to stay unchanged under local rescaling. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted by Physical Review D, studies spacetimes with a 2+2 direct product structure. The sources are separated electromagnetic and Yang-Mills fields.

They prove every such configuration admits at least two independent, commuting non-null Killing vectors, and they use those symmetries to find general solutions. As a special case they generalize the Birkhoff-Riegert theorem to all spacetimes containing a two-dimensional subspace of constant Gaussian curvature. The authors then sort the solutions into Weyl equivalence classes and tie them to known solutions in both Weyl and Einstein gravity. The work maps out what this alternative gravity permits.
arxiv-2512-18582:
Haoxiang Luo and five co-authors sketch an AI partner for the engineers who will run 6G wireless networks. Sixth-generation systems promise complexity beyond manual oversight or rigid automation. Their Wireless Copilot, posted to arXiv in December 2025, pairs a large language model with a cognitive framework so operators can state intent in plain terms.

The Copilot translates high-level goals into precise, optimized, and verifiable network actions, sitting as a new layer between people and infrastructure. The authors walk through its use in low-altitude wireless networks that support 6G, covering design, configuration, evaluation, and optimization. A case study on intent-based resource allocation shows stronger adaptability than rival approaches. They close with a roadmap toward a broader human-AI ecosystem for running future networks.
arxiv-2512-18682:
Yuchen Li and four coauthors tackle a slow step in engineering design in this 2025 paper. When simulations are costly, turning loose design wishes into a precise optimization problem is done by hand and eats expert time. Language models could automate the step, but earlier attempts either drifted from the design intent or needed solver feedback to filter training data, feedback that costly simulations cannot supply. Their framework, APF, works without any solver in the loop.

APF builds its own fine-tuning data through a generation and annotation pipeline, then trains models to output accurate, runnable optimization models. On antenna design tasks it beats existing methods both in how faithfully requirements are formalized and in the quality of the radiation efficiency curves produced.
arxiv-2512-18782:
Garry Goldstein takes on the Hedin equations, an exact framework for the many-body problem that is almost impossible to solve as written. Their functional-derivative form defeats direct numerics. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, replaces them with a ladder of integral equations, Hedin approximations I, II, III, and beyond, whose solutions converge to the true ones.

The first rung is exactly the famous GW approximation, so the ladder reads as a systematic improvement of GW. Goldstein tests the scheme in zero-dimensional field theory, where the equations also count Feynman diagrams. Higher rungs capture more diagrams for the self-energy; rung II already beats the best vertex-correction methods, and rung III nearly matches the exact answer. The approach offers computational physics a principled way to buy accuracy step by step.
arxiv-2512-18882:
Tylor Adkins and a large collaboration check whether the Crab Nebula's polarization angle wobbles, and use it to hunt axion-like particles. The Crab, or Tau A, calibrates polarization measurements across millimeter astronomy, so its steadiness matters. The team analyzed 90 GHz data from the Simons Array's 2023 season. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, follows up earlier POLARBEAR hints of oscillation.

No global oscillation signal appears. They cap the amplitude at 0.12 degrees with 95 percent confidence across the frequencies searched. Read as an axion search, that bound limits the axion-photon coupling below 3.84 times ten to the minus twelve, scaled by mass, for particle masses between 4.4 times ten to the minus twenty-two and 7.2 times ten to the minus twenty electron-volts. The earlier hints are neither confirmed nor fully excluded, leaving the case open.
arxiv-2512-18982:
Tuo Wu leads ten co-authors in sketching a wireless architecture for 6G smart cities: fluid antennas fused with intelligent surfaces. Antennas that move gain fresh spatial diversity. Surfaces that steer reflections reshape the signal environment itself, though alone they suffer double path loss and little processing power. Their vision article, posted to arXiv in December 2025, unites the two into one system.

Five pillars structure the design. Base stations gain large-scale beamforming, and user devices gain the finest spatial diversity. Three new surface types join them, including enormous facade surfaces that restore line-of-sight links using surface waves. A two-timescale controller coordinates slow network beamforming with fast device adaptation. Simulations close the piece, supporting robustness across uses from wireless power transfer to integrated sensing. City-scale connectivity planners get a concrete blueprint, challenges included.
arxiv-2512-19282:
Alexander Pigazzini and Magdalena Toda prove a local barrier to flattening Berry curvature in spin-orbit coupled atomic condensates. Berry curvature acts like a magnetic field in momentum space. Even when the total Chern number vanishes, they show, the curvature cannot simply be ironed flat point by point.

Their arena mixes the momentum torus with two phase circles, carrying a Kaluza-Klein metric and a connection whose torsion encodes synthetic gauge fields. A harmonic part of the torsion defines a mixed cohomology class. Careful pointwise curvature work then yields a three-level structure: the physical metric resists reduction at every stage of a path toward a flat product metric.
arxiv-2512-19482:
Lapo Dispoto, Fedor Ignatov, Atsushi Oya, and Yusuke Uchiyama bring a transformer to the MEG II experiment, which hunts a forbidden muon decay. Its drift chamber drowns in pileup hits, with a third to a half of all hits being junk, and clean positron tracks must be dug out of that noise.

The model works as a classifier that discards pileup hits before tracking. Trained on chamber data, it raised hit purity sharply. Tracking efficiency rose by about fifteen percent and resolution by about five percent at top muon rates. The team estimates the gain as roughly ten percent more sensitivity to the rare decay's branching ratio.
arxiv-2512-19582:
Tommaso Rainaldi, Victor Ale, Matt Grau, and Dmitri Kharzeev add trigonometric gates to the continuous-variable quantum toolbox. Hybrid machines that mix qubits with qumodes, quantum oscillators, suit bosonic field theories well. Existing gates, though, are built from polynomial functions. That is an awkward fit for periodic, non-perturbative interactions.

Their ancilla-based method implements trigonometric gates whose arguments are arbitrary Hermitian functions of the oscillator quadratures, in unitary and non-unitary forms. The lattice sine-Gordon model is the showcase. They prepare ground states, simulate real-time dynamics, compute vertex correlation functions, and extract kink profiles. Fourier-style gates, they argue, widen what hybrid simulators can reach.
arxiv-2512-20082:
Chaithra, Kamesh Kadimisetty, and Biju Mohan build a stock-sentiment system that listens to the market's reply. Sentiment tools tend to score news text in a vacuum. They skip whether prices agreed the next day. Their frame targets India's NIFTY 50 index. It fine-tunes a three-billion-parameter LLaMA model on the SentiFin data set. Feedback loops are layered on top of that base.

A retrieval pipeline pulls in context from many sources. It picks by embedding similarity. A feedback module checks each call against the next day's returns. It then recalibrates how far each source is trusted. A reinforcement agent learns source-weight policies over time. On NIFTY 50 headlines from 2024 and 2025, the system beat baselines. It won on accuracy, F1 score, and fit with the market.
arxiv-2512-20282:
Anand Rai and co-authors compute the thermodynamic and transport properties of hot, dense quantum chromodynamic matter. Such matter is expected in low-energy heavy-ion collisions, where baryon density is high. They compare three effective approaches: the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, a chiral effective model, and a hadron resonance gas model.

Flow measures come from the Boltzmann equation in the relaxation-time approximation. The authors track how each quantity varies with baryon chemical potential or net density. The Lorenz ratio rises steeply at low density, signalling a strong break with the Wiedemann-Franz law, then nears its standard value. The shear-viscosity-to-entropy ratio stays nearly flat before climbing slowly. Parallels with graphene's electron-hole plasma are also discussed.
arxiv-2512-20482:
Revanth Gangi Reddy and a large team built SweRank+, a system that finds the code a bug report is actually about. In big multilingual codebases, mapping a natural-language issue to the functions needing change is the slow first step of every fix. Older rankers were largely Python-only and searched in a single pass.

SweRank+ couples two parts. SweRankMulti embeds code cross-lingually and reranks candidates with a language model, trained on a curated multilingual dataset. SweRankAgent then searches iteratively over multiple turns, keeping a memory buffer of candidates instead of committing to one shot. Benchmarks across several languages show the multi-pass agent improving on single-pass ranking. Both components set new state-of-the-art results for issue localization.
arxiv-2512-21682:
K. Nihongi, H. Tanaka, M. Hagiwara, and a team study the quantum antiferromagnet cesium iron chloride under extreme magnetic fields and pressure. The material's iron ions sit on a triangular lattice, a geometry famous for frustrating magnetic order. At zero field its ground state is a nonmagnetic singlet.

Pulsed-field magnetization measurements show the magnetization rising linearly between about four and eleven tesla, pausing at a plateau, then jumping sharply near thirty-two tesla. Electron spin resonance data trace the low-field behavior to one angular momentum manifold and the jump to a level crossing with the next. Under pressure, the singlet phase shrinks while the high-field transition breaks into a pattern of fractional steps. The authors explain the steps with a spin one-half framework whose states are not time-reversal partners. That construction produces three-body interactions on triangular plaquettes, a coupling textbooks omit.
arxiv-2512-22482:
Longfei Fang, Yongtao Li, Huiqiu Lin, and Jie Ma prove a spectral version of supersaturation for color-critical graphs. A graph is color-critical when deleting one special edge lowers its chromatic number; cliques and odd cycles qualify. Supersaturation asks more than whether a forbidden pattern must appear. It asks how many copies appear once a graph is pushed past a threshold. Here the threshold is measured by the spectral radius, the adjacency matrix's largest eigenvalue.

Their first theorem concerns near-Turán graphs with a few added edges. Beyond their spectral radius, many copies of any color-critical graph are forced. The extremal graphs have exactly that near-Turán form. A second theorem handles the stronger max-threshold condition. Together the results completely resolve a problem posed by Ning and Zhai.
arxiv-2512-23182:
Xuefeng Liu and Michael Plum close a long-standing gap in verified eigenvalue computation. Engineers and mathematicians computing vibration frequencies with the finite element method get sharp upper bounds from standard high-order elements, but guaranteed lower bounds of matching quality have been elusive. Existing rigorous routes, based on special low-order elements, do not extend to high-order methods, and the nonstandard alternatives are awkward.

Their two-stage algorithm works with ordinary high-order finite elements on graded meshes, which concentrate mesh points where the solution varies fastest. The output is a rigorous lower bound as sharp as the corresponding upper bound, shown on the Laplacian and Steklov eigenvalue problems over square and dumbbell-shaped domains. Tests stress the accuracy and efficiency of the method on strongly nonuniform meshes. The authors present it as a competitive answer to a problem that has resisted the toolkit for years.
arxiv-2512-23382:
Xiamiao Zhao, Yiyan Zhan, and Mei Lu work in extremal graph theory, which asks how large a structure can get before a forbidden pattern must appear. Their subject is the Turán number of Berge paths in hypergraphs, a generalization where each edge of an ordinary path is matched to a larger hyperedge containing it. The arXiv title, on extremal results for Berge disjoint paths, governs over the catalog entry.

Earlier researchers had settled the Turán number for single Berge paths and partly for sets of disjoint odd-length ones. Zhao and her co-authors give the exact value for the general case. Any number of disjoint Berge paths, for hypergraphs of uniformity at least three and paths long enough relative to that uniformity. The result completes a line of work going back to the classic Erdős-Gallai theorem on paths.
arxiv-2512-23582:
Guillaume Neuttiens and Jonas Sauer prove well-posedness for the time-periodic Cahn-Hilliard-Gurtin system, a model of phase separation that extends the classic Cahn-Hilliard equation with extra mechanical effects. Their setting is the half space, and the solutions they seek repeat periodically in time. Systems of mixed order, where equations of different types couple, need boundary conditions of a matching mixed character.

To supply them, the authors introduce a new class of complementing boundary conditions that generalizes the classical Lopatinskii-Shapiro conditions from elliptic and parabolic theory. They show the classical conditions are generally insufficient for mixed-order systems, while their extension restores well-posedness and maximal regularity for the periodic problem. The result gives this phase-field model a firm base on a half-space. It tells users when the model has one clear answer and when it does not.
arxiv-2512-23682:
Dmitri Orlov and six co-authors model the interior of ITER, the international fusion experiment, under its baseline operating scenario with neon impurities injected to protect the divertor. Predicting performance as one piece means coupling core transport to the exhaust region, something earlier studies often treated separately. Their workflow constrains core calculations directly with existing divertor simulations that include neon seeding.

Stationary temperature and density profiles were computed across a scan of effective ion charge, and the power crossing into the scrape-off layer was tracked. That power varied by more than a factor of one point seven across the scan, matching the divertor prediction only inside a narrow window of impurity level and heating power. Rotation changes shifted results modestly, and charge-exchange radiation proved tiny. The study gives ITER operators clear guidance on impurity control and heating plans. The goal is plans both halves can live with.
arxiv-2512-23982:
Hung-Fu Chang, Mohammad Shirazi, Lizhou Cao, and Supannika Mobasser study how professional programmers actually use AI coding tools, and what schools should do about it. Most earlier research examined individual users or classrooms, leaving industrial practice underexplored. The team instead analyzed fifty-seven curated YouTube videos from late 2024 and 2025 in which practitioners reflected on working with large language model tools, including vibe coding and agentic coding workflows.

Practitioners reported real productivity gains and lower barriers to entry, alongside a shift of the bottleneck toward code review. Their concerns ran long: code quality, maintainability, security flaws, ethics, erosion of foundational problem-solving skill, and entry-level engineers arriving underprepared. The authors argue computer science curricula should pivot toward problem-solving, architectural thinking, and code review, with early project-based courses that integrate the tools rather than banning them.
arxiv-2512-24382:
Dongwook Choa, Jiawei Hu, Siu-Cheong Lau, and Yan-Lung Leon Li build an equivariant version of Lagrangian Floer theory. The setting is Liouville sectors with a Lie group symmetry. Partially wrapped Fukaya categories organize the theory. Symmetry should let physicists and geometers pass to quotients without losing information.

A correspondence theory does that passing. Equivariant Floer cohomology upstairs relates to ordinary Floer cohomology of the quotient. Symplectic quotients with nodal singularities get special study. There the correspondence becomes an isomorphism on cohomologies. That outcome was conjectured by Lekili and Segal. The paper proves it in this setting. The work serves symplectic geometry and mirror symmetry. Symmetry reduction is a basic move in both fields, and this gives it a Floer-theoretic foundation.
arxiv-2512-24682:
Ke Xie, Xingyi Zhao, Min-Yue Chen, Yu-An Chen, and co-authors introduce CellSecInspector, a tool that searches cellular network rules for security flaws automatically. Modern 3GPP specifications are huge, linked, and fast changing, so manual review misses deep links between clauses. Their system turns procedures into structured state, condition, and action records.

Those records are chained into full network functions and checked against nine basic security properties under four attacker scenarios. The tool also generates test cases from what it finds. Readers in mobile security get an end-to-end method for finding specification weaknesses that rule lists and small hand-made checks often miss.
arxiv-2512-24782:
Ranfang Zheng, Zheyu Lin, and Xu Kong build a classifier for tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole, tailored to the Wide Field Survey Telescope. Their goal is finding candidates from light curves alone, with little reliance on outside catalogs, which suits faint and distant galaxies. Two modules can work separately or together.

One module fits light curve parameters, and the other is a Transformer network that classifies the curve. Training used several thousand simulated or collected light curves. Astronomy readers get a tool for both live alert streams and archives, built to flag rare stellar disruptions early.
arxiv-2512-24882:
Yuki Fujimoto shows that open string spectra describe the masses of mesons and baryons well. The exponential spectrum from string theory is fixed by a single Hagedorn temperature, with no other free parameters. Fitting physical hadron spectra gives consistent temperature values for both mesons and baryons, near a third of a gigaelectronvolt.

Earlier phenomenological fits had suggested different values for the two families, so the agreement is notable. The fitted temperature also matches typical string tension from lattice calculations. Hadron physics readers get a parameter-light string picture of the mass spectrum. Unity between meson and baryon spectra supports the open string and diquark viewpoint.
arxiv-2512-24982:
Isaac Kim and Tuomas Laakkonen show any Clifford plus T circuit can be controlled with constant T-depth overhead, defying a natural counting expectation. A circuit of CNOT gates can contain very many gates, suggesting a controlled version would need comparably many Toffoli gates. Instead, the Toffoli count drops to at most the number of qubits, and depth can be made constant at a modest extra cost.

Measurement-based uncomputation reduces Toffoli depth further to one. Corollaries give constant T-depth controlled Clifford circuits and more. Quantum computing readers get major savings for controlled operations, which are ubiquitous in algorithms and error correction.
arxiv-2601-00282:
Qianli Wang leads six coauthors in asking whether shrinking a language model also dulls its self explanations. Quantization cuts model size and speeds up serving. Models also explain their own outputs in words. Those explanations support trust in high stakes use. No one had checked what compression does to them. The study tests two explanation types across three methods.

Natural language reasons and counterfactual examples both count. Several bit widths are tried for each method. Quality and faithfulness slip by moderate amounts overall. User judges see bigger drops in coherence and trust. Larger models hold faithfulness better under compression. Their plain explanation quality is not spared, though. No single method wins across all measures. The authors urge case by case validation. Compression stays useful, they conclude, when its explanation cost is measured first.
arxiv-2601-00482:
Abhiram Bellur and eleven colleagues demonstrate how several AI agents can work alongside a developer on a fiddly coding task: coordinated renaming. Renaming one identifier in software often forces matching renames in many related places across files. Doing that by hand is tedious and error prone, while simple heuristic tools suggest far too many wrong changes.

The team's approach assigns agents to propagate a rename through related identifiers, combining language model judgment with real refactoring tools. Unlike a plain language model, which misses cases because it cannot see or edit the whole project, their agents interact with the code directly. The work is presented as a model for agents extending a developer's reach on routine but demanding maintenance, rather than replacing human involvement.
arxiv-2601-01082:
Quality diversity search looks for a set of solutions that are both good and varied across traits a user cares about. Bryon Tjanaka, Henry Chen, Matthew Fontaine, and Stefanos Nikolaidis note a flaw in leading methods when the trait space has many dimensions. Solutions with near traits fall into the same grid cell and get the same score, so the search stalls.

Their method, Discount Model Search, replaces the grid with a smooth learned model of those scores, so near solutions can still be told apart. The team adds two new test domains where traits are whole images, and users show what they want with a set of example images instead of hand-built measures. Across these domains and standard benchmarks, the new method beats the leading grid method and other rivals. It opens quality diversity search to rich, high-dimensional goals.
arxiv-2601-01182: Andrii Shidlich surveys results on how well a family of smooth functions of several variables can be approximated. The family is a generalized Wiener class, a set of functions defined by limits on how fast their components fade. The paper gathers new and known estimates for key measures of approximation quality, covering both linear methods, which use fixed building blocks, and nonlinear ones, which adapt to each function.
arxiv-2601-01382:
Six authors led by Man-Yu Duan propose a cleaner hunting ground for an exotic particle made of four quarks. Two states seen in recent experiments, with a doubly charged member, hint at a genuinely exotic family that no two- or three-quark picture explains. The authors suggest looking in a specific decay of the B meson into a kaon plus a D meson pair, using data reported by Belle II.

Working in a molecular picture, where the exotic state is a loose pairing of two known mesons, they estimate how strongly it would show up in the mass distribution of that decay. Depending on the fitting scheme, the share comes out near ten percent or near seven percent, with sizable error bars. The signal should stand out clearly in this channel. Sharper measurements at Belle II and LHCb could settle what this four-quark state really is.
arxiv-2601-01582:
Gerhard Hiss and Caroline Lassueur close a step in sorting building blocks of finite group representations. For a prime p, each block with a cyclic defect group carries an extra invariant, described by Linckelmann, that largely fixes its source algebra class together with a tree diagram. Sorting those invariants is the series goal.

Earlier parts dealt with general cyclic blocks and then, for odd primes, narrowed the problem to certain classical groups and their simpler quotients. In Part III, the pair finish that narrowed task for special linear and unitary cases. The result feeds a wider program that sorts blocks up to a strong form of sameness.
arxiv-2601-02082:
Testing self-driving cars against pedestrians on real roads is dangerous. Engineers use simulators instead. But fake walkers that chase difficulty over realism can teach cars to be needlessly timid. Yueyang Wang and three co-authors generate stress-test scenarios. Their source is a pedestrian model modeled on human thinking. It has realistic spread between people. It also varies within one person over time.

The human-like walkers were swapped into the CARLA simulator. Gap-acceptance patterns became more believable. Vehicle braking became smoother. The built-in rule-based walkers did worse on both counts. Risky interactions arose only for certain simulated individuals under certain conditions, underlining how much human variability matters. The scenarios then serve to tune vehicle controllers toward behavior that is both safer and more efficient.
arxiv-2601-02182:
The Tayler-Spruit dynamo builds magnetic fields in stably stratified stellar interiors. It was long assumed to settle into steady patterns. Paul Barrère and three co-authors simulate it in a spherical shell. The outer sphere rotates faster. Far richer behavior appears.

Alongside the known stationary and hemispherical dynamos, the simulations show new behavior. Magnetic reversals and complex time dependence appear for the first time. They link tightly to breaking of the flow's symmetry at the equator. In a typical run, two large-scale magnetic modes of opposite symmetry couple. The coupling runs through that symmetry breaking. Richer regimes likely involve more modes. A restless dynamo could reshape expectations for neutron star magnetic fields and their emissions.
arxiv-2601-02482:
Stephen DiKerby and co authors report the first resolved spectrum of an iron emission line doublet from G0.11-0.11. A molecular cloud near the center of the Milky Way, taken with the XRISM Resolve instrument. Such clouds glow in the iron K alpha line either because an X ray source lit them up in the past, through fluorescence, or because cosmic rays ionize them. Telling the two apart has been hard without very sharp spectra.

The line complex splits cleanly into its two components at the expected energies, and each line is barely broader than the quantum mechanical prediction, leaving little room for other broadening. The cloud's radial velocity is measured as precisely as radio observations achieve. The sharp spectrum also tests for secondary features, opening a new way to decide between the reflection and cosmic ray accounts.
arxiv-2601-02982:
Nicolás Bernal and three co-authors test theories of cosmic inflation in universes with an extra spatial dimension. They study two models of inflation. One is simple monomial inflation. The other is the simplest alpha-attractor model. Both are placed inside three setups with extra dimensions: the Dark Dimension, with one flat extra dimension, and two Randall-Sundrum setups with a warped extra dimension and one or two branes.

For each case they derive the expansion equations and compute the slow-roll parameters. They then fit the models to data from the Planck, BICEP, and ACT observations. Monomial inflation is strongly disfavored in every scenario. Alpha-attractor inflation, by contrast, fits current observations very well. The extra-dimensional versions also offer more flexibility than the standard four-dimensional case.
arxiv-2601-03482:
Stefan Konigorski and three co-authors ask whether large foundation models can truly personalize health advice for one person rather than an average patient. Such models are changing prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, yet a model that shines in one study can fall to chance in another. The authors call this the generalizability paradox and link it to other tensions, such as privacy versus performance.

They point to N-of-1 trials, crossover self-experiments long treated as the gold standard for personal causal evidence. Those trials test treatments within one person, so they can settle what works for that person while keeping data local. The paper weighs how much causal understanding personal recommendations really need. Its message: prediction alone may not earn trust in medicine.
arxiv-2601-03682:
Shaojie Wang and Liang Zhang argue that language models fail at math less from weak calculation than from weak logic. Their analysis finds errors about logical relationships, which variables connect and which operation applies, behind over ninety percent of wrong predictions. Standard step-by-step fine-tuning barely reduced those errors, because the logic stays implicit in long worked solutions.

Their framework, First-Step Logical Reasoning, trains models on the first planning step alone: choosing the variables and the operation from the problem statement. Isolating that step gives explicit supervision for logical understanding while staying light and token-efficient. The idea reframes math training: before teaching a model to write full solutions, teach it to read a problem's structure correctly, since every later step inherits that first decision.
arxiv-2601-06782:
Sungtaek Son, Eardi Lila, and Kwun Chuen Gary Chan wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on care plans built for each patient. Such plans are called individualized treatment regimes, or ITRs. A plan gives a treatment based on facts about that patient. The paper works with data from studies that watch patients, not trials that assign care.

Past methods can fail when each patient record holds a great many facts. Too many facts can hurt how well a plan works and how clear it is. The authors cut the list of facts down to a small set. That small set still holds the gap in results between one treatment and the next. In this way the plan can stay sharp while it stays simple to read and use.
arxiv-2601-07082:
Valentin Nkana Ngan and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with efficient hyper-reduced-order model for segregated solvers for geometrical parametrization problems. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors propose an efficient hyper-reduced order model (HROM) designed for segregated finite-volume solvers in geometrically parametrized problems. The method follows a discretize-then-project strategy: the full-order operators are first assembled using.

Finite volume or finite element discretizations and then projected onto low-dimensional spaces using. A small set of spatial sampling points. Selected through hyper-reduction techniques such as DEIM. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07182:
Ruiyi Ding and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers PRPO. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Policy optimization for large language models often suffers from sparse reward signals in multi-step reasoning tasks. Critic-free methods like GRPO assign a single normalized outcome reward to all tokens, providing limited guidance for intermediate reasoning .

While Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer dense feedback, they risk premature collapse when used alone. As early low-reward tokens can drive policies toward truncated outputs. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07382:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by J-B. Roux and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers superspace worldline formalism approach to quantum gravity. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Using the ADM formalism, we show that the Hamiltonian formulation of Quantum Gravity is exactly.

In the form of a worldline (WL) formalism in the superspace. We then show that the Keldysh partition function reduces to the partition function of Euclidean 3D gravity. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07582:
Huhai Zou and colleagues present ES-Mem, a memory design for dialogue agents that must remember over long conversations. Memory lets an agent stay coherent across many sessions and adapt over time. Without it, long-term interaction breaks into disconnected chats. Their 2026 preprint builds memory around event segmentation.

Event segmentation splits a stream of experience into meaningful episodes. ES-Mem uses that idea to organize what a dialogue agent stores and recalls. Well-placed boundaries can make retrieval cleaner than storing one long transcript. The design targets long-term dialogue, where relevant facts may sit far in the past. Readers building assistants and companion agents get a memory approach modeled on how events naturally divide.
arxiv-2601-07682:
Emiliya Poghosyan and coauthors align an electron beam with sub-pixel accuracy to study advanced detectors. Hybrid pixel detectors are radiation hard, fast, and have high dynamic range. They now serve diffraction work and even imaging work with electrons. Their pixels, though, are about ten times larger than those of direct detectors made for imaging. Spread from hits inside them is also stronger in them.

Machine learning study of them needs a beam spot known with great care. Sub-pixel alignment squeezes position knowledge finer than the pixel grid. That precision helps separate detector effects from real sample signals. The work supports using these robust detectors in electron microscopy.
