A laser fuses powder into a hard protective skin. Surface quality of titanium parts decides safety in service, yet no clear guidance existed on the best laser power for this coating. The team varied power across a narrow band and examined the coatings' structure, phases, chemistry, and hardness.

Power proved decisive. At the two lower settings, long cracks ran through the coating and bonding to the base metal was poor, risking peeling. At the middle setting the coating bonded cleanly with no obvious defects, formed new strengthening phases, and reached the highest hardness measured. One step higher, cracks returned and performance fell. The authors offer the middle setting, and the reasoning behind it, as a reference point for coating titanium parts in aerospace manufacturing.
plos-pone-0356382:
Timothy Mulvany and seven colleagues test how the way a tumor is outlined on a scan affects computerized measurements used to diagnose children's brain tumors, in this 2026 study. Radiomics extracts numbers from MRI scans that machine learning can turn into diagnoses, but humans draw tumor boundaries differently. Using scans from just over one hundred young patients, the team shrank and expanded expert-drawn outlines to imitate cautious and generous drawing, then watched what happened to the measurements.

Expanding outlines disturbed nearly all measurements, and far more than shrinking them did. Diagnosis models trained on expert outlines lost accuracy under either change, but less when training included the altered outlines and only the steadiest measurements. The authors advise that when boundaries are ambiguous, leaving doubtful tissue out beats including it, and that model builders should plan for drawing variation from the start.
plos-pone-0356482:
Lisha Zou and three colleagues build a decision aid for the earliest stage of drug discovery in this 2026 paper. Virtual screening ranks thousands of molecules against a disease target, but labs can only afford to test a shortlist, and raw ranking scores say little about how much to trust them. Their package, TASC-VS, adds test-time adaptation, statistical calibration, and uncertainty-aware ranking to turn ranked lists into fixed-budget choices.

On a curated fifteen-target benchmark, the full package beat a strong comparator on enrichment and on the quality of its top twenty picks, though some gains lost significance after strict statistical correction. A separate stress test on another benchmark favored the simpler rival. The authors are frank about the limits: the method offers calibrated shortlist support on the tested subset, and broader use needs fresh validation.
plos-pone-0356782:
Maria Hjorth and Anna Forsberg report a qualitative study, published in 2026, on setting up nurse-led follow-up care for people with liver cirrhosis. Six clinics tried the new arrangement, and the researchers interviewed nurses, doctors, and managers repeatedly over several years of rollout. Their analysis looked for what helped the change take hold and what got in its way.

They found just over twenty influencing factors, split almost evenly between barriers and supports. Staff shortages, unclear roles, and weak leadership support hindered the work. Some staff also felt a moral strain when patients who needed the extra care could not all receive it under the trial's random assignment. On the positive side, the follow-up was seen as safe and worthwhile, and managers who backed the nurses strengthened their standing in the team. Simple tasks nurses could own outright worked best.
plos-pone-0356882: Iqra and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in pure mathematics. They prove new Newton-type inequalities, bounds named for a classic rule for estimating integrals. The work covers a class of curved functions shaped by a hyperbolic form, using fractional integrals of the Riemann-Liouville type. Number checks back up the proofs. Such bounds help scientists estimate quantities that cannot be computed exactly.
plos-pone-0357382:
Xuan Wang and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE on shrinking three-dimensional animation files so they stream and render smoothly on modest devices. Animation data is bulky and repeats heavily between frames, but older compressors cut it into blocks with sloppy boundaries and leave redundancy behind. Their scheme tidies scattered vertex data with an improved clustering method, carves the animation into blocks adapting to how the scene moves, and polishes the result with boundary editing and matrix reorganization.

Across four datasets, the optimized algorithm compressed files to roughly a seventh of original size, beating a leading comparison method widely while cutting reconstruction error substantially and keeping structural similarity high. On mobile devices, loading times fell by over two thirds and rendering frame rates rose by nearly half. The method is presented as practical support for virtual reality, games, and digital twins on limited hardware.
plos-pone-0357482:
Sangrak Son and colleagues trial a smart watering system that feeds liquid organic fertilizer to greenhouse lettuce only when plants seem to need it. Organic fertilizer costs a lot, so feeding on a fixed calendar wastes money. Cameras measured leaf canopy size every few days and shared data online. In the smart beds, a sensor switch ran the pump only when canopy growth lagged behind hand-fed beds by a set margin.

Lettuce weight and leaf area ended up nearly equal in both setups. The fixed schedule, however, used about four times as many feeding events and left far more unused nutrients in the growing mix. Son and colleagues say growth-guided feeding can cut fertilizer bills sharply while keeping yields, a useful result for small greenhouse growers.
plos-pone-0357782:
Elena García-López and Fabrice B. R. Parmentier published a 2026 experiment in PLOS ONE on how an unexpected sound distracts people in the middle of a task. In their setup, volunteers identified where a visual target appeared while tones played in the background, most of them standard and a few rare and deviant. The key question was whether a deviant sound affects a person differently when the correct next action repeats the previous one versus when it changes.

Deviant sounds slowed people when the response repeated, in both the two-choice and four-choice versions. That braking effect did not depend on how many choices were available. The same sounds sped up response changes, though, and that benefit shrank when the choice set grew. The split suggests distraction works through two mechanisms: one inhibiting action repetition, one helping switching, with only the second sensitive to context.
plos-pone-0358182: Feng and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that can blind people with diabetes. They hunted for new marker genes tied to two cell stresses: low oxygen and a copper-driven cell death called cuproptosis. They then probed how those markers might drive the disease. Fresh markers could lead to earlier tests for a condition often found late.
plos-pone-0358482: Mutuyimana and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how suffering is voiced in Eastern Africa. They built a new survey, a Cultural Scripts of Trauma Inventory, tuned to local ways of expressing pain after trauma. Imported surveys can miss local idioms of distress. A tool built from local scripts can help counselors hear what patients truly mean.
plos-pone-0358882:
Matthew Wassall and colleagues worked in 2026 on telling apart the activities of people who use lower limb prostheses, using motion sensors worn in everyday life. Knowing whether a prosthesis user is walking, climbing stairs, sitting, or standing matters for judging how well the device serves them. Laboratory tests capture only a slice of that life, so the team used inertial sensing, the motion tracking built into small wearable devices, under real world conditions.

The study builds classification methods that read those sensor streams and sort them into activities. Reliable real world measurement would let clinicians see how a prosthesis performs across weeks, not minutes. It could also guide better fitting and fairer comparisons between devices.
plos-pone-0359282: Özel and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on easing pain after open-heart surgery. A cut through the breastbone, called a median sternotomy, leaves strong pain as it heals. The trial tested elastic therapeutic taping, sticky bands meant to support tissue and ease pain. Patients were assigned at random to taping or standard care. A cheap, drug-free aid would be welcome after such major surgery.
plos-pone-0359782:
Peter Oloche David published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It proposes the Genomic Equity Accessibility Framework, shortened to GEAF. The framework models what such therapies cost people and how fairly they are shared: genomic and regenerative treatments, built on genes and lab-grown tissues, that often carry very high prices.

The author stresses that the framework's measures are built to fit together in a disciplined way. Such a model gives policymakers a structured way to ask who can actually get these therapies and who is priced out. Health economists and access advocates are the readers for a tool built on fairness.
pmc-11223882:
Madeira, Madhusoodanan, Lee, and co-authors describe the 2024 state of the Job Dispatcher tools at EMBL-EBI. Their framework gives scientists free access to popular programs for analysing DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. Users reach the tools through a shared web service rather than installing each program alone.

Along with the tools, the service supplies the sequence datasets those programs need. That pairing lets a researcher run a standard analysis even without local computing power. Keeping such shared services current matters more each year, as sequence data grows faster than most single labs can handle.
pmc-13121982:
Ahammed Mekkodathil leads a 2026 narrative review of electrolyte-based indices in traumatic brain injury. Electrolytes are charged minerals in blood, and their imbalance can worsen swelling and cell harm after a head injury. Simple ratios built from routine lab tests could help doctors judge risk quickly and cheaply.

The review covers the glucose-to-potassium ratio, osmolality, a measure of fluid concentration, an ion shift index, anion gap, and combined disturbance scores. The glucose ratio and osmolality showed the strongest power to predict death and poor recovery. Others look promising but need more testing. Correcting sodium and calcium values for glucose and protein levels prevents misreading. Standard thresholds and larger studies are the next steps.
pmc-13188982:
Ingrid de Souza e Sousa is first author on a 2026 review of new drug targets for chromoblastomycosis, a chronic fungal skin infection classed as a neglected tropical disease. The fungi resist standard antifungal drugs, burrow under the skin, and form protective biofilms, slimy cell layers, making treatment long and often unsuccessful.

The authors' group found the fungi use surface enzymes, protein-cutting secretions, and a signaling protein called calcineurin to grow, change form, and grip host cells. Blocking those systems with known inhibitors, including some HIV drugs and immune drugs, impaired the fungi. Metal compounds built around a chemical scaffold called phenanthroline also killed them potently. New treatment strategies follow from these targets.
pmc-13195182:
Sifan Cao is first author on a 2026 preclinical study of a robot and augmented reality system for jaw tumor surgery. Removing facial tumors and rebuilding the jaw demands exact bone cuts and plate placement. Freehand template methods risk tissue injury and inconsistent alignment, especially when fitting a straight leg bone into the jaw's curve.

The proposed system pairs robot-assisted bone cutting, aligned by optical registration to the preoperative plan, with augmented reality guidance that projects the virtual jaw model into the surgeon's view. A calibration method reduces marker errors. Tests on cadaveric and animal specimens showed favorable cutting and alignment accuracy and low overlay error. The workflow is feasible in preclinical settings, the authors conclude.
pmc-13202082:
Farm work in rural India strains backs, shoulders, and joints, and a 2026 plan headed by Gurjeet Kaur plans a scoping review of that burden. The plan focuses on agriculture-related musculoskeletal disorders among vulnerable rural groups, including tribal groups, marginal farmers, and agricultural laborers.

Following established scoping review guides, the team will search several major databases plus grey literature for English studies issued from 2010 onward. Extracted data will cover farming techniques, disorder patterns, risk factors, programs, and access to healthcare in each study. A narrative and thematic synthesis will then map knowledge gaps and regional gaps to inform occupational health plans.
pmc-13202182:
Care for fluid and air problems around the lung varies between hospitals, and a 2026 quality standard by Mark E Roberts sets minimum expectations for the United Kingdom. The British Thoracic Society document defines markers of high-quality, cost-effective care for adults with pleural disease in primary and secondary care settings.

Roberts and co-authors derived each statement from the society's evidence-based pleural disease guideline, following the national quality standard process as their model. The standards are meant for clinicians and services delivering pleural care, and also for commissioners, planners, and patients judging what care should look like. Together they translate guideline recommendations into concise, auditable statements for everyday practice.
pmc-13202682:
Two mushrooms new to science are described from southwestern Guizhou in a 2026 taxonomy study from Heng-Ting Chen. The research article names Collybiopsis guizhouensis and Collybiopsis anlongensis, two small agaric fungi in the family Omphalotaceae, based on specimens collected in China.

The team combined microscopic morphology with a three-gene phylogenetic analysis using ribosomal and protein-coding markers. Each species landed in its own distinct, well-supported branch of the family tree in both maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses. Clear structural gaps from known relatives backed the molecular split, and the descriptions add to a genus whose small, plain fruiting bodies long hid its true diversity.
pmc-13235882:
Lin and colleagues offer a new way to estimate how much charge an electric vehicle battery holds. That figure, the state of charge, is a core reading in any battery management system. Guessing it wrong shortens range estimates and can harm the battery, so carmakers need methods that stay accurate as conditions change.

The team pairs a temporal convolutional network, a neural model built for time series, with an Unscented Kalman Filter. The network learns patterns in the battery's recent history; the filter then steadies the output and cuts its wobble. Tested on lithium-ion batteries, the combined method aims at accuracy with smooth, trustworthy readings a driver can rely on.
pmc-13240982:
Lebrecht's team at Imperial College London gauged what sets winning human-like virtual influencers apart on Instagram. The dataset covered 157 female virtual profiles, all large accounts. Coders scored realism, identity steadiness, and whether real humans appeared alongside. Reach and like rates were weighed across images and videos.

Bigger accounts led the top content, mainly on video. Among the top clips, openly computer-made personas outnumbered realistic ones. Nearly four in five top accounts kept a stable look and consistent story. The authors conclude tidy, legibly virtual personas engage fans better than realism alone.
pmc-13241382:
Lenga and colleagues at Heidelberg asked whether one quick status question can track recovery after lumbar spine surgery. Two hundred fifty-seven patients answered mobile surveys every two to three days. Six weeks produced one thousand six hundred twenty-seven postoperative check-ins. The single Global Postoperative Status score was tested against pain and medication diaries.

Worse status scores lined up consistently with heavier pain burden. Patients reporting frequent pain peaks scored far lower than pain-free peers. Scores also dropped stepwise as painkillers escalated to combined opioid regimens. The authors stress this is exploratory validity only, pending prospective confirmation.
pmc-13241582:
Lahiri's team at the University of Florida tested whether camera trap orientation changes which animals get recorded at carrion sites. Carrion feeds both vertebrate scavengers and invertebrates, yet most designs target one group. The team deployed horizontal and vertical cameras across 17 carrion placements. The site was Panther Swamp National Wildlife Refuge in Mississippi.

Both designs tallied similar total richness, but the species lists differed sharply. Vertical cameras caught more flesh-eating invertebrates, including blow flies and carrion beetles. Horizontal cameras, with their wider view, recorded more white-tailed deer wandering past. The authors advise pairing both orientations to capture the whole carrion food web.
pmc-13242282:
Janelle Bellot and co-authors explore cell biology in this 2026 study of YAP, a protein that helps cells grow and survive. Under stress from very salty conditions, YAP gathers into droplets called condensates, but what those droplets do was not clear.

The team used a tagging method to list proteins that touch YAP in its spread-out and droplet states. The partner list changed a lot once droplets formed, shifting from grouping genetic material to switching genes on. Three partners, named JUNB, TCF12, and IFI16, sat inside the droplets. Removing JUNB or TCF12 stopped droplets from forming at all and blocked the genes YAP normally turns on.
pmc-13242382:
Söylemez's team at Mersin profiled circular RNAs in the blood of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients. Forty-one patients faced 41 matched healthy controls. Five candidate circRNAs were measured by PCR after RNase treatment. The study is the first to test these rings in this epilepsy syndrome.

Two circRNAs ran sharply high in patient blood; a third ran low. Two others showed no difference between groups. The high and low markers both tracked drug resistance. Sex-split patterns emerged too, hinting at marker promise worth follow-up testing. All were blood-based tests, with blood drawn from both groups.
pmc-13242482:
Yusuf Sülek and co-authors asked whether longer spinal fusions speed up wear in the hip and knee. Their cohort study appeared in the Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery in 2026. They reviewed patients aged forty to sixty-five who had lumbar surgery between 2010 and 2021 at one center. Groups ranged from decompression without fusion to fusions spanning four or more vertebrae, and joint space was tracked on imaging.

Hip joint space narrowed fastest in the long-fusion group, then the short-fusion group, then the no-fusion group. Each added fused level raised the odds of severe hip narrowing, while knee wear showed no clear difference between groups. Back and hip function scores were recorded alongside the imaging. The authors advise closer hip monitoring for patients who receive extensive fusions, so degeneration is caught early. The pattern fits the idea that a stiffer spine shifts load onto the hips.
pmc-13243882:
An Huang, Haopeng Hong, and Yonghui Sun profiled colon cancers by the side of the bowel they grow on, layering genes, proteins, and protein switches. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Left-sided and right-sided tumors arise from different embryonic tissue and already behave differently in the clinic. The team ran exome, protein, and phosphoprotein sequencing on eighty tumor-and-normal tissue pairs to find out why.

Left-sided cancers were driven mainly by chromosomal instability and grew dense in blood vessels. Right-sided cancers leaned on microsatellite instability instead, a scrambling caused by failed DNA repair. Their immune neighborhoods also split: right-sided tumors showed stronger antigen display by M1 macrophages. The share of repair-deficient tumors reaching instability differed by side too. The authors argue these differences explain why targeted and immune therapies land unevenly, and they offer the atlas for tailoring treatment by tumor side.
pmc-13244382:
Molly Milano, Alec Giakas, and Eric Tecce describe a spinal abscess that crushed the cord and then starved it of blood. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Surgery in 2026. A man in his sixties came to the emergency department with sudden paralysis of both legs and intense lower back pain. Imaging placed the damage at the fourth thoracic level, where an epidural abscess was compressing the cord and a secondary cord infarction had followed.

Spinal cord infarction is uncommon and its outlook for recovery is generally poor, with causes that often stay murky. The authors walk through the hospital course to show how the two injuries compounded each other. Published guidance for such cases is thin, and their report adds one fully told case to a sparse literature. For emergency teams the lesson is speed: back pain with sudden leg paralysis is a surgical clock.
pmc-13245082:
Li and co-authors published this short correction notice in Molecular Medicine in 2026. It amends their 2025 paper on how alpha-synuclein clumps abnormally in the brain during repeated low-oxygen episodes, and how a compound called Danshensu methyl ester may protect nerve cells from that damage.

The notice fixes the author credit on the original paper. Juan Li, Na Zhang, Ziyin Zhang, and Jinsai Fu are now marked as equal contributors and co-first authors, which the first version had failed to state. No data, results, or conclusions change; the correction simply puts the shared credit on the record for anyone citing the study.
pmc-13246982:
Coniglio and co-authors mined sawmill waste for antifungal chemistry in this 2026 Bioresources and Bioprocessing study. In Uruguay, Pinus taeda plantations feed a large timber industry whose knot-rich offcuts are usually discarded, yet knots concentrate the tree's defensive compounds. The team extracted those compounds with ethanol, tuning temperature, alcohol strength, and solvent ratio to find the best recipe.

Optimized extractions recovered about a fifth of the knotwood's weight, rich in phenolic antioxidants, mainly stilbenes and terpenoids. In laboratory assays the extracts strongly slowed two wood-rotting fungi, nearly stopping one of them within a week. The authors present knotwood residue as a realistic feedstock for natural wood preservatives, turning a disposal problem into a product within a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13247182:
Seas wrote this 2026 editorial in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. It introduces a journal supplement on managing infectious diseases where resources are scarce. Infections still claim a huge share of global disability and death, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. The supplement gathers studies on practical responses, from antibiotic stewardship to HIV and tuberculosis care.

The previews include a stewardship program in a Botswana children's surgical unit. They also cover telehealth supporting stewardship in the rural United States, long-acting HIV prevention and shorter tuberculosis regimens in Peru, artificial intelligence reading chest X-rays for tuberculosis, and mobile clinics preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Mozambique. The editorial's message is that progress combines simple clinical tools, digital innovation, and community education.
pmc-13248482:
Paudyal and co-authors tested machine learning for spotting hidden udder infection in dairy cows, published in 2026. Subclinical mastitis shows no obvious signs yet lowers milk quality, and cell counts in milk are the usual clue. The team combined heat camera images of udders with milk measurements from one hundred ninety-four Holstein cows.

Sampling each quarter of the udder gave nearly eight hundred data points. A random forest model using both image and milk features reached strong accuracy, with milk lactose among the strongest signals. Heat images alone performed noticeably worse. The authors say combined data looks promising, but larger studies must confirm the approach before farm use.
pmc-13249582:
Wen and co-authors sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of a rare Chinese shrew, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Sorex cansulus lives only in China and is classed as near threatened. The team described the animal's form and its mitochondrial DNA, then compared forty-three shrew species across the five tribes of the red-toothed shrew subfamily.

Selection, not chance, had shaped most of the genome's protein-coding genes, and all ran under strong pressure to stay unchanged. Family trees backed several name changes, including splitting this shrew from a close relative as its own species. Three other species shared an odd extra transfer RNA gene, forming their own branch and raising questions about its function.
pmc-13249682:
B. Penninx and co-authors examine how advice on using biological medicines changed after approval, in this 2026 study covering 2006 to 2025. Biologicals are drugs made by living cells, and doubt often remains about their real-world benefit and safety once they reach patients.

The team compared first and current official product summaries for drugs approved in Europe between 2006 and 2010, and checked them against clinical guidelines. Official changes appeared in 47 percent of cases, mostly widening use and mostly backed by maker-funded studies. Guidelines disagreed with the official text in 75 percent of cases, usually urging narrower use. The authors link funding source to the direction of advice.
pmc-13250182:
Khachidze and co-authors chart falling birth rates in the country of Georgia and project where they lead. Their 2026 BMJ Open study uses national statistics and the national birth registry, covering well over half a million births from 2014 to 2024. The team modeled past trends and forecast the decade ahead.

Fertility fell from a little over two children per woman to well under two across the study years. The steepest drops came among teenagers and women in their early twenties, while mothers grew older on average. If recent trends hold, the models project fertility near one child per woman by 2034. The authors warn that this shift could strain Georgia's economy and its social systems in coming years.
pmc-13250382:
Amito and colleagues survey malaria parasites in northern Uganda for gene changes tied to drug resistance. Their 2026 Journal of Parasitology Research study enrolled fever patients at Gulu Regional Referral Hospital between April 2022 and January 2024. Parasite DNA was sequenced for resistance genes in the multidrug and kelch families.

Among three hundred fifty-three recruits, about three in five carried falciparum malaria, confirmed by rapid tests, microscopy, and genetic checks. Fever, chills, and headache dominated the reported symptoms. Resistance-linked variants were widespread, including changes in the kelch gene associated with artemisinin resistance in about one sixth of isolates. The authors urge ongoing monitoring of these markers to protect malaria control in the region and beyond.
pmc-13250882:
Sun and co-authors examine a long non-coding RNA that seems to protect kidneys in diabetes. Their 2026 Renal Failure study compares samples from about one hundred diabetes patients and a similar number with diabetic kidney disease. The RNA, called LINC00472, also gets tested in kidney cells stressed by high sugar.

Levels of the RNA ran low in kidney disease patients and in sugar-stressed cells, and they tracked closely with kidney function measures. Adding extra copies calmed the cells, cutting scarring genes and inflammatory signals. A small partner RNA reversed those gains when boosted, and a signaling gene downstream completed the chain. The authors propose the RNA as both a diagnostic marker and a possible treatment lever for the disease.
pmc-13253782:
Agnieszka Kałmykow-Piwińska and Katarzyna Witkowska study flood pollution in a 2026 paper from Poland. They asked how the September 2024 flood changed trace element levels in floodplain mud where the Nysa Kłodzka River meets the Odra Valley. The team mapped the site and took 112 samples from 56 places.

Lab tests on 44 samples showed surface mud held more trace elements than deeper, pre-flood layers. Lead and cadmium rose clearly, and several scoring tools confirmed higher pollution and higher risk to living things. The authors say floods move and spread pollutants across floodplains, not just wash them away.
pmc-13253982:
Shaghayegh Moradi Alamdarloo and co-authors study urinary injuries during major birth surgery in a 2026 paper from Shiraz, Iran. They reviewed patients with placenta accreta spectrum, where the placenta grows too deeply into the womb, who had cesarean hysterectomy at Namazi Hospital from 2015 to 2024.

In all, 115 patients, or 23.09 percent, had a urologic injury during surgery. Heavy blood loss of 3,000 milliliters or more was strongly tied to injury, with adjusted odds of 7.10. The deepest form, placenta percreta, carried higher risk than accreta. The authors urge expert team care and careful planning before surgery.
pmc-13254482:
Abdoulaye Kone and colleagues describe malaria patterns in Bamako, Mali, in a 2026 study. They enrolled fever patients at two community health centers, one urban and one suburban. All ages joined at the urban site, while the suburban site enrolled children under five years.

Malaria from Plasmodium falciparum was found in sixty-eight percent of fever patients at the urban site and about sixty-one percent at the suburban site. Severe cases appeared at the suburban site, including cerebral malaria in about fifteen percent of its cases. Treated mosquito net use was lower in the suburb, far lower in the suburb than in the city. The authors urge keeping control efforts up even in the dry season.
pmc-13256482:
Siqing Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 Delphi study, a method that builds expert agreement through repeated survey rounds. Their goal was a mobile health program to cut sitting time in older adults, who may sit for up to thirteen hours a day. Long sitting is linked to heart disease, diabetes-type disorders, memory decline, and early death, yet few tested phone programs target it in this age group.

The team first built a draft program from past studies, clinical guidelines, interviews, and a survey. Sixteen experts in old-age care, behavior science, and health promotion then refined it over two rounds, with every expert responding both times. They settled on 27 items in three parts: building capability, creating opportunity, and raising motivation, using tools such as goal-setting, feedback, and social support.
pmc-13257782:
Melissa L deJonge and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing virtual and in-person exercise programs for college and university students. Physically inactive students with signs of mental ill health joined a six-week structured program led by supervisors. The team measured anxiety and depression symptoms, social connectedness and relationship quality, and overall well-being before and after the program, across three phases of the project.

The in-person group had 87 students and the virtual group 62. Both forms cut symptoms and improved social inclusion and well-being, with moderate-to-large effects, and outcomes did not differ significantly by delivery mode. Gains in social inclusion helped explain better well-being in both groups. The authors say online exercise programs can widen access to mental health prevention for students.
pmc-13262582:
Alimujiang Yusufu and colleagues show that where bone cement lands inside a crushed vertebra decides how well the repair works. Vertebroplasty injects cement through a needle to stabilize osteoporotic fractures. Their 2026 review of one hundred forty-five first-time patients sorts X-rays by cement coverage into three groups.

One year on, patients whose cement spread widest or crossed the spine's midline reported the least pain. Their vertebrae also regained more height and refractured less often. Scanty coverage lagged on every measure. Pushing beyond two-thirds coverage added nothing further, giving surgeons a clear target: cross the middle, then stop.
pmc-13262882:
Ali Sultan Khazaal Nazal and colleagues use computer methods to search for a new HIV blocker in a 2026 journal article. HIV-1 protease is an enzyme the virus needs to mature, and drugs against it are a mainstay of treatment, though resistance grows. The team built a shape-based model from a known blocker complex and screened a drug library for matches.

One candidate, shortened to BAN, emerged from the screen. Docking tests predicted it binds slightly more strongly than the reference blocker. Simulations over 100 nanoseconds showed many tight hydrogen bonds and strong total binding energy. Yet the candidate also made the enzyme more flexible and broke stable salt bridges. The authors propose it as a new scaffold needing lab validation.
pmc-13262982:
Ludmila Anjos de Jesus and colleagues describe nursing technician training in Brazil's federal education network in a 2026 journal article. These mid-level courses prepare the largest share of the nursing workforce for direct patient care. The team analyzed the official teaching plans of 26 courses, using a structured outline and content analysis, to map how the courses are organized and taught.

Shared aims included quality training rooted in social needs and active teaching methods that engage students. Weaknesses included gaps in how plans were assembled and mismatches between stated goals and practical placements. Internship arrangements varied inconsistently between courses. Focus on the Brazilian public health system was still weak, the authors found, and they urge updates to strengthen training.
pmc-13263282:
William Alves de Melo Júnior and co-authors study mouth sores and quality of life in children with leukemia in a 2026 journal article. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, and its drug methotrexate often causes painful mouth inflammation. All patients in this Brazilian university hospital study also received light therapy for the mouth as routine care.

The cross-sectional study covered 113 patients aged 5 to 18 treated from 2020 to 2024. Most, 85 percent, reported a high impact on quality of life. Worse sores, older age, higher drug doses, and slower healing all tracked with worse quality of life. In adjusted analysis, sore severity and healing time stayed significant. The authors note the design cannot prove the light therapy's own effect.
pmc-13264582:
Maria A Papanikolaou and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on the Hippo signaling pathway, a chain of signals that controls cell growth, in brain tumors of children. These tumors are the second most common cancer in children, and standard care can harm the growing brain. Targeted drugs aimed at this pathway offer a possible new route.

The review explains how the pathway links with many other signal chains that drive growth. In high-grade tumors, switching on two partner proteins, YAP and TAZ, helps tumors grow, and blocking YAP slowed tumor growth in lab animals. YAP activity can also help tell severe tumors from milder ones. The authors map which tumor subsets might suit drugs against this pathway.
pmc-13264982:
Xiayun Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 study of brain excitability in generalized anxiety disorder, a long-term condition of excessive worry. Its brain basis is unclear, so the team used magnetic brain stimulation to probe the motor cortex on both sides, and measured two key brain chemicals in blood.

They compared 30 unmedicated patients with 30 matched healthy controls. Patients showed an uneven pattern: the left motor area was harder to excite and gave weaker responses, while the right gave stronger responses than in controls. The left-to-right balance was clearly reduced. Two other measures did not differ after strict correction. Blood levels of glutamate and GABA, the main go and stop chemicals, were also off balance. The authors suggest the paired measures as objective markers to support clinical judgment.
pmc-13267982:
Nobuyuki Okamoto and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a groin abscess with a hidden cause. Their patient was an 84-year-old woman with advanced breast cancer and a known groin hernia. Four days after breast surgery, a mass in her right groin began to grow. Scans showed a fluid pocket, and a needle draw confirmed pus.

Simple care calmed the abscess for a time, but it returned near the start of the large bowel about a month later. Surgery then revealed a partly burst appendix. Inflammation had spread behind the belly lining to the groin, outside the hernia sac, an unusual route. Removing the appendix solved the problem, with no return at three months. The authors urge early imaging for groin swelling in hernia patients.
pmc-13269782:
Robert S Wong and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Cx36, a protein that forms direct channels between nerve cells, often called electrical synapses. New detailed structures showed charged spots where two half-channels dock together. The team altered those spots and measured whether working channels still formed.

Computer calculations and electrical recordings in paired engineered cells were combined. At least three charge-matched pairs at each docking face were needed for a working channel. These charge patterns also seemed to keep Cx36 pairing with itself rather than with other brain channel proteins. The authors say the findings explain how these junctions form and choose partners, guiding future treatments for channel faults.
pmc-13269982:
Gabriela Plasencia and co-authors published a policy review in 2026 on language access in United States health care. Over 68 million Americans speak another language at home, and Spanish speakers form 62 percent of that group. The review covered studies, federal rules, and professional guidelines from 2004 to 2025.

Professional interpreters and language-matched care are recommended, yet barriers persist in practice. The authors call for payments that reward better language support and stronger penalties for poor performers. Health systems should test and use bilingual staff skills in an organized way. Language support must also be built into technology standards. The goal is safer care and better experience for patients who prefer other languages.
pmc-13270882:
Xinhe Wang is lead author of a 2026 journal article re-analysing single-cell gene data from a mouse model of oxygen-induced retinopathy, an eye disease like the one that can blind premature babies. In this disease, low oxygen in the retina drives abnormal new blood vessels that may pull the retina loose.

Using a public data set of mouse retinal tissue, the team sorted cells into ten types and compared gene activity between normal and diseased eyes. Several genes were turned up, including Hnrnpu and Vamp2, and others, including Xist, were turned down. Network analysis flagged hub genes such as Srsf1 and Sf3b1, and the authors discuss how changes in these genes may shape the disease.
pmc-13271282:
Mohamed A. Mabrok wrote a 2026 benchmark study on how breast X-ray classification results are reported. Deep learning papers on mammography often report scores per breast side or per patient, and that choice, he argues, makes results across studies hard to compare fairly.

Using 706 patients with four-view mammograms from a Chinese database, Mabrok tested six model designs crossed with three ways of combining views, under patient-level cross-checking. Side-level scores beat patient-level scores by an average of 17.5 percentage points, far more than the gaps between model designs, which were under three points. A large transformer model trailed every simpler network despite having many more parameters. The lesson is that reporting level drives headline performance.
pmc-13271382:
Donald S. Herzog is lead author of a 2026 cattle feeding study on adding rumen-protected lysine, an essential protein building block shielded from stomach digestion, to lower-protein grain diets for beef cattle. Lower protein diets could cut costs and nitrogen waste, but only if growth does not suffer.

Two experiments tested a standard 14.4 percent protein diet against reduced diets at 12.4 and 11.6 percent protein with lysine added. Ninety steers showed no diet effect on weight gain, feed intake, efficiency, or most carcass traits, though the lowest-protein group had a lower dressing percentage. Six heifers in a rotation design were used to measure nitrogen balance, tracking urine and manure output.
pmc-13271582:
Naoki Iso is lead author of a 2026 development and validation study of VRactice, a virtual reality system for upper-limb rehabilitation training that adds feedback on body position. Virtual reality can aid motor learning, but few studies have checked its tracking accuracy against gold-standard motion capture, especially for arm reaching with shop-bought setups.

Sixteen healthy adults, average age 25.3, performed reaching tasks while tracked at once by VRactice and by a professional Vicon system, with sensors on hand and elbow. The study compared the three-dimensional paths from both systems over the half second before peak reach. The design tests whether the cheaper virtual system measures movement closely enough for rehabilitation use.
pmc-13272182:
Yiquan Ji and Bao Chen wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study of C-reactive protein patterns after spine surgery and the effect of vancomycin powder placed in the wound. That study, a secondary analysis of a randomised trial in lumbar fusion patients, supported the protein's level on day seven as a rule-out marker for surgical site infection.

The letter praises the work, then argues the analysis missed pathogen type. Aggressive bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus provoke strong inflammation, while low-grade organisms may raise the protein only slightly despite real infection, so one threshold could miss slow infections. It also notes monitoring stopped at seven days, too early for delayed, biofilm-linked infections, and urges combined microbe and marker models.
pmc-13272282:
Martin Seiser leads a 2026 study that builds a low-cost frame to hold broken long bones still from outside the body. Such frames are vital where commercial systems are too costly or hard to obtain. The team made the frame from threaded rods, washers, and nuts sold for building work.

Five designs were tested on young cow bones with a set fracture gap, under repeated up-and-down loading. The commercial frame was stiffest, but the Steinmann pin and two-sided smooth wire designs were close, and no clear gap separated them from it. The authors call the result a first proof of concept, needing more tests before patient use.
pmc-13272682:
Tao Yang leads a 2026 study linking a protein called AKAP1 to glycogen build-up and liver cancer in mice. Glycogen is a stored form of sugar, and its handling is rewired in many cancers for reasons that are not clear. The team raised or lowered AKAP1 in mouse livers.

Lower AKAP1 cut liver glycogen and slowed both chemical-induced and gene-driven liver cancers, while higher AKAP1 did the reverse. AKAP1 helps a partner protein break down the message for an enzyme that frees sugar, raising glycogen. A peptide that blocks AKAP1 from reaching its site lowered glycogen and curbed cancer in mice, with no clear toxicity seen.
pmc-13272882:
Azar Darvishpour leads a 2026 study of wisdom, sense of coherence, and quality of life in older hospital patients in northern Iran. Sense of coherence means feeling that life is understandable and manageable. The team surveyed 200 patients in hospitals in eastern Guilan in 2024, using standard scales for all three measures.

Most participants were men aged 60 to 74. Both wisdom and sense of coherence linked positively to quality of life, and together the model explained 41.5 percent of its variation. Sense of coherence had a slightly stronger link than wisdom. The authors suggest that programs building these inner resources could help older patients feel better and cope with illness.
pmc-13274482:
Weimo Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 review article on the electron buffer effect, an idea for keeping catalysts in their best working state. During electricity-driven reactions, a catalyst's electronic structure can shift irreversibly, draining activity and stability. A buffer support can lend or take electrons reversibly, much as a chemical buffer steadies acidity.

The review explains how this steadying keeps active sites at the right oxidation state and tunes how reaction intermediates stick and release. It sorts buffer materials into metal-based and non-metal-based families and surveys their roles in key reactions such as splitting water and reducing carbon dioxide. The authors close with the measurement challenges of proving and precisely controlling the effect.
pmc-13274682:
Tao Meng and colleagues wrote a 2026 review article on turning genetic findings about osteoarthritis into useful clinical tests. Osteoarthritis, the wear-and-pain joint disease, varies hugely between patients, yet doctors lack early risk tools. Gene studies have found many risk spots, but most are small, noncoding, and active only in certain joint tissues.

The review maps a route from gene signal to biomarker. First, pin down the likely effector gene, then place it in the right cells using single-cell and spatial maps of cartilage and bone. Promising outputs include polygenic risk scores, compact molecular test panels, and imaging-plus-omics models. Pitfalls include ancestry limits and tissue access, and the authors set out standards for safe deployment.
pmc-13275082:
Emma L Hutton and co-authors present a 2026 quality improvement report on empowering nurses to lead change in a specialist acute stroke unit. Happy, engaged nurses are linked to safer care, so the project aimed to lift both staff experience and patient outcomes. The team used the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, a test-and-learn method, inside a daily team framework.

They tracked nurse and patient satisfaction surveys plus safety indicators: falls, pressure injuries from hospital care, catheter infections, and hand hygiene. The report describes significant improvements in falls, pressure injuries, and hand hygiene adherence, while patient satisfaction scores rose. Nurse satisfaction results also improved. The authors stress the changes were relatively easy to implement yet highly impactful.
pmc-13275982:
Sedef Akçaalan and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study on pairing a plant compound with gene silencing against breast cancer. The compound is quercetin, found in many foods. The gene, XBP1, helps cancer cells survive stress and has been tied to breast cancer growth.

Working with two breast cancer cell lines, the team applied quercetin, switched off XBP1, or did both. Each step alone slowed cell growth and colony formation. Together they worked better than either one. The combined treatment raised signals that drive programmed cell death. It also shifted markers tied to how cancer cells spread, in a direction linked to less spreading. The authors suggest pairing gene-based tools with plant compounds deserves further study as a treatment strategy.
pmc-13276282:
Kagisho Madikadike Molabe and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on genes behind eggshell quality in a South African chicken breed. Cracked eggs waste food and money and let germs in. The Potchefstroom Koekoek is a local breed valued for hardiness, and shell thickness is a key trait for its eggs.

The team kept one hundred hens and collected three hundred fifty eggs over nine weeks of laying. They measured shell traits and read DNA from blood and egg-making tissues. Two single-letter DNA changes in a gene called SCNN1G tracked with shell thickness. Birds with one letter form laid thicker shells than birds with the other. The gene was most active in the magnum, the tube section where egg white forms. The authors say such markers could guide breeding for stronger shells.
pmc-13277082:
Bea Klos leads a 2026 study of smell in children and teens with obesity during a stay-in weight loss program. Smell shapes eating behavior, yet little work has tested it in young patients. Sixty young people, about thirteen years old on average, joined a program mixing food therapy, activity, stress care, and behavior work for about thirty-eight days.

Smell tests covered detection, telling odors apart, and naming odors, before and after the program. At the start, scores were mostly in the normal range for their age. After weight loss, only odor naming improved a little; other scores held steady and did not track weight change. Self-ratings of smell also matched test results poorly, the team found.
pmc-13277782:
Clayton C McIntyre leads a 2026 study asking whether a single moment of brain activity can identify a person. Brain network fingerprinting uses patterns of linked activity, like a fingerprint, to tell people apart. Most work averages over whole scans. This team instead estimated links from single scan frames, split-second snapshots, using a phase-based method.

Given enough reference data, single frames could be matched to the right person. Finer maps of brain regions made matching easier. Tasks were also easier to spot within a person than across people, meaning task patterns are more personal than shared. Individual variation may drive much of what single-frame studies see, the authors conclude, so designs must account for it.
pmc-13278382:
Meghan E Carey leads a 2026 study of depression treatment for autistic young people on Medicaid, the United States safety-net health program. Getting treatment after a depression diagnosis can lower suicide risk, yet access is uneven. The team tracked 44,074 autistic enrollees aged eight to twenty-nine for five months after a new depression claim, grouping similar treatment paths.

Four paths emerged. About thirty-nine percent got little or no treatment, while only about twenty-five percent were treated continuously. Others declined gradually or started late. Continuous treatment was less likely for Black and Hispanic enrollees and for those with intellectual disability, and most likely for the youngest group and for females. Many autistic enrollees get no depression care at all.
pmc-13279282:
Parisa Mazdarani and James Edward Miles report a 2026 lab study of a knee surgery for cats. Cat knee joints, called stifles, can lose steadiness when a key ligament tears. Past bone cut methods failed to restore steadiness in cat limbs. The team test a method called CBLO, which levels the shin bone top by a cut set from a rotation point.

Ten cat hind limbs were pressed in a rig that kept hip motion free. Tests ran with the joint whole, after ligament cut and after surgery. Surgery cut the shin slope from near twenty four degrees to near nine degrees. Yet joint shift stayed like the cut ligament state, not the whole state. In this model, the cut did not restore steadiness.
pmc-13279482:
Alexander Darup and colleagues report a 2026 study of antibiotic powder placed in joints at hip and knee replacement. Joint infection after replacement is a grave side effect that can need more surgery. From January 2023, their centre added one gram of vancomycin powder in the joint before closure as a shield. The study asks if the powder cuts infection rates and if it harms wound healing.

Charts held one thousand four hundred ninety nine first hip and knee replacements from 2022 to 2023. Of those, eight hundred eighteen got the powder and six hundred eighty one did not. The title gives the core result: the powder acts as just a partial shield. Infections were pushed later in time, not stopped for good. Time to infection, wound issues and infection rates were all compared across the two groups.
pmc-13279682:
Raphael Fougeray and colleagues report a 2026 study of moth outbreaks on the coast of French Guiana. The ashen moth Hylesia metabus has females with stinging scales that cause severe skin reactions. Outbreaks hit coasts of Venezuela and French Guiana, yet stay local and hard to forecast. The team ask what habitat and climate traits mark outbreak prone sites.

Field work at thirteen sites read forest shape, tree species mix, canopy cover and bird attack rates on prey. Climate models added rain and heat patterns for each site. Outbreak prone sites held low tree density overall. They also showed small daily heat swings and sharp seasonal shifts between dry and wet seasons. Bird predation rates were weighed as a further check. Such trait maps could warn health teams where skin outbreak risk runs high.
pmc-13280382:
Nick Rucks and colleagues present a 2026 proof of concept framework for live death risk monitoring after stem cell transplant. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which transplants donor blood stem cells, treats high risk blood cancers. Early mortality stays significant, with about six to eleven percent dead in the first one hundred days. Static pre transplant scores cannot track risk as care unfolds. Their framework updates risk in real time from routine clinical data.

Deep learning models forecast seven day mortality risk from twenty two lab values of the past fourteen days, plus five demographic features. An explainability method shows which inputs drive each forecast over time. The approach was evaluated on eight hundred ninety one patients in Dusseldorf from 2004 to 2019. An independent cohort from the MIMIC-IV database gave a second test. Live, explained risk could help teams act before decline sets in.
pmc-13280582:
Antonija Poplas Susic and team give a 2026 Delphi study that sets Community Health Centres as a care model for Europe. Such centres have existed in Europe for more than five decades. They gain praise as models for comprehensive, equitable and integrated primary care. Yet a shared European definition was lacking. From an international federation definition, a refined set of thirty five key statements was built through expert consultations.

A two round Delphi study engaged thirty one experts from sixteen countries. Five point Likert questionnaires rated acceptability and feasibility of each statement. All thirty five statements were rated acceptable and feasible, with mean scores above three. Top rated elements held respect for human rights and access irrespective of socioeconomic status. Interprofessional teamwork also ranked high. A common framework can guide centre setup across diverse European systems.
pmc-13280982:
Philani Ezekiel Mkhize and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a pregnant woman who passed far too much urine. She was thirty-six and twenty-eight weeks pregnant. Her blood salt was high, her potassium was low, and her urine was very weak. The cause seemed to be an enzyme from the placenta that breaks down the hormone that holds water in the body. A lab-made form of the hormone, which the enzyme cannot break, helped her fast.

After birth, though, her symptoms came back. Scans pointed to swelling in the stalk of the pituitary gland, the small gland that releases the hormone. That is a second, separate cause in the brain itself. She went back on the lab-made hormone. The authors warn that two causes can hide in one patient, even when the first seems clear.
pmc-13281282:
Ish Sethi and colleagues compared trainee and senior doctors on a hard choice in a 2026 study. The choice is which sick children should get a heart and lung support machine. Such calls vary a lot from doctor to doctor. The study ran at one large children's referral hospital. Trainees in child critical care filled in surveys soon after a child's breathing support began or rose. Senior doctors rated the same children.

Trainees ruled out about one in five children for the machine. Children who arrived with poor daily function were far less likely to be picked. Trainee and senior calls agreed only to a fair degree. The authors say how a child functioned before illness sways these calls. Clearer shared rules could help trainees and seniors land in the same place.
pmc-13281582:
Weihao Lin and colleagues found an old drug class that may revive a lung cancer therapy in a 2026 study. New pills that block a flawed cancer gene helped many patients at first. But tumors in time learn to resist them. The team screened close to two thousand approved drugs on resistant cancer cells. Cholesterol pills called statins stood out. They killed resistant cells by choice and shrank tumors in lab and animal tests.

Resistant cells had ramped up a fuel path that builds cell fats and tags. Statins block the head enzyme of that path. Silencing that enzyme copied the statin effect. The path feeds a growth switch that keeps resistant cells alive, and statins cut it off. Paired with the gene pills, one statin delayed resistance and hit tumors harder in animals, with fair tolerance. The authors propose trials of the cheap pairing.
pmc-13281882:
Al-Safi Noman and colleagues studied digital tools and birth and death records in Yemen in a 2026 paper. Sound records of births and deaths guide health planning. In war-torn settings, weak systems blur those counts. The team surveyed one hundred nineteen staff across thirty-two public health sites in Sana'a. The survey scored tech gear, software, staff skill, and networks. It also scored how well sites register, cover, and publish their statistics.

Stronger tech went hand in hand with stronger statistics work. The link was large in their model, explaining much of the gap between sites. Tech use itself sat at a middling level across sites. The authors read the pattern as a case for investing in systems and training. They caution that a one-time survey shows links, not proof that tech alone caused the gains. In a fragile state, they argue, even linked gains are worth chasing.
pmc-13282382:
Tim David and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study on using sound and milling to take apart self-assembled molecular cages. The cages form from palladium metal centres and linking molecules, a family with uses in catalysis, sensing, and drug delivery. Building them is well understood, but controlled disassembly was scarce. The team attached polymer chains to the cage parts so outside forces could pull on them.

Ultrasound sent shear forces through the chains, stressing the metal centres until links broke. In one cage type, that released the anticancer drug cisplatin on demand. Ball milling, grinding in the solid state, achieved full and reversible activation too. The method also dismantled a giant twelve-centre sphere, among the heaviest discrete assemblies reported. Computer simulations mapped the force needed to break the metal links and the step-by-step pathway. The authors offer force as a general tool for responsive materials.
pmc-13282482:
Wiebke Bennecke and co-authors present a 2026 physics study achieving three-dimensional imaging of electron orbitals with a table-top ultrafast light source. Orbitals are the quantum shapes that describe where electrons live in molecules. A method called photoemission orbital tomography rebuilds them from electrons knocked out by light. Extending it to three dimensions at femtosecond speed, a millionth of a billionth of a second, had been out of reach.

The team paired a new spectroscopy method, ultrafast momentum microscopy, with a tunable extreme ultraviolet source built in the lab. A tailored algorithm rebuilt the full three-dimensional picture from sparse, undersampled data. That pairing sped up collection and cut how much data is needed. They proved it by imaging the frontier orbitals of an organic semiconductor on a silver surface.
pmc-13282682:
Mahsa Boustani and co-authors present a 2026 study of hydatid cyst disease in patients in northwest Iran, including the genetics of the parasite behind it. The disease comes from the larval stage of a tapeworm, Echinococcus granulosus, forming cysts in organs. The team recorded two hundred ninety-five surgical patients in Urmia treated between 2010 and 2021, and tested seventy-four preserved cyst samples with gene methods.

Cases were more often female, and the liver and lung were the commonest cyst sites. Villagers and people with little schooling featured heavily among patients. DNA was extracted from all tested samples, though only about a third could be sequenced for each of two genes. Every sequenced sample belonged to the same genotype, G1, the sheep strain, with no variation in the stretches read.
pmc-13282982:
Italian health records show what first-line leukemia care really looks like in Valentina Perrone's 2026 population study. New targeted drugs have changed first care for this common adult leukemia. Routine data can show what trials cannot, such as cost and real drug use.

Health records for about nine million residents covered patients who started care from 2019 to 2022. A total of 1,479 patients began first treatment in the study window. Standard chemotherapy stayed the most common first choice, above all in older patients. Ibrutinib users had lower death risk and longer time to next treatment. Yearly cost per patient was high and driven mainly by drug costs.
pmc-13283182:
Half the hedgehogs reaching a Lombardy rescue center carried drug-resistant gut bacteria, S Raineri and associates found in 2026. Hedgehogs can signal the health of local environments. The team checked dead hedgehogs from a wildlife rescue center in Lombardy.

Gut samples from 49 hedgehogs were tested for resistant Escherichia coli strains. Resistant strains appeared in 25 animals, just over half of the group. Most strains resisted many drugs, including key penicillin-type drugs in all cases. Gene tests found TEM most often, then SHV and CTX-M types. Seven strains carried two resistance genes at once. All strains stayed sensitive to colistin and florfenicol in lab tests.
pmc-13283382:
Jun Zhang and Jingru Ma present a 2026 review of nature-inspired polymer particles for liver cancer immune therapy. Liver cancer is often found late and responds poorly to standard care. Immune drugs help some patients but fail many others with this cancer.

The particles copy cell surfaces or use targeting tags to reach tumors. They can hide from immune patrols, stay in blood longer, and release drugs slowly. Animal studies show better immune cell entry into tumors with these designs. Cancer vaccines and cell reprogramming are covered as partner strategies. Checkpoint drugs worked in synergy with particles in some animal work. Safety and scale remain open hurdles.
pmc-13284482:
Marta Ballester Martinez, Giuseppe Filomeni, and Salvatore Rizza present a 2026 laboratory protocol for growing three mouse liver cell types together. Work on metabolic liver disease needs models that keep how liver cells interact in the body. The protocol covers hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells, and Kupffer cells taken from the same mouse liver.

Steps include liver perfusion without a pump, enzyme digestion, and sorting cells by density steps. Hepatocytes are then grown in a defined, serum-free fluid made to mimic plasma. Keeping conditions close to the body should help labs study normal liver work and disease change with all three cell types present, rather than one type alone.
pmc-13285682:
A cell-cycle brake drug supercharges antibody-guided cancer bombs, Xiao Guo and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Antibody-drug conjugates haul poison straight to tumor cells, either wrecking DNA or jamming division spindles. The WEE1 blocker azenosertib stalls cells at damage checks, a natural partner for both poison types.

Paired with two DNA-wrecking conjugates, the blocker deepened DNA harm and cell death, stretched response length, and beat resistance in patient-grown mouse tumors. With spindle-jamming conjugates, pairing worsened division chaos and froze cells mid-split longer. All pairs worked better and stayed tolerable in animals. The authors pitch azenosertib as a near-universal booster for this drug class.
pmc-13286182:
Takuma Shimoyama and colleagues probe how people judge minds in edible robots in a 2026 psychology experiment. Eating a thing that seems to have feelings can stir the same moral pinch as eating an animal, a puzzle known as the meat paradox. Their food-like agents could move and make sounds, letting the team vary the show while the food itself stayed the same.

More than a thousand viewers watched two video clips of the agents and rated what kind of mind each seemed to hold. Ratings split into two strands: a sense of doing, and a sense of feeling, and each strand favored a unlike clip. Hesitation about eating the agent also shifted between the clips, while guilt stayed level across both. Oddly, neither mind strand tracked hesitation or guilt in the end, a loose end the authors flag for the study of food and feeling.
pmc-13286282:
Pravesh Parekh and a large team present FEMA-Long, a faster statistics engine for repeat-measure studies, in a 2026 methods article. Studies that weigh the same people again and again bog down when the math insists on tidy, unchanging correlation patterns. Real growth and aging bend those patterns, but flexible fits were too slow for genome-scale data. Their extension lets correlation flex freely, curves bend smoothly, and gene effects change with time.

Test runs showed the engine matches careful answers while finishing thousands of times sooner. Applied to a Norwegian birth cohort, it tracked length, weight, and body mass in 68,273 babies across their first year. Heritability and gene correlations shifted month by month rather than holding still. Several gene variants acted only at certain ages, exactly the kind of fleeting signal the tool was built to catch.
pmc-13286982:
Ruolin Wu and a nine-author team redate the birth of flowering plants using the whole fossil record in a 2026 evolutionary study. Molecular clocks often place flowering plant origins deep in the Jurassic or earlier, while fossils suggest a Cretaceous debut, a standoff called the Jurassic gap. Instead of hand-picking a few fossils, the team fed more than 25,000 fossil occurrences into a statistical bridge model to estimate each lineage's age from its full record.

Those data-driven age densities then constrained 110 nodes on a tree of 644 flowering species built from 83 genes. The combined analysis rejected any origin after the Jurassic closed. It settled on a short, late Jurassic history for the crown group, narrowing the long quarrel between rocks and molecules. The authors offer the two-step method as a more objective way to marry fossil and genetic clocks.
pmc-13287082:
Zohreh Hajibarat and Abbas Saidi mine public gene data for soybean stress defenses in a 2026 computational study. Drought, salt, and heavy metals together erase huge shares of the world's soybean harvest. Rather than rerun experiments, the team integrated expression data from 112 samples across stress types. They layered differential expression, correlation shifts, and two machine learning rankers to find genes that respond again and again.

Thirty-seven candidate genes survived the combined filters, clustering around amino acid building, energy and carbon metabolism, and oxidative stress handling. Three genes on chromosome 16 drew the strongest multi-layer support. Cousin genes in wild soybean and two related beans suggest part of the response is ancient and shared. The authors offer the shortlist as hypotheses for lab validation and for breeding hardier varieties.
pmc-13287582:
Reham M Abdel-Hameed and colleagues built spongy crystal materials in 2026 from copper, zinc, and metal waste to pull a harmful farm chemical, carbofuran, out of waste water. Three versions carried rising amounts of acid groups on their inner surfaces, and uptake was tested in the lab.

The version richest in acid groups took up the most chemical, at 389.2 milligrams per gram of material. The plainest version managed 162.5 milligrams per gram. Uptake over time and across strengths fitted standard surface models well. The authors present acid-rich crystals from waste metal as a cheap route to cleaning pesticide-laced water before release.
pmc-13288582:
Rehab M Abdelhamid and colleagues test soaking legume seeds in liquid from a soil bacterium in a 2026 plant study. They isolated Streptomyces griseoviridis, profiled its cell-free culture filtrate, and primed common bean and faba bean seeds at several strengths before measuring sprouting and early growth.

Chemical analysis found plant hormones in the filtrate, led by gibberellic acid and zeatin, plus fatty compounds such as oleic acid. A 25 percent mix suited common bean best, lifting germination and shoot length, while a weaker 10 percent mix suited faba bean, which reached full germination sooner. Protein and pigment levels also rose, and computer docking hinted at how one indole compound might steer metabolism. Effects clearly depended on species and dose.
pmc-13288682:
Annemieke Wargers and colleagues listen to teenagers themselves through focus groups in a 2026 study tied to the European SEEDS project. Eight discussion groups brought together 35 adolescents aged 13 to 15 from lower-income areas of Spain, the Netherlands, Greece, and the UK, framed by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

Teenagers knew healthy habits mattered yet often skipped them anyway. Friends and peers mostly discouraged activity outside physical education lessons, good ties with teachers helped, and families shaped eating more than movement. Cramped schools, little free time, canteens short on healthy choices, and the COVID-19 pandemic all got in the way, while required PE lessons and school clubs pushed activity upward.
pmc-13288882:
David R Strong and colleagues build a yardstick for anti-smoking social pressure in a 2026 analysis of thirty years of United States surveys. Tobacco supplements to a national population survey ran nine times from 1992 to 2022 and reached 1,462,050 respondents, who were asked how willing they were to restrict smoking across ten everyday settings.

Answers formed one strong scale, stable across years, that tracked tightly with state smoking rates over the whole period. Living in a high-pressure state cut the odds of smoking about as much as living where cigarette prices were highest, in their adjusted comparisons. State programs aimed at norms may deserve part of the credit for the long national decline.
pmc-13289082:
Andrew Steptoe, Alanna Jo Shand, and Camille Lassale study diet and well-being in older adults. Data came from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. It holds 3,296 adults aged 50 and up. Diet was scored in 2018 and 2019. Well-being was scored then and in 2020.

High scores meant a Mediterranean-style diet. Such scores tied to higher well-being at the start. The link held after many checks. It held past low mood and income too. High scorers lost less well-being in the pandemic. That held past their starting scores. Diet may guard mental health in old age.
pmc-13289382:
Marie Eriksson, Elena M Gutierrez-Farewik, and Åsa Bartonek traced a 2026 long-term record review on walking in myelomeningocele, a spinal birth defect also called MMC. Lesion level predicts walking ability, but stiffness and other factors can hold people back. The authors compared childhood walking patterns with adult patterns in the same people years later.

Of 59 adults, 29 had three-dimensional gait testing as children and again as adults for comparison. Mean age rose from 11.6 years at first testing to 25.9 years at adult testing, with a median gap of 15.0 years between visits. Most kept walking without aids, yet hip, knee, and ankle measures worsened and speed fell even in that steady group. Community walking dropped sharply by adulthood.
pmc-13289782:
Li Chen and coauthors describe a 2026 look at how rare stomach gland tumors appear on endoscopy. Oxyntic gland neoplasms include a benign adenoma and two cancer types from acid-making glands, and they often lack an obvious cancer look. Records came from one major center for histology-proven cases between January 2019 and July 2025, with three imaging modes reviewed.

Among 156,240 upper endoscopies, only 35 patients had these tumors, a rate of 0.028 percent as reported. Lesions were small, with a median of 6 mm, and clustered in the upper stomach. Color often matched nearby lining or looked mildly red, with branching vessels in about a third. Enlarged openings and vessels marked benign forms on magnified views.
pmc-13290082:
Mary E DeFeo, Yuanyuan Liu, Zhiwei Zhou, Steven K Higginbottom, and Dylan Dodd screen a 2026 set of gut bacteria for making indole-3-acetic acid, a tryptophan product reported to calm inflammation. Which organisms make it well, and by what oxygen-free path, was unclear. Liquid chromatography screening covered 206 human gut isolates to settle how common strong production really is among gut residents.

Only five strains passed the measurement cutoff, and high output was confined to two acetogen species in the screen. Production rose with amino acid breakdown through OFOR enzymes, yielding many branched and aromatic acids alongside. In germ-free mice colonized with one producer, those products appeared in body fluids with distinct handling. Carbon tracing showed released carbon dioxide gets recycled.
pmc-13290782:
Round doughnut-shaped solids of revolution hide infinitely many Möbius bands as minimal surfaces, Mario Schulz proves in a 2026 geometry paper. Free boundary minimal surfaces meet the solid's boundary at right angles and minimize area, and Schulz asks which topologies can arise inside toroids.

The proof uses equivariant variational methods. In toroids of revolution that are round and strictly mean convex, Schulz constructs infinitely many distinct embedded Möbius bands meeting the boundary freely, plus infinitely many embedded annuli of the same type. Each surface's area scales in direct proportion to the size of its symmetry group. The result adds Möbius topology, long out of reach for such constructions, to the list of shapes minimal surface theory can guarantee inside curved containers.
pmc-13290982:
Hai Zhao, Jiaxin Yang, and Fan Yang review UBE2 enzymes in cancer in a 2026 article. These enzymes help run the system that tags proteins for disposal. Their role in picking targets inside tumors has had less study. The immune side of that role is a key focus.

Three ideas frame the review. One enzyme can help or harm a tumor by tissue type. Many enzymes feed into a few shared pathways. Some act right where tumors meet immune cells. The authors weigh marker uses and drug ideas with care. Most proof comes from few tumor types and past cohorts. Firm trials must come before clinic use, they warn.
pmc-13291782:
Dilara Yiğit and colleagues report a 2026 animal experiment testing whether emodin, a plant-derived anthraquinone, protects rat leg muscle from ischemia-reperfusion injury. Twenty-four male Wistar rats were split into four groups: sham, emodin alone, injury alone, and injury plus emodin. Injury was produced by clamping the lower aorta for 45 minutes, then restoring flow for 120 minutes.

Injured muscle showed higher malondialdehyde and lower catalase activity, signs of oxidative damage. Emodin at 20 mg/kg lowered the malondialdehyde levels and partly restored catalase, though superoxide dismutase and glutathione did not change. Tissue damage such as fiber disarray, swelling, and neutrophil buildup also eased, without vanishing. The authors call the protection partial and urge work on the pathways involved.
pmc-13291882:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued a 2026 safety opinion on dextransucrase made by a genetically modified Bacillus subtilis strain, DP-Eyp97, from Genencor International B.V. The enzyme is meant for sugar processing that builds oligo- and polysaccharides in place. Panel members, with Holger Zorn among the listed authors, reviewed the production strain, the manufacturing route, and expected intake.

The strain met the qualified presumption of safety standard, and the enzyme carried no living cells or leftover DNA. Estimated intake reached up to 27.598 mg of total organic solids per kilogram of body weight daily in European groups. Given that record, the panel skipped toxicity testing. A sequence check found no match with known allergens, though a small allergy risk could not be ruled out, and the panel declared no safety concerns.
pmc-13292682:
Carolina Viza Amorim and co-authors write a 2026 letter testing whether the BRAFV600E mutation can separate high-grade dysplastic moles from early melanomas, a distinction pathologists often sweat over. The mutation drives growth but also freezes cells in senescence, appearing in most ordinary moles yet only about 6 percent of in-place melanomas. The team assayed archived high-grade dysplastic nevi from patients with dysplastic nevus syndrome.

Twenty-five lesions with the strongest atypia anchored the topography analysis, most sitting on the trunk. The mutation rate matched the 70 to 80 percent range typical of dysplastic nevi generally, far above the 5 to 10 percent seen in early melanomas. Eight of nine patients had a personal melanoma history. The authors suggest a positive result favors a benign high-grade mole, while negative lesions deserve suspicion.
pmc-13293482:
Claudia Zuluaga-Quintero, Luis Eduardo Diaz Barrera, and Luisa Villamil review, in a 2026 paper, the two-sided role of Actinobacteria in fish farming. These versatile bacteria are common in water systems, yet their help and harm in aquaculture were poorly pulled together.

Only a minority of studies moved past dish tests to live fish, and nearly half lacked firm naming of their strains. Streptomyces stood out as the most reported genus on both sides. Some strains fought major fish germs by jamming signals and biofilms, while kin of the same group caused off-flavors in water and rare infections. Genome-level naming is urged before farm use.
pmc-13293682:
Keishi Shintomi and colleagues rebuild, in a 2026 study, chromosome packing in a dish to learn how a protein machine called condensin I is switched on and off. Chromosomes must condense before cell division and loosen after, in step with the cell cycle.

Using a small set of purified proteins, the team showed two phosphate tags activate the machine: one frees it from self-blocking tail regions, the other, on a central subunit, gives full power. Adding a phosphate-removing enzyme pulled the machine off rebuilt chromosomes and undid packing. Frog egg extracts showed the two tags rise and fall on unlike schedules in real division.
pmc-13293982:
Eleanor I Lamont and coauthors give a 2026 protocol for pulling bacterial RNA out of host-heavy samples before sequencing. Pathogen signals drown in host RNA, and bought probes often miss parts of the transcriptome. Their transcript-capture method builds 150-base biotinylated probes at home from bacterial DNA spanning the whole genome, then fishes matching cDNA from standard libraries.
