Enrichment tops 200-fold in lab, animal, and human infection samples. Gene coverage passes 80%, giving near-complete bacterial transcriptomes where noise once blocked analysis. A snapshot of what bacteria actually do inside a host can reveal weak points that pure lab cultures hide.
pmc-13294182:
Jacob S. Heng and a large team report a 2026 eye case in a patient with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with CAR T cells. Engineered T cells can cross into protected sites like the brain and eye, clearing hidden disease, but entry can spark local inflammation at tumor sites, called tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity. Eye involvement has rarely been described.

Both optic nerve heads developed masses with retinal disease that mimicked fungal infection inside the eye. Spotting the true cause early mattered, since infection treatment and inflammation treatment pull opposite ways. The authors show that team-based care can manage ocular toxicity well and urge eye checks when vision changes follow cell therapy.
pmc-13294482:
Vivek Singh and colleagues freeze twelve snapshots of the human mitochondrial ribosome small subunit mid-assembly in a 2026 structural study. Building the subunit correctly is vital, since it makes energy machine parts and faults cause severe disease. Particles pulled from human cells were sorted by cryo-microscopy into distinct late stages covering platform, decoding center, and RNA tail folding.

Two familiar proteins gained new jobs: PUS1, known for transfer RNA editing, and mtIF2, known for starting translation, both act as assembly helpers. Stepwise RNA folding and protein docking appear tightly choreographed. The modular path explains how the subunit earns translation skill only when fully mature.
pmc-13294682:
Jonathan Rees, Nico M Franz, and Beckett Sterner describe a 2026 method for aligning biological species checklists. Checklists list taxonomic groups and underpin research articles, project databases, and major resources such as the Catalogue of Life. Matching records between two checklists is a necessary first step before data can be combined.

Their exemplar-based approach uses sample members of each group to link records across lists. It avoids heavy manual preparation, handles very large checklists efficiently, and respects how taxonomic concepts relate to each other. Open-source code in the List Tools library lets others apply the method for data integration and quality control work.
pmc-13295782:
Ziwen Zheng and colleagues set out a trial of guided needle sampling for swollen chest glands in a 2026 protocol. Standard ultrasound-guided needle sampling can miss the telling tissue in small specimens. A laser microscope threaded through the needle could steer sampling live, rivalling a freezing biopsy method that few centres offer.

Five Chinese centres aim to enrol 640 adults whose glands measure at least 10 millimetres and need a firm diagnosis. Patients are split evenly between laser-guided needle sampling and freezing biopsy, grouped first by cancer likelihood. Matching the biopsy method's success rate within a set margin is the main test, with safety and procedure time also tracked.
pmc-13296182:
Sevil Ceyhan Dogan and Kenan Goren test, in 2026, whether bone drugs used for osteoporosis might also act against breast cancer, using computer methods alone. They model three bisphosphonates, checking their chemistry, predicted safety and fit against proteins tied to tumours and bone turnover.

All three compounds showed plausible links to targets involved in tumour growth and bone breakdown. Zoledronate came out strongest overall in the modelling. The authors suggest these familiar drugs might help manage cancer-related bone disease beyond simple bone protection. They stress that laboratory experiments must confirm the predictions before any clinical claim.
pmc-13296282:
Xingru He and colleagues examine, in 2026, how the layout of parks, rivers and wetlands shapes bird variety across southwest China. Fast urban growth is shrinking such blue-green spaces, and bird richness offers a handy gauge of ecological health.

Links proved complex and curved rather than straight. Green spaces mattered more overall than water areas, with their size and edge length especially influential. The authors argue that planning which enlarges and connects green patches can lift urban wildlife. Their results give city builders concrete guidance for healthier, more wildlife-friendly development.
pmc-13296982:
A three-dimensional imaging pipeline is built in 2026 by Jiajia Wang and co-authors for the mouse trigeminal ganglion, the relay hub for whisker touch signals. Flat methods miss its spatial layout, so whole-head fluorescence sectioning mapped cells at fine resolution.

Two zones emerged: one packed with cell bodies, one rich in fibres. Neurons serving three named whiskers sat across both zones with overlapping but biased territories, and one whisker's neurons spread widest front-to-back. The authors say the atlas sharpens understanding of how whisker touch signals map onto the ganglion's internal three-dimensional anatomy.
pmc-13297082:
Tianqi Chen and co-authors build, in 2026, a brain-inspired vision system that learns to detect line orientation without labelled examples. A front end mimicking early visual processing feeds a self-organising map, which settles into orderly patches responding to distinct angles.

The system held up under noise, scarce training images and restricted early experience, and adjusted when new stimuli arrived after training. The authors present it as a testbed for how self-organisation shapes perception, and as a step toward artificial vision that learns in a more biology-like way from raw experience alone.
pmc-13297282:
Xianglong Ou and colleagues pretreat, in 2026, mice with a seaweed-derived sugar for four weeks before triggering severe pancreas inflammation. This illness kills often and lacks good treatments, so the team check injury, gut barrier and microbes under the sugar's protection.

Treated mice showed lower digestive enzyme leaks, less tissue damage and muted inflammatory signals in pancreas and gut. A key inflammatory pathway quieted while an antioxidant axis woke, gut lining seals strengthened and fewer bacteria escaped to the pancreas. Gut microbes regained variety with helpful kinds enriched. The authors propose the sugar as nutrition-based support.
pmc-13297982:
Autopsies in northern Pretoria reveal pneumonia and HIV-linked infections still dominate infection deaths, report Moshawa Calvin Khaba and colleagues in a 2026 ten-year review. They examined 55 autopsy cases from 2012 to 2021 where infection was the final cause of death at a South African tertiary service.

The deceased had a median age of 31 years and 67% were women. HIV was present in 35%, and AIDS-defining illness in 27%, with widespread tuberculosis the commonest of those. Multilobar pneumonia caused 36% of deaths and septic shock 18%. Notably, 60% of the group was HIV-negative. The authors argue autopsy findings expose diagnostic gaps that better testing before death could close.
pmc-13302982:
Blending a metabolism score with a frailty count sharpens risk forecasts in early cardiometabolic disease, Yaocheng Luo and colleagues report in a 2026 cohort analysis. Data from China's CHARLS and America's Health and Retirement Study covered people at CKM stages zero through three. Their combined triglyceride-glucose-frailty index was tested against later heart events and death.

Risk climbed steadily across index quarters in a dose-response pattern, bending twice along the way. The pattern held across subgroups, and the index sorted future cases with moderate accuracy in both cohorts. The authors offer it as a supporting gauge for sorting risk in early to mid stages, while calling for more checks on its clinical worth.
pmc-13307182:
Joan Somja described two overlapping skin lymphoma forms in one older man in a 2026 case account. A 68-year-old carried slowly growing dark plaques on his legs and buttock fold for 25 years, matching mixed hyperpigmented and poikilodermatous mycosis fungoides.

Unlike the usual net-like pattern, lesions formed broad, sharp-edged sheets of darkening in the reported description. Whole-body scans found no spread beyond skin, and tissue plus immune tests confirmed the lymphoma with a single T-cell clone. Staging reached IB, and doctors chose watchful waiting given the calm course.
pmc-13307382:
Marlus da Silva Pedrosa and co-authors examine in 2026 how zinc uptake through the AdcABC system shapes daily life in Streptococcus mutans, a key tooth decay bacterium. They compared normal cells, cells missing adcBC, and restored cells, with high and low zinc on hand.

Cells without the uptake system grew poorly and used many sugars less well, while added zinc restored growth but not all measures of cell activity. Acid tolerance did not change, yet clumping and surface growth did depend in part on uptake. Gene activity for stress and metal balance also shifted, showing that zinc acts through more than one route.
pmc-13307782:
In 2026, Junyue Zheng and co-authors test whether glyphosate, the world top weed killer, helps drug resistance genes spread in the gut, using zebrafish as a stand in. Fish faced glyphosate, its breakdown product AMPA, or the antibiotic oxytetracycline, alone and in pairs, and gut gene counts were compared.

Glyphosate alone raised the share of resistance genes by a factor of 1.67 in the fish gut samples. Paired with the antibiotic, the share rose by a factor of 2.30 in those samples, a joint push past either agent alone. AMPA showed no such push in this work. Human meaning stays unclear, so tests in closer models must follow before health claims can stand.
pmc-13308582:
Satish Kumar and co-authors compare in 2026 two ultrasound guided nerve blocks for pain after radical breast surgery in a double blind randomised trial. Women aged 18 to 70 years got either an erector spinae plane block or a rhomboid intercostal block before their operation.

Total fentanyl use in the first 24 hours after surgery was the main score for the trial. The back muscle block group used a mean of 2.67 units per kilogram, versus 3.68 in the rib block group, a firm gap. Pain scores and drug use during surgery did not differ in a clear way. Less opioid need favours the back block where teams can offer it.
pmc-13309382:
Joëlle M. Posthumus led a 2026 feasibility study on judging a urostomy from photographs after bladder surgery. A urostomy diverts urine through an opening in the belly after the bladder is removed and a bowel segment is used. Nurses lack shared rules for what a healthy opening should look like.

Photos from 49 patients treated in one center during 2022 were scored by two experts with set criteria. Place, color, and shape of the opening could be judged in most photos, while height could not be measured without a scale in the image. Lighting and angle varied a lot. The authors say standard photo rules are needed before wider use.
pmc-13309482:
Javier Jiménez-Garrido presents a 2026 mathematics article on the Stieltjes moment problem inside broad function spaces set by growth rules. The problem asks when a list of numbers can serve as the moments of some function. The new setup allows a larger home for the moment map than past work used.

When a function can be sent to its moment list, the article studies whether that map misses values or merges distinct functions, and in some cases settles both questions. Results also cover fast-growing rule sets where a key shifted-moments condition fails. A recent Borel-Ritt type result on sector functions drove the new framing. Readers in analysis and ultradifferentiable function theory are the audience.
pmc-13309582:
Omar Hahad and co-authors review links between dirty air before birth and poor birth outcomes in a 2026 article. Breathing polluted air during pregnancy ties to low birth weight, early birth, and stillbirth in many studies. How the harm happens, and which weeks matter most, stay less certain.

Study searches across three databases gathered population findings and lab evidence on body pathways. Higher fine particle exposure in mid-pregnancy linked to lower birth weight and higher early birth risk in the cited work. Proposed pathways include chemical stress, swelling, hormone disruption, vessel problems, and gene-mark changes. The authors call for sharper work on timing and on how pollutants act together.
pmc-13310582:
Shaymaa Shurrab and co-authors follow the first two reported cases of a rare metabolic disorder into the teen years in a 2026 article. The disorder stems from faults in the CA5A gene, which weaken a mitochondrial enzyme and trigger ammonia buildup, acid imbalance, and low blood sugar in newborns. Long-term course data were almost absent.

The sister, now 16, and her brother, now 14, both presented as newborns with ammonia-driven brain symptoms and the same gene change on both copies. The sister had three further illness-triggered crises, the last at age eight, an unusually late pattern, while her brother stayed stable. Glucose infusions, a single gut dose of carglumic acid, and at times vein lipids treated the crises. The authors chart management for such episodes.
pmc-13310882:
James Woodforde led a 2026 systematic review on changing culture in community sport clubs. Grassroots clubs are asked to boost inclusion, health, and safety, and culture shapes whether those goals land. How often culture change plans have been tested was unknown.

Five databases were searched through June 2025 for tested plans in community settings. Twelve studies met the bar, most small and based on interviews. Themes covered safety and fairness, inclusion of marginal groups, and adult conduct in youth sport. Plans that paired personal learning with club wide change and steady outside help showed the best shifts. Proof is young and mixed, so firm claims await stronger tests.
pmc-13311082:
Erik Bergqvist studies math self beliefs and student engagement in group problem work in a 2026 paper. Confidence in math skill and math self image both foretell engagement, yet their split roles beside math anxiety are rarely modeled together. Swedish upper secondary students were tracked over a two week problem solving unit.

Seventy seven students gave data at two time points. General math confidence linked positively to every engagement facet, while math self image linked only in narrow ways. Math anxiety tied mainly to mental disengagement. Past achievement seemed to reach engagement through general confidence. Teachers should build broad confidence and ease anxiety together.
pmc-13311182:
Nina Dhollander and a large team weigh colposcopy accuracy for sorting HPV positive women in a 2026 review. Global guidance lists colposcopy as one triage route after a positive HPV screen, yet its true accuracy in screening groups needed pooling. Past studies that reported full outcome counts were gathered across major databases.

Eleven studies with 13,311 women in total met the bar. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were figured for two grades of cell change, and colposcopy was compared with cell test triage where data allowed. Bias and proof certainty were graded with standard tools. Results should guide screen programs on when scope triage earns its cost.
pmc-13311282:
Yuji Tachibana and co-authors examine the 2026 imaging study of virtual non-contrast pictures made from contrast liver CT scans. If the made-up images match true plain scans, patients could skip one scan pass.

Thirty-one patients had three-phase liver scans on a second-generation spectral CT machine between August 2024 and February 2025. Virtual plain images were built from each phase and checked against true plain scans in numbers and by eye. Average gaps stayed within the preset 10 HU limit for all phases. Images built from the last phase looked cleanest, with fewer vessel leftovers and better overall quality.
pmc-13311782:
Lidija B McGrath and co-authors describe adults with congenital heart disease covered by Medicaid in a 2026 United States study. Medicaid coverage marks low income, whose effect on this growing patient group is poorly charted.

Claims data from all states covered 260,535 adults with heart defect codes from 2016 to 2018. Women made up 63.1 percent, and the average age was 40.2 years in this group. Rhythm problems, mental health diagnoses, and high blood pressure each affected over two fifths. A quarter had a disability, and heavy emergency visit use was common. The picture shows wide medical and social need.
pmc-13312082:
Raymond Vanholder and co-authors write a 2026 commentary for World Kidney Day arguing that kidney care must change to serve both patients and the planet. Today's model centers on late-stage disease and in-center dialysis, which the authors call unsustainable because of its costs, environmental load, and poor results for quality of life.

They welcome the 78th World Health Assembly's recognition of kidney disease as a serious threat and call for care built on early detection and prevention. Transplantation and home dialysis serve patients and the environment better, dialysis itself should be made greener without lowering quality, and conservative care deserves a place for frail older patients. The piece asks governments, professionals, and the public to act together on awareness and patient-centered change.
pmc-13312182:
Dongxue Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 study of two receptors, the vitamin D receptor and the calcium sensing receptor, in parathyroid cancer. This rare cancer resists radiation and chemotherapy, so complete removal at first surgery is the only curative option, and its molecular drivers remain poorly understood.

Both receptors help govern parathyroid hormone output and cell growth, and both were already known to fall in benign parathyroid adenomas. The team found the two receptors downregulated in parathyroid cancer as well, with signs the pair interact during tumor development. Long non-coding RNAs tied to the vitamin D receptor emerged as candidate diagnostic markers. The authors present these molecules as leads for earlier detection and for understanding how this uncommon cancer arises.
pmc-13312582:
Vincent Corbel and a large group of regional specialists write a 2026 commentary on the resurgence of chikungunya in South America. The mosquito-borne virus re-emerged across the Americas over the past decade. In 2025 alone, 18 countries reported more than 313,000 cases and 170 deaths, with transmission still expanding into 2026.

New vaccines show promise, the authors note, but missing world guidance, safety questions in some groups, supply limits, and thin data on lasting protection block large rollouts. Meanwhile climate change is reshaping the Aedes mosquitoes that carry the virus, shifting where they thrive and how they resist insecticides. The commentary argues the outbreak exposes surveillance and control systems that react after the fact instead of acting early, and calls for a proactive regional strategy before the next wave.
pmc-13312782:
Dilek Erden reports a 2026 quasi-experimental study on whether teaching nursing students cooperatively sharpens their creative thinking and self-directed learning. The course under study prepares third-year students to educate patients themselves, a task that rewards both inventiveness and the ability to steer one's own learning.

Ninety-one students took the Education in Nursing course in the 2022-2023 year, with questionnaires given before and after. Creative thinking dispositions rose overall, including the self-discipline, innovation-seeking, courage, and curiosity parts of the scale. Self-regulated learning levels and motivation also climbed after the course. Several threads linked the two gains, with learning strategies tying positively to self-discipline by the end. Erden concludes that building the course around cooperative learning helped students grow both more creative and more independent as learners.
pmc-13313082:
This 2026 letter by Öztürk comments on a study of blood inflammation indices in thyroid nodules. The original paper compared three combined blood counts as clues to whether a nodule is cancerous. Öztürk praises the comparison but questions how the authors judged the indices' value for predicting outcomes. Simple correlation tests, he argues, cannot show independent predictive power.

He notes the study ran no receiver operating analyses and no adjusted regression models for outcomes such as spread to lymph nodes. His own study of 376 patients with thyroid cancer found one index did predict distant spread and high risk category independently. The monocyte count alone also tracked stage and spread. Öztürk concludes the indices may flag aggressive cancers rather than diagnose them, and the original null result may reflect method limits.
pmc-13313182:
Qiqi Xia and colleagues compare two strains of Japanese encephalitis virus in a 2026 study of why genotype V of the virus has come back. This type was last seen in the Muar strain in 1952 and then seemed to vanish for more than 50 years, while newer strains differ from Muar in their genes.

The team set the new XZ0934 strain against Muar in cultured cells and in mice. XZ0934 grew to higher levels, spread more in the blood, and killed more mice, showing it is both stronger and faster to copy itself. Changes in the tail end of its genome, the 3 prime untranslated region, reshaped folded parts of that tail and changed output of a short viral RNA. Those small changes help explain the sharper power of the returned strain.
pmc-13314582:
Hirotaka Tao offers a new frame for how chronic inflammation seeds early cancer, in a review from 2026. Long inflammation is known to feed tumors both by piling up mutations and by failing to rebuild tissue in neat three-dimensional order.

Most accounts treat scarring, failed repair, immune faults, and tissue disorder as parallel strands, Tao argues, without showing how they lock together across scales. His review pulls proof from inflammation, matrix biology, force sensing in tissues, tumor settings, and development. It names a shared layer: the mechanics of the extracellular matrix, the scaffold around cells. When that scaffold stiffens and warps, repair can stay busy while order keeps slipping, a failed morphogenesis that primes early tumors. The frame may guide new ways to stall cancer at its roots.
pmc-13314782:
Pia Ritter and colleagues read brainprints to spot broken language networks in tumor patients, in their 2026 study. Brain tumors often warp language wiring, but the warp differs from person to person, and group averages wash that out.

The team built a resting-state connectivity fingerprint for each person, a personal profile of language network links. They studied 27 right-handed patients with a left-side brain tumor near language areas, at three times: before surgery, right after, and three months on, as the design states. A healthy reference came from 30 people, whose prints stayed steady over time. Patient prints exposed odd links that group math would miss, and those prints were tied to language test scores. Personal maps could steer surgery and rehab for each patient.
pmc-13316082:
Courtney E Stewart and a large team ran a pilot trial in 2026 on a growth hormone releasing hormone analog. They asked whether it can aid thinking and brain wiring in adults, from normal cognition to mild impairment. Age-linked decline ties to a weaker hormone axis, and boosting growth hormone can help cognition, but direct effects of the releasing hormone were unproven.

Twenty-two adults took low-dose tesamorelin at 1 milligram or placebo for ten weeks in a double-blind design. Body makeup, fatigue, sleep, physical performance, glucose handling, cognition, and brain structure and connectivity were measured. Low-dose treatment showed no direct link with clear changes, and machine learning explored subtler patterns.
pmc-13316182:
Yifan Zhang and colleagues built a bone scaffold in 2026 inspired by liver cell exosomes, using liver-to-bone signaling to speed skull defect repair. Exosomes carry messages between tissues that keep the body in balance, and liver-derived vesicles strongly accelerated healing of critical cranial defects in their tests.

The vesicles were anchored with a polydopamine coating onto a printed scaffold of a polycaprolactone polymer and nano-hydroxyapatite. The scaffold boosted stem cell sticking and growth, while the vesicles raised vessel growth and bone differentiation. Gene sequencing showed the vesicles switch on the PI3K and AKT pathway in stem cells.
pmc-13316282:
Xueying Xu and a large team introduce in 2026 a mechano-immunotherapy idea, calming how macrophages sense stiffness to limit scar capsules around implants. The model drug RN-1734 blocks the TRPV4 sensing channel, and in dishes it cut calcium entry and inflammatory cytokine release from a macrophage line.

Effects depended strictly on context, working only on stiff gels at 10 percent weight per volume and not on softer 5 percent gels. In animals the drug eased capsule growth around rough electrospun scaffolds but not smooth hydrogels, even though hydrogels released about six times more drug.
pmc-13316782:
Johanna Klutmann and co-authors found a 2026 way to watch medical students think during a digital family medicine exam, capturing whether they reason forward from data or backward from answer choices. Seeing the process, not just the score, could sharpen teaching.

Fifth-year students in two exam rounds recorded their reasoning on extra research questions, giving 210 students in the large cohort. Forward reasoning appeared far more often than backward, and top scorers used both styles more than weak scorers. Feedback during learning did not shift the style choice, though follow-up questions might. The method offers schools a quality check on their questions and a window into skills that marks alone hide.
pmc-13317582:
Adjeng Pratiwi Djatmiko and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, healing plants of the Anak Dalam tribe of Jambi, Indonesia. They judge the plants' promise for diabetic wounds, which heal slowly, infect easily, and can end in amputation. The tribe's forest knowledge is deep but barely tested for this use.

Searching five databases for work from 2015 to 2025, the team examined 40 plants. Four stood out, including gotu kola, guava, and betel, with chemistry tied to wound closing steps such as fiber building, new vessel growth, and skin regrowth. Flavonoids and kindred compounds drove antioxidant, calming, and germ-fighting effects. Most proof, though, comes from dishes and animals, so the list is a candidate pool, not a verdict.
pmc-13317682:
Ashlyn Zebrowski and co-authors ran a 2026 randomized pilot on what helps people adopt virtual reality therapy, a digital treatment for anxiety, pain, and distress whose real-world uptake lags its promise. How a tool is introduced may matter as much as what it does.

Participants were split three ways: unguided use, self-guided use with support materials, or use backed by a prescriber consultation. Brief exposure lifted acceptance scores across all groups, though ratings stayed in the neutral band, marking early shifts rather than enthusiasm. Measures covered usability, faithfulness of use, and tolerance, with exit interviews adding color. Provider support shaped the early experience most. The pilot maps which supports deserve testing in a full clinical trial.
pmc-13318082:
Yun Zhang and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review, randomized trials of virtual reality therapy for thinking and mood in Parkinson's disease, an illness that dulls both as it progresses. Headset programs promise playful, repeatable training, yet trial verdicts have clashed.

Thirteen trials with 430 patients met the rules, mostly sound on randomization but shaky on blinding. Pooled results showed a moderate lift in overall thinking scores and a larger easing of depressive symptoms with VR care. The depression gain's forecast range crossed zero, warning that future settings may see less. Evidence grading tempers enthusiasm. VR looks promising for minds and moods, the authors conclude, but bigger, tighter trials must firm the claim.
pmc-13318882:
Tae Rim Kim and colleagues offer a 2026 narrative review comparing people who smoke regular cigarettes with people who vape. Quitting help may need to differ between the two groups. A planned search from 2010 to 2025 across four databases found 76 studies. Mindset, habits, and responses to help were compared.

Cigarette users showed stronger bodily withdrawal and automatic, learned habits. They did best with planned, high-intensity help mixing therapy and medicines. Vape users showed reward-driven use and lower felt risk. They engaged more with digital tools using games, peers, and flexible goals. The authors propose two playbooks: full quitting and relapse control for smokers, and stepwise digital plans for vapers. Matching by age and fitting health systems round out their plan.
pmc-13319082:
Anna Yu. Popova leads a very large team reporting a 2026 blood-test survey of hepatitis B immunity in Belgrade, Serbia. Blood samples from 2,533 residents were tested in May 2024. Three markers split current infection, past exposure, and protective antibodies. Age and vaccination patterns were read alongside.

Current infection prevalence was low, at 1.0 percent overall in their results. Past exposure markers reached 8.7 percent, and protective antibodies reached 21.6 percent across the city. Infection markers climbed steeply with age, peaking in the over-70 group. Protection ran the other way, highest in young children. Vaccination coverage fell from 82.3 percent in minors to 4.6 percent among retirees in their figures. Few residents knew their own infection history. The authors urge adult screening and catch-up vaccination.
pmc-13319482:
Xiaoyan Zhang and co-authors follow teens over time in a 2026 study of hard childhood events and early body aging. Hard events in childhood have been tied to worse health in later life, but proof in the teen years is still thin. The team also asked whether race and sex change the picture when they are weighed together.

Records for 1655 young people came from a long running United States birth study, with hard events logged from ages 3 to 9. Spit samples at ages 9 and 15 gave gene based age scores. Two event patterns showed in each group, and one age score linked most clearly to those patterns. Girls in some groups showed older scores than boys.
pmc-13319882:
Jordan A Neely and co-authors argue for home town screening hubs in rural Kansas in a 2026 commentary on chronic disease and cancer. Rural areas carry heavier illness loads and higher death rates than cities, with long drives, few staff, and low income all blocking routine checks. Early spotting of disease is a proven way to cut that burden, yet rural uptake stays low.

Blood pressure checks are put forward as an easy front door, since one visit can open checks for heart, sugar, blood, and mood risks at once. Pairing simple tests with lab work and social support checks adds depth without a hospital trip. Town based drives could bring fair early care to places clinics barely reach.
pmc-13320182:
Samuel O Ajoseh and co-authors profile metabolism in lesser known Acinetobacter germs in a 2026 genome based study. The wider germ family thrives in many settings, resists drugs, and can cause harm, yet its side branches get far less study than its most feared member. Gene maps for 19 side branch isolates were used to forecast their chemical pathways.

A total of 104 pathways across 32 groups were forecast, and 96 ran in all isolates, covering core jobs such as protein building and energy making. Twenty pathways tied to harm and drug resistance, and most of those also ran in all isolates. One branch alone carried genes to make iron grabbing tools, a first report for that branch. The maps guide hunts for weak spots.
pmc-13320482:
Meziane Brizini and co-authors review recent care for the most common brain tumour in children in a 2026 article. These low-grade gliomas grow slowly and survival is high, yet tumours often need repeat treatment and can harm thinking and daily function over time. Care depends heavily on where the tumour sits.

Recent gains rest on gene testing that sorts tumours by growth signals, most often in the RAS and MAPK paths. That sorting guides drugs aimed at BRAF, MEK, and RAF targets for chosen patients. The review also covers spinal fluid tests, smart imaging, and checks of daily function. Open questions include how long targeted drugs should run and how to spread testing fairly.
pmc-13320582:
Duc Thanh Tran and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare bone lymphoma with a lasting break. Primary lymphoma of bone makes up only a small share of bone cancers, and the diffuse large B-cell type is the most common form. The patient was a 42-year-old man with disease in the upper arm bone near the shoulder.

Small biopsy samples first made the tumour hard to separate from other round cell cancers, until marker tests gave a firm answer. After chemo and radiation, the weakened bone broke and would not heal, badly limiting shoulder use. Surgeons rebuilt it with a reverse shoulder replacement plus the patient's own bone treated with liquid nitrogen, restoring limb function.
pmc-13321382:
Jiali Wang and co-authors study how storage humidity shapes strawberry aroma after harvest in a 2026 experiment. Berries lose water in storage, which can spoil scent and taste. Fruit was held for eight days at either high humidity, 90 percent, or low humidity, 45 percent, and scent compounds plus membrane fats were tracked.

Low humidity sped water loss and raised total scent compounds by about 17 percent, yet balance worsened rather than quality improving. Fresh green and floral notes fell, while fat derived scents built up, and a membrane damage marker rose by 43 percent under dry storage in the study. High humidity better kept aroma by limiting membrane oxidation.
pmc-13322882:
Han Wang and co-authors position periostin as a driver and marker in allergic rhinitis, in a 2026 review. Periostin sits downstream of interleukin-4 and interleukin-13, linking type 2 immune activity with lasting change in the nasal lining, a pattern that standard drugs do not always control.

According to the review, periostin weakens the surface barrier, draws in eosinophils and promotes fibrosis, feeding a cycle of inflammation and repair. Levels in varied samples track disease severity and response to steroids and biologic drugs. The authors propose grouping patients by periostin level to guide personal treatment, and they discuss direct targeting of periostin for hard-to-treat tissue change.
pmc-13322982:
Rauf A Salamzade, Lindsay R Kalan and Cameron R Currie link multicellular life in microbes to richer chemical output, in a 2026 study. Single-celled microbes that evolved to work as groups gained cell types with set roles. That step is tied to greater complexity in life.

Across bacteria and fungi, single-celled groups showed weak capacity for special compounds. Groups that gained multicellular growth, such as mycelium and fruiting body formers, showed large gains in that capacity. Those same groups also held more enzymes for breaking down plant sugars. The authors offer the pattern as a guide for hunting new drugs against resistant infections.
pmc-13323482:
Qin Hu, Hua Jin, Lan Hu and Xu Li review mitochondria along the gut-kidney axis, in a 2026 article on kidney health. Mitochondria run energy metabolism and signalling in gut and kidney cells, and gut microbes can shift their activity in both organs.

Healthy mitochondria guard the gut barrier, steer intestinal metabolism and keep microbial balance. Faults in their creation, movement, recycling and DNA feed kidney damage in chronic kidney disease, working through inflammation, oxidative stress and ferroptosis. Two-way traffic between gut and kidney mitochondria forms a loop the authors map in detail. Diet change, probiotics and faecal transplant are floated as non-drug ways to tune mitochondria and protect kidneys.
pmc-13323582:
Lisa Bearpark and co-authors compare life expectancy loss by sex after aortic valve surgery for infective endocarditis in Sweden, in a 2026 register study. Their cohort held 2,585 patients operated between 1997 and 2022, drawn from national registers including SWEDEHEART, with about a fifth women.

Women were older at surgery, carried more other conditions and had more added valve work than men, and died more often over a mean seven years of follow-up. Life expectancy loss hit the young hardest, reaching about fifteen years for a 50-year-old woman in their estimates. After standardisation, women showed higher net survival than men, a contrast the authors explore for care planning.
pmc-13323682:
Qiong Li and co-authors link an early pregnancy lipid index to preeclampsia in a 2026 multicentre cohort study. Their set held 2,162 patients with preeclampsia and 36,660 normal controls, with the atherogenic index measured before twenty weeks from triglycerides and HDL cholesterol.

Higher index quarters carried higher risks of preeclampsia and of gestational diabetes combined with preeclampsia after adjustment, though effects were modest. Each small step up in the index added a single-digit percentage to risk in the reported models, and the dose pattern curved rather than running straight. Age, body mass and parity did not change the link. The authors propose the cheap index as an early risk marker.
pmc-13325082:
Ketlyn P. da Motta and a large team test a selenium-bearing quinoline against cancer pain in mice in a 2026 animal study. Pain from tumor growth and from the chemotherapy drug vincristine often overlap and resist standard care.

Mice received Sarcoma 180 cells in a paw, with some also given vincristine over days 2 to 6. The compound, called 4-PSQ, was fed by mouth from days 8 to 17. Tumor and drug exposure caused pain sensitivity, swelling, and oxidative imbalance in tissues. Treatment eased the pain behavior, slowed tumor growth, and restored key ATPase enzyme activity. Tissue checks confirmed tumor mass and immune cell influx. The results back 4-PSQ as a possible add-on for cancer pain.
pmc-13325282:
Rudorwedu B Shanduka and colleagues review pairing bacteria-eating viruses with synbiotics as a swap for antibiotic growth promoters in poultry in a 2026 article. Misuse of those antibiotics bred resistant germs and left residues in food.

The team screened 152 studies from 2016 to 2025 through seven databases under PRISMA rules. Bacteriophages strike target germs while sparing helpful gut microbes, and synbiotics blend prebiotics with probiotics to aid gut function and immunity. Each works alone, yet almost no trials test them together in live birds. The authors call for animal validation, standard doses, and farm-scale trials before the pairing can be trusted at industry level.
pmc-13326782:
Eva Berg, Niels K.N. Focke, and Knut Brockmann ask how often childhood epilepsy hides behind a migraine label in a 2026 study. Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures, once called Panayiotopoulos syndrome, often brings headache that mimics migraine.

Charts and EEG records covered 186 children aged 3 to 14 referred for migraine or headache over two years. Clear epilepsy was confirmed in 6.5 percent, 12 children, helped by drug response. Another 23 children, 12.4 percent of the group, met the signs but never got seizure medicine. In all, 18.8 percent received a possible to definite epilepsy diagnosis. Missed recognition during visits explained most gaps.
pmc-13327882:
Juri Backes and co-authors blend machine learning with a body-network model to forecast sepsis in a 2026 study. Sepsis is hard to catch early, and pure data models forecast well but explain little, while mechanism models explain but lack clinical proof. Their Latent Dynamics Model couples oscillators standing for organs and immune cell groups.

Patient data are mapped into the model's low-dimensional settings, and learned paths through that space flag organs heading toward failure while staying readable to clinicians. Trained on real intensive care records from the MIMIC-IV cohort, the hybrid reached competitive scores against standard measures. The learned paths showed believable patterns of decline, recovery, and stability, offering forecasts with a story attached.
pmc-13328182:
Lingli Ma and co-authors review PANoptosis in diabetic retinopathy in a 2026 article. PANoptosis fuses three cell death programs, apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis, into one inflammatory route that may drive diabetic retinal damage. Evidence spans patient samples, diabetic animals, and high-sugar cell cultures, with uneven strength.

The authors map the PANoptosome signal networks, non-coding RNA control, and immune-metabolic cross-talk, and weigh candidate markers from gene signatures to death molecules. Treatments range from small-molecule blockers to gene tools and nano-delivery, yet blocking the pathway everywhere could weaken host defense and retinal immunity. Marker-guided, eye-local, stage-timed dosing is their recommended path over blanket suppression.
pmc-13328282:
Sultanah Alsudays reviews the dimensions of employee AI anxiety in a 2026 systematic review. As workplaces adopt artificial intelligence, worry about it has grown into a research field of its own. Following structured review guidance, Alsudays sorts prior work by theory, setting, traits, and method.

Conservation of Resources and Social Cognitive Theory anchored most studies, which clustered in China and Türkiye and in healthcare settings. General AI anxiety drew the bulk of attention, while narrower worries, about job replacement, ethics, learning, group effects, and system setup, stayed underexplored. Regression was the standard tool. Sharper dimensions and wider settings would give managers a truer map of workforce unease.
pmc-13328782:
Yu-Mi Kim and colleagues compare ballet training with weight-bearing exercise in a 2026 trial with women who have obesity. Twenty-three women were split into a control group of 7, a ballet group of 10, and a weight-bearing group of 6. Both training groups met for 60 minutes three times a week, with effort rising over time.

Only the ballet group lost clear amounts of weight and body fat, while muscle mass stayed steady in all groups. Both training groups gained back strength, flexibility, and left-side balance. Ballet alone also lifted sit-up results and right-side balance. Knee strength and stamina improved in both groups at the two test speeds used. The authors suggest ballet can match standard training for leg function.
pmc-13329482:
Martin Hausberg, Gert Gabriëls, and Helmut Hopfer comment in 2026 on a study of nerve regrowth in transplanted kidneys. The study by Ohki and co-authors, as framed in the comment, used repeat graft biopsies from 50 living donor recipients at three points: 3 months, 1 year, and 3 years. Staining for a nerve marker tracked whether sympathetic nerves returned to the graft.

The comment calls the design novel but urges caution. Many grafts could not be read cleanly under the plan, since staining stayed positive from the start in nearly half the group. Grafts with regained staining leaned toward higher blood pressure, more blood pressure drugs, and more scarring. Yet grafts positive throughout looked alike, so a firm causal claim is not yet earned, the authors argue.
pmc-13330682:
Alejandro Martínez Pradeda and colleagues describe a digital monitoring system for blood cancer care in a 2026 article. The SiMON-PRO-Hematology platform was built by pharmacists, blood specialists, nurses, and software engineers. It aims to track drug care and patient-reported outcomes together, since standard follow-up often misses how patients feel.

Patients fill outcome forms on tablets by themselves. Responses join clinical and lab data inside the system, firing live alerts and guiding structured pharmacist actions. Analysis tools track change over time, adherence, and group comparisons. Work spans care, management, and research areas. No new patient data were gathered for the design report. The authors claim less duplicate paperwork and faster safety spotting.
pmc-13331282:
Yuki Numata and colleagues report emergency clip repair of a mitral valve during aortic valve implant in a 2026 case. A 78-year-old woman with tight aortic narrowing had transfemoral implant surgery. Right after balloon widening, her circulation collapsed and heart-lung support began. Scans showed the front mitral leaflet sucked forward, causing severe leakage without clear outflow block.

The aortic valve was placed, yet severe leakage and instability held. Drugs failed to settle her state. Clip repair through a catheter followed 3 days later as a bailout. Leakage fell from severe to mild and stability returned fast. She left hospital in the best symptom class and stayed well at 6 months.
pmc-13332982:
Sanjana Singarayer and colleagues lay out a framework in 2026 for standardizing the side-effect playbooks that accompany cancer drug trials. For new products, toxicity management guidelines sit beside the trial protocol and tell sites how to adjust doses and treat harms early, but each trial has tended to write its own.

The framework was developed across AstraZeneca's antibody-drug conjugate portfolio. It runs in three stages: gather information from internal files and published labels, compare products side by side, then write conservative guidance that avoids brand framing. Antibody-drug conjugates, a fast-growing class, serve as the test case, turning varied advice into clear action steps for key risks. The authors build in room for patient and setting differences, routes for justified departures, and periodic updates, and argue the model can extend to other drug types and disease areas.
pmc-13333282:
Mulu Bayray Kahsay and Natasa Nord present three years of paired solar and power data from a zero emission building laboratory in Trondheim, Norway, in a 2026 dataset paper. High-latitude sites face low sun angles, snow, and long dark winters, making them a hard test for building-integrated solar panels.

Hourly records for 2023, 2024, and 2025 pair incoming solar radiation with photovoltaic output. The panels face north, east, west, and south, plus a pergola tilted at 60 degrees and a roof at 30 degrees. Radiation came from class C pyranometers and output from current and voltage readings across three inverters, filtered and reorganized into yearly tables. The authors say the synchronized data can validate solar models, benchmark forecasting methods, and reveal year-to-year swings and slow performance decay. The dataset is openly posted on Mendeley Data.
pmc-13333782:
Alessandro L. Colosio and co-authors measured how exercise intensity affects the repeatability of breathing gas measurements in a 2026 cycling study. Labs rely on oxygen uptake and related values, so knowing when those numbers wobble matters.

Forty-two healthy adults completed a ramp test plus six steady cycling trials spread over moderate, heavy, and severe intensity domains, each lasting six minutes. Two metabolic carts recorded oxygen uptake, carbon dioxide output, and ventilation. Values rose with intensity but did not drift between days. Variability shrank as work hardened, dropping below 5 percent for oxygen and carbon dioxide measures in the severe domain, and reliability coefficients were excellent. The domain-specific benchmarks help researchers judge real change against measurement noise.
pmc-13336382:
Panfeng Zhao and co-authors looked at biodegradable zinc implants in a 2026 article tracking the field toward clinical use. Implants that dissolve safely after healing would spare patients removal surgery, and zinc offers a friendly breakdown profile among metals.

The review covers zinc's body roles, current implant systems, and applicable standards. To fix corrosion speed, antibacterial performance, and compatibility, researchers alloy zinc with magnesium, manganese, or lithium, modify surfaces, and add working coatings. The authors survey how breakdown is tested in dishes and animals, sum up preclinical results and the state of clinical trials, and collect regulatory requirements from home and foreign authorities. They close with the mechanism and translation bottlenecks that still block routine adoption.
pmc-13336482:
Shiru Jiang and co-authors etched random gold mazes with femtosecond lasers to make encryption hardware that stores no keys in a 2026 study. Physical unclonable functions promise hardware-level security, but shrinking them raises the cost of reading and storing their responses.

Laser-driven plasmonic heating and Marangoni convection scramble gold near-percolation films into maze patterns no one can copy. The mazes serve as two independent unclonable functions at once, one optical and one electrical. Because the microscale wiring carries nanoscale detail, responses can be captured on site and keys generated in real time during encryption, so nothing secret sits in memory. The team demonstrated the storage-free process on an integrated circuit platform, sketching a shift toward on-demand security.
pmc-13336982:
Dongyu Bai, Ri He, Junxian Liu, and Liangzhi Kou survey machine-learning molecular dynamics for ferroelectric materials in a 2026 perspective. These materials hold a switchable electric polarization behind memories, sensors, and brain-like chips. How their polarization flips and domains move at atomic scale decides how well devices work.

First-principles methods are accurate but too slow and small for real dynamics. Learned force fields carry near-quantum accuracy into large, long simulations of switching, domain birth and motion, and twisted polar textures. The authors flag hard problems: long-range electric forces, coupled spin and lattice motion, and training data hunger. New long-range-aware and spin-aware models plus large pre-training could make the method truly predictive for device design.
pmc-13337082:
Samadhi Kulasooriya and co-authors chart how balance-sensing hair cells age in a 2026 mouse study. Age-related vestibular decline troubles many older people, but its molecular roots were vague. Single-cell gene profiling of young and old mice showed old vestibular hair cells carrying classic aging marks: senescence, failing power units, and sloppy protein upkeep.

Imaging and electrical recordings matched the gene story: hair bundles decayed and sensing activity fell before the cells themselves died. Bundle failure thus looks like an early driver, not a late symptom. Comparing ear regions revealed shared and distinct aging signatures between balance and hearing cells. The map may guide treatments that protect bundles and preserve balance in later life.
pmc-13337382:
Olle Ringden and colleagues follow three pancreatic cancer survivors for up to two decades in a 2026 report. Pancreatic ductal cancer rarely allows long survival. Eight patients originally had radical Whipple surgery with no distant spread; two received donor stem cell transplants in an earlier trial, and the six untreated controls died within one to four years.

A third transplant patient, a 60-year-old man treated elsewhere, joins this follow-up. One survivor remains alive 21 years after diagnosis with no recurrence, despite later oral cancer surgery. Another died of esophageal cancer 19 years out, and the third stays cancer-free at 15 years after graft rejection and further surgery. The authors suggest donor cell therapy may add anticancer effects worth testing.
pmc-13337782:
Xuanrong Zheng and colleagues trace genes behind curled leaves in a wild strawberry in a 2026 study. Moderate curling can be a useful breeding trait. A curled mutant of Fragaria nilgerrensis came from a chemical mutation library, but its control network was unknown.

Cell wall features and gene activity were compared between mutant and normal plants. A gene called FnFLA16 changed cellulose-related traits and promoted curling when tested. A second gene, FnWRKY17, was shown to bind directly to the FnFLA16 promoter in yeast and reporter assays. Together they form a control pair that explains the curled shape and offers a breeding target.
pmc-13337882:
Won Fen Wong introduces a 2026 editorial collection on how viruses dodge host defenses. RNA and DNA viruses have evolved ways to blunt sensing, alter immune cells, and reshape tissues so infection persists. Lasting infection is framed as an immune disease as much as an infectious one.

Examples range from SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A to HIV-1 and human papillomavirus. Even with better drugs and vaccines, evasion still limits lasting protection. The collection gathers work on innate sensing blocks, signaling changes, and tissue shifts that drive chronic illness. Understanding those tricks is presented as key to stronger antivirals and vaccines that hold up over time.
pmc-13341182:
Stopping thyroid hormone tablets safely is the theme of a 2026 letter by Sun Wook Cho, who adds iodine exposure as a missing piece. About one-quarter of patients in recent studies manage to discontinue levothyroxine, especially those on lower doses with lower starting TSH and shorter treatment.

Cho argues these patterns point to thyroids with preserved reserve rather than permanent failure, and notes subclinical hypothyroidism often normalizes on its own in older adults. Population iodine intake could quietly suppress gland function and later allow recovery. Framing deprescribing this way may help doctors pick candidates whose hormone therapy was never truly permanent.
pmc-13342182:
A decade of research on pyruvate kinase deficiency is charted by Wanyi Zhao's team in their 2026 bibliometric analysis. The inherited enzyme defect is the top cause of congenital non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia, and records from 2015 to 2025 were mapped with network tools.

Screening distilled 90 core papers from 649 records, with an extra PubMed check adding 15 matching items. Themes visibly migrated from genotype cataloguing toward PKR activators such as mitapivat and preclinical gene editing. The authors cross-checked across databases to guard against selection bias, finding a field pivoting from description to targeted therapy.
pmc-13342482:
Lelou and colleagues investigated in 2026 how stress hormones called catecholamines, the family that includes adrenaline, act on liver cancer cells. Nerves of the sympathetic system, the body's fight-or-flight wiring, reach into liver tumors, but their direct effect on tumor cells was unclear. The team mapped nerve fibers in ten human tumor samples and tested the hormones on liver cell lines and on primary human liver cells.

Dense, twisted sympathetic fibers crowded the non-tumor tissue at the tumor's invasion front. Mature liver-like tumor cells carried both receptor types for these hormones and broke the hormones down into known waste products. Exposure switched on inflammation, growth, and tissue-remodeling programs tied to loss of mature identity and to a shift that helps cells spread. The same program marked aggressive tumor subtypes with poor outlook. The authors suggest blocking this nerve signal as a new treatment angle.
pmc-13346082:
Yongda Yue and co-authors test adding a circulation drug to keyhole spine surgery for narrowed lumbar canals in 2026. Patients received either two-portal endoscopic decompression alone or the surgery plus limaprost, a prostaglandin drug, with pain, disability, and function tracked for six months across five visits.

The drug group beat surgery alone on pain scores, disability, Japanese Orthopaedic scores, muscle strength, and overall outcome grades, though canal width measures never budged. Pain relief peaked strongest at one month and nerve recovery at three months. Patients aged 65 or older, leaner patients, and those with central-type narrowing benefited most. The pairing offers a practical add-on for the right stenosis profile.
pmc-13347082:
Qingjia Zeng and a large team build models to predict quick hospital arrival after stroke, in a multicentre study from China issued in 2026. Records for 1,327 patients from six hospitals were split by time, training on 2019 to 2022 cases and testing on 2023 to 2025 cases. Early arrival meant arrival within 24 hours of symptom onset.

Six model types were compared, and a multilayer perceptron did best on the later test set, reaching an AUC value of 0.9020 with a sensitivity of 91.5 percent in the reported run. Explanation tools showed which record features pushed each prediction. Testing on later years, rather than a random split, gives a tougher check on real clinic use.
pmc-13349782:
Malek Marian and co-authors reported a plant study in 2026 on cold-tolerant bacteria taken from alpine rose-family plants. They tested whether two such bacteria could change how apple and strawberry plantlets respond to freezing.

Plantlets received either a control solution or one bacterium each, Pseudomonas GRAN103 for apple and Duganella ALCN104 for strawberry, then faced normal warmth or three hours at about minus 6 degrees. Treated plantlets leaked fewer electrolytes under freezing, a sign of less cell damage. Gene activity patterns under cold differed between treated and untreated plants and between the two crops. The work hints that helpful microbes might raise frost tolerance in fruit growing.
pmc-13349882:
Manuel Panzardi and a large team ran a pilot study in 2026 on delivering diabetes self-management education by video in two health systems. Adults with type 2 diabetes, high blood sugar readings, and at least one heart-related condition were invited to six monthly online group sessions.

Sessions led by diabetes educators covered the disease, daily habits, peer support, and goal setting, in both a community health centre and a private nonprofit system. The team measured recruitment, attendance, and engagement, and interviewed patients, providers, and staff about benefits and barriers. Group education works in person, but moving it online fairly across very different systems needs practical testing like this.
pmc-13350482:
Dmitrijs Rots and a large team reported a child in 2026 whose case may define a new inherited brain development syndrome tied to the EHMT2 gene. The boy had global developmental delay, autism, low muscle tone, distinctive features, a brain malformation, heart disease, and other birth differences.

Genome sequencing of the child and parents found he carried two changed copies affecting EHMT2, a gene whose partner gene is already known to cause Kleefstra syndrome. A handful of earlier patients with single changed copies showed overlapping features and chemical marks on DNA. Adding a recessive case sharpens the argument that this gene belongs on diagnostic lists.
pmc-13351682:
Jiayuan Liu, Xiangying You, and Yuyao Huang pool evidence in 2026 on breathing problems in long-term survivors of childhood and teen cancer. Better survival has grown the survivor group, yet late lung harm is poorly counted. Seven databases were searched to December 30, 2025 for studies of 5-year survivors diagnosed before age 21.

Eleven studies with 128,509 survivors were included, and study quality was mostly high. Pooled share with any breathing complication was 35 percent, though results varied greatly between studies. Reduced forced vital capacity affected 19 percent. The authors also sort risk factors linked to higher rates, giving follow-up teams a clearer sense of how common late lung problems are.
pmc-13351882:
Koichi Takaishi and co-authors study mental blocks that stop bystanders from using a defibrillator in 2026. Early shock delivery greatly improves survival after cardiac arrest outside hospital, yet devices often sit unused. Survey answers from a simulated arrest linked empathy traits to willingness to act.

Willingness peaked for rushing over to the person and for phoning for aid, and bottomed out for using a defibrillator. Caring concern about others linked to greater willingness for every rescue step. Seeing another person's view linked to willingness to fetch and use the device. Personal distress linked to lower willingness for device steps. Results point to training that builds confidence, not just device access.
pmc-13354282:
Norman-Vivaldi Montúffar-Otero leads a 2026 bibliometric study of the most-cited work joining swallowing disorders and cognitive impairment. The two problems overlap often in older adults and in brain disease, yet the field's structure was unmapped. Scopus was searched through October 10, 2025, retrieving 1,190 records, and the 100 most-cited papers were charted in depth.

The top set spans 2009 to 2022, since newer papers lack time to gather citations, and totals 30,872 citations. Tiers split into 11 hyperclassics above 500 citations, 20 top-class papers, and 69 classics. Stroke led the topic mix. Analysis in R with bibliometrix tools mapped performance, collaboration, and journal links across the corpus.
pmc-13356582:
Glenn Briffa and co-authors review in 2026 how to spot and treat complex regional pain syndrome early after a wrist fracture. This chronic pain disorder can follow a broken distal radius and cause long disability, yet its signs overlap with normal healing. The team searched two databases for studies from 2000 to 2026 and kept 26.

Signs of the syndrome can arise early, though formal diagnosis often lags by weeks or months. Strong early pain, heightened pain sensitivity, female sex, older age, and low vitamin D raised risk. Early movement and planned rehab linked to better function. Imaging was weak for early diagnosis, making repeated clinical checks the key tool, the authors say.
pmc-13357082:
Weifei Liang and co-authors built in 2026 a survival prediction model for liver cancer based on mitochondrial function, the cell's energy system. Liver cancer outcomes vary widely, and faulty mitochondria help drive it, yet their predictive value was unclear. Using gene data from 370 patients, they grouped tumors by energy-pathway patterns and built an eight-gene scoring model, then tested one key gene in cells and mice.

Three tumor subtypes emerged with distinct energy and immune profiles. The model predicted one-, three-, and five-year survival well and beat standard staging. One gene, MRPS15, proved to fuel tumor growth by sustaining energy output, making it a candidate target.
pmc-13358582:
Jingsi Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study on a little-known gene in lung adenocarcinoma. The gene, C1ORF112, helps cells copy and repair DNA. The team found it runs high in these tumors and links to shorter survival. They traced how a switch protein called E2F8 turns the gene on.

Using patient data, single-cell maps, lab tests, and mouse models, they showed the gene helps tumors grow and spread. Turning it down weakened the cancer cells. Work like this matters because this lung cancer still resists many drugs. A gene that drives growth and can be measured may serve as both a warning sign and a drug target.
pmc-13358682:
Arens and co-authors improve a fast way to test how plants handle drought in a 2026 study. When water runs short, air bubbles can block the water pipes inside a plant, a failure called embolism. Knowing how much dryness a plant can bear before its pipes fail is key to forecasting drought deaths. The team refined a method that uses air pressure to chart that limit.

They tested three South African plants with very different builds: two shrubs and a reed-like grass. For the grass they found a gentle way to track water stress without cutting the plant. A cheaper, faster test that works across plant types could widen drought research worldwide.
pmc-13361682:
Areeb Ansari and co-authors review artificial intelligence in vascular surgery in a 2026 paper. AI is entering this field fast, above all in reading vessel scans, planning operations, guiding tools during procedures, and watching patients afterward. The team searched PubMed and Scopus for studies joining AI with diagnosis or treatment in vessel care. They also checked the reference lists of the papers they kept.

The review weighs how AI sharpens diagnostic precision, speeds workflow, and may improve patient outcomes. New uses include smoother operating room flow, navigation help inside vessels, training platforms for surgeons, and decision support at the bedside. The authors balance the promise against the proof, mapping where AI already earns its place and where claims run ahead of evidence.
pmc-13361782:
Mollie VanNatta Day and co-authors studied kidney harm from a common antibiotic pair in a 2026 paper. Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam is a workhorse duo for serious infections, but whether the pair itself injures kidneys has been hotly debated. The team reviewed adults at their academic hospital who got both drugs for at least 48 hours between May 2019 and March 2023. In all, 350 patients qualified.

Kidney injury struck 89 patients, about a quarter of the group. The team compared those harmed with those spared across many traits: other kidney-stressing drugs, infection site, blood pressure support, treatment length, and drug levels in blood. pmc-13408982:

pmc-13415282:

pmc-13415482:

pmc-13419082:

pmc-13427082:

pmc-13433582:

pmc-13434282:

pmc-13434382:
