Activity jumped 223 fold over plain ruthenium oxide, while life grew a thousand fold by one key count. A full cell ran past 1,000 hours at plant level current. Precious metal use fell by four fifths.
pmc-13435982:
Aach and colleagues published in 2026 the protocol for a German multicenter trial testing whether exoskeleton-based feedback therapy beats conventional therapy for walking after chronic spinal cord injury. The trial enrolls patients who keep some leg movement despite a long-standing injury. Robotic assistance may retrain walking in ways standard physiotherapy cannot, but proof against an active control has been missing.

One hundred eighty patients across eight injury centers and fifteen rehabilitation centers will be assigned at random, half to Hybrid Assistive Limb therapy and half to usual care. Both arms train sixty minutes, five times a week, for twelve weeks. Success means a clear gain on at least one of three walking measures, scored by assessors who do not know the assignments. Quality of life, pain, and bladder function are also tracked to six months.
pmc-13436682:
Quy Quoc Tran and coauthors report a 60 year old woman whose heart attack masked a body wide clot storm in 2026. Severe rheumatic mitral narrowing plus atrial fibrillation and patchy blood thinning set the stage. She arrived in shock with ST elevation on her heart trace.

Heart imaging showed clot blocks in several small branches with clean artery walls. Suction cleared flow, yet shock, kidney failure, and leg ischemia deepened. Body scans then found clots in gut, spleen, kidney, and leg arteries. She died of multiorgan failure despite care. Heart attacks from clots warrant whole body checks when decline persists.
pmc-13437182:
Behrad Yadolahi, Mehdi Taghian, and Leyli Sadri reviewed new fiber-based systems that deliver drugs straight to diseased gums and mouth lining. Their 2026 systematic review searched five databases for English studies from 2015 to 2025 and kept eight papers, half original studies and half reviews. The carriers were mostly electrospun fibers, thin strands spun from polymers, or sticky patches that cling to wet tissue.

Spinning reliably produced even, porous mats with fibers about 250 to 500 nanometers wide, the review reports. Loads such as doxycycline, curcumin, and neem extract leaked out slowly, over hours or up to a week. The mats stuck firmly, lowered several inflammation markers, and killed up to 98 percent of target bacteria, with no sign of irritation. Yet methods varied widely between studies, and bias risk was rated moderate. The authors ask for shared making rules and long-term stability tests before clinic use.
pmc-13437282:
Mark Windheim and Khadija Aichane-Simon review a viral protein that human adenoviruses use to quiet the immune system. Species D, the largest group, alone carries a protein called E3/49K. Their 2026 review explains how this protein targets CD45, a switch on white blood cells that helps control their activation.

The protein sits in the cell surface and also sheds a soluble piece, the only secreted protein known from these viruses. Both forms grip CD45 tightly, force it to pair up, and block its normal enzyme action. That grip dampens T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells at once. The authors link this trick to how these viruses adapt and persist in people. They also raise a hopeful flip side: a tool this precise at calming immunity might one day serve medicine against unwanted immune attack or in cancer care.
pmc-13437482:
Zhi-Lie Cao and co-authors rework the story of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, a rare inherited condition bringing skin bumps, lung cysts, and kidney tumors. Faults in the FLCN gene cause it, and textbooks long classed it among disorders of runaway mTORC1 signaling. New structural and gene-wide studies, reviewed in 2026, show the gene's product instead steers that switch selectively, choosing which targets it may reach.

Losing both copies in kidney cells locks growth factors in the cell core and rewires fuel use, driving tumors. Losing one copy is enough to weaken lung and skin structure, without the full tumor program. This lens settles an old paradox about signals seeming both too high and too low. The authors point to fresh therapy targets, aimed at the trapped growth factors and rewired enzymes. Their pitch is organ-specific precision care.
pmc-13438882:
Chaves and colleagues evaluate a hypertension control program in a large South Florida health system in this 2026 longitudinal study. Leon Medical Centers serves Medicare beneficiaries who are overwhelmingly of Hispanic origin, a population in which program effects were little studied. The system launched a multicomponent program in 2011 with team-based care, standardized measurement, pharmacy and transport support, and culturally tailored engagement, and the team tracked control rates through 2018.

The patient sample grew as the program matured. It rose from 4,710 to 21,540 people in total. Average age rose too, from about 73 to about 77 years. After full implementation, the adjusted odds of controlled blood pressure were about five to six times higher than before. Crude control rates reached roughly ninety percent using time-averaged readings, while single-visit readings consistently underestimated control and agreed only fairly with the averaged measure.
pmc-13439182:
Maélie Caussé and co-authors report a hydrogen-rich compound that survives the trip back to normal pressure, in 2026 work on hydride chemistry. Squeezing hydrogen with metals past 100 gigapascals can form odd materials with rich hydrogen lattices, some prized as possible superconductors. Most fall apart once pressure drops. The team heated a hydrogen-loaded yttrium and iron mix in a diamond anvil cell, starting near 60 gigapascals.

Crystallography and computer searches mapped the new compound, Y3Fe4H20, built from iron and hydrogen units sharing edge atoms around yttrium centres. Brought back to room pressure, the material held its form for tens of hours before changing. Keeping such phases stable without pressure is a key step toward studying and using them in ordinary labs.
pmc-13440682:
Silva and colleagues report a 2026 study of voice and swallowing after total thyroid removal, surveyed in the late recovery period. Seventeen women, at least six months past surgery without node dissection or radiotherapy, completed two questionnaires. One covered thyroidectomy-related voice and throat symptoms, and one covered thyroid-related quality of life.

The median symptom score sat in a range showing persistent complaints for many women, and the team analyzed how voice and swallowing self-ratings relate to overall quality of life scores. Even without nerve injury or added treatments, patients report lasting changes in how the voice feels and how swallowing works, complaints clinics can dismiss as minor. Documenting them with validated instruments makes the case for routine late follow-up and speech therapy referral pathways after thyroid surgery, not only early wound checks.
pmc-13440782:
Naito and colleagues reported a 2026 MRI study on severe facial pain. Trigeminal neuralgia brings short, stabbing pain attacks on one side of the face. A blood vessel pressing the nerve explains many cases, but not all. The team asked whether skull shape itself raises the risk of pain.

They measured scans from 20 patients, 20 people with facial spasm, and 16 controls. Both pain and spasm groups had a shallower back skull space than controls. The gap between key nerves ran smaller in both patient groups as well. On the painful side, nerve spacing shrank further still in the pain group. A cramped skull space may set the stage for nerve trouble. Such measures may one day flag at-risk patients before pain begins.
pmc-13441982:
Jiangwei Yang and colleagues pool trials of acupoint stimulation added to standard care for obsessive-compulsive disorder, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Acupoint methods span needle acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and skin-surface electrical stimulation. Twenty-three randomised trials with 1,713 participants were gathered from seven databases to February 2026, with bias graded by standard Cochrane tools.

Adding it improved symptom scores clearly beyond control care on the standard Yale-Brown scale. Anxiety and global impression scores also moved favourably. The largest gains appeared where the method joined both medication and cognitive behavioural therapy together. Reported adverse events ran far fewer in treated groups than in medication controls. Subgroup hints pointed to point sets including PC6, a wrist point, and to twenty to forty sessions as favourable ranges, though those readings rest on few studies. The authors call the adjunct promising and comparatively gentle.
pmc-13442382:
Tania Sharmin and Colleen McDowell review two eye receptors, alpha4 and alpha9, in a 2026 paper on fluid pressure inside the eye. Each receptor pairs with a beta1 partner to form alpha4beta1 or alpha9beta1. Both sit in the meshwork and canal that drain fluid from the front of the eye.

The review sets out how these receptors link cells to the mesh around them and sense stretch and pull. It traces their contact with a fibronectin piece called FN+EDA, a contact that can raise drain blockage. Links with the TLR4 and TGF-beta paths also get close attention, since those links may drive scar-like change in the meshwork of eyes with glaucoma. The authors frame both receptors as fresh drug targets.
pmc-13442982:
Shen Ju Liang and colleagues report a 68-year-old woman with vessel inflammation plus two rare turns in a 2026 case paper. Her illness, microscopic polyangiitis, most often wounds kidneys and lungs. She came in short of breath at rest, with huge thirst and urine flow that pointed to a gland fault in her brain.

Blood tests showed a p-ANCA mark at a titer of 1 to 10 strength, plus myeloperoxidase antibodies. Brain scans confirmed gland injury, and steroid plus immune globulin care helped at first. One week in, a kidney artery balloon burst, and her blood count fell from 95 grams per liter to a low of 47 grams per liter. A dye-guided plug sealed the bleed, and she rallied well on strong drug pulses.
pmc-13444182:
Sou-Hyun Lee and Kyung-Hwa Kwak review how birth anesthesia shapes later mind health in mothers in a 2026 paper. Postpartum depression and trauma stress can dent mother-child bonds and life quality for years. Their review sweeps risk marks before birth, mode of birth, drug care, and long outcomes.

Full sleep anesthesia for cesarean birth tied to higher severe depression and self-harm risk in the pooled work. Epidural pain care, judged as a yes-no mark, showed no shield against either state. Relief quality, pain during surgery, failed spinal care, and forced switches to full sleep looked like the true levers. Ketamine drugs near birth may cut early depression risk, with long gains unproven. The authors urge trauma-aware talk as core care.
pmc-13444282:
Masayuki Endo and colleagues report two cases of coronary subclavian steal treated through vessel tools in a 2026 paper. The state starves the heart when a narrowed shoulder artery robs flow from a bypass graft. A 75-year-old man held a hard, chalky narrow spot in his left subclavian artery near its start.

Stepwise balloon widening, then a covered stent, fixed his flow. The twin case, an 83-year-old man, had a tight spot with slim room between two branch mouths, plus disease in both spine arteries. Balloons guarded both branches while the stent went in, which kept heart and brain flow safe. The authors tailor each plan to lump shape and branch maps, a rule they urge for this rare steal state.
pmc-13445382:
Wenyan Lu and colleagues design a new compound that hits two targets at once for Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 drug study. The starting drug blocked a family of enzymes that loosen gene control, and it also propped up a growth signal that fades in the Alzheimer brain. The team reshaped that drug to do both jobs more strongly.

Their lead compound, W2A-28, blocked only the first three enzymes of the family and spared the rest. In cells it raised the growth signal, and in lab tests it held up well in liver samples and crossed barriers with ease. In brain organoids grown from Alzheimer patients, it cut tau tangles and amyloid levels, which marks it as a candidate worth animal testing.
pmc-13445482:
Fatemeh Fereidooni and colleagues pool past studies on tranexamic acid, a drug that slows bleeding, given during bladder removal surgery, in a 2026 review. The surgery saves lives in bladder cancer yet often brings heavy blood loss and transfusions. Whether the drug helps here, and at what risk, stayed unsettled.

Four studies, one trial and three cohort studies, met the search rules, with sizes from sixty-four to nine hundred thirty-six patients. Those given the drug lost less blood and needed fewer transfusions, above all after surgery. No rise in vein clots appeared, and pooled results linked the drug to lower death rates after surgery. The small study count tempers the claim, so the authors frame the drug as promising.
pmc-13446182:
Caterina Benedetto and colleagues report a seventy-year-old man with a rare cancer of the tear gland, treated with limited surgery and carbon ion radiation, published in 2026. Tumors of this gland are very rare, and the standard path is wide removal that can cost the eye, followed by radiation. His tumor caused no symptoms and was found as a primary ductal adenocarcinoma.

Surgeons removed the growth with a careful, tissue-sparing operation, yet some disease stayed behind. Carbon ion treatment then cleared the tumor in full, with only mild side effects, since the heavy particles drop their dose with sharp precision. The case shows an eye-saving route for a cancer whose rarity leaves long-term odds murky, and it adds weight to particle therapy for orbital tumors.
pmc-13446482:
Barry L. Westcott reports the crystal structure of a cobalt salt built from a paired-ring ketone ligand, in a 2026 study. Two ligand molecules grip the cobalt ion through a ring nitrogen and the ketone oxygen, while two water molecules cap the top and bottom spots. The shape lands near a stretched octahedron, with the metal on a center of symmetry.

The salt matches copper and nickel cousins reported before, yet its water bonds run far shorter than the copper form, a gap chalked up to the copper ion's known distortion. Tetrafluoroborate anions take hydrogen bonds from the bound waters and stitch the units into layers, with weak extra contacts from the sulfur ring. The report completes a trio of like structures across three metals.
pmc-13447082:
Qi Li and colleagues review how a mother's high-fat diet in pregnancy may raise her child's later risk of Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 paper. The diet stokes low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress in the mother, which reshapes the womb through the placenta. The fetal midbrain cells that make dopamine, the very cells lost in Parkinson's, take selective harm.

Two paths reinforce each other in the account: a stuck-on insulin resistance and inflammation axis, and a choked clean-up system for worn cell power plants. Together they leave dopamine cells with thin reserves for adult life. The authors gather early warning marks across inflammation, clean-up molecules, gene tags, and diet records, and they weigh food, anti-inflammatory, and clean-up boosting plans for prevention.
pmc-13447182:
Dae Young Cheon writes in 2026 about what blood pressure patterns at hospital discharge may reveal after a heart failure flare. The two to three months after discharge carry high risks of death and return to hospital, yet few tools flag who is most at risk at that moment. A study discussed here measured pressure over a full day just before patients went home.

In three hundred patients, unusual night-time patterns, where pressure rose or fell too far, linked to worse short-term outcomes. Higher swing in pressure across the day seemed to reflect illness severity rather than add risk on its own. Cheon frames discharge monitoring as a snapshot of nerve and hormone strain at a fragile handover point. That reading may help teams target closer follow-up where it matters most.
pmc-13447282:
Lulu Xie and co-authors test how shade and soil pathogens together shape Korean pine seedlings in a 2026 controlled experiment. Young pines struggle to establish under dense forest canopy in northeast China. Low light and rising soil disease pressure both threaten survival, yet their combined effect on root choices was unclear.

Seedlings grew under three light levels and four pathogen doses, with survival, growth and leaf and root traits measured. Shade alone cut survival, growth, photosynthesis and plant mass, while high pathogen doses deepened the harm and sharply raised deaths. Leaves responded to light only, growing thinner and richer in nitrogen under shade. Roots shifted strategy under pathogen pressure, moving from thin, gathering roots toward thicker roots richer in defensive chemicals, a trade-off the authors link to forest renewal.
pmc-13448282:
Chung and colleagues are tracing how T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer, enters the central nervous system. Their 2026 laboratory report focuses on the meninges, the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, where this leukemia often settles. Current prevention uses chemotherapy injected into the spinal fluid, which can harm children's developing brains, so a targeted alternative matters.

Chung used a mouse leukemia driven by the NOTCH1 gene and found leukemia cells clustering early under the back of the skull. That spot is rich in bone marrow and tiny channels linking marrow to the meninges. With advanced microscopy, the team is testing whether cells travel through those channels. They are also testing whether a signal chemical called CXCL12, made by meningeal support cells, guides them via its receptor CXCR4. Blocking that route could one day limit brain spread without blanket chemotherapy.
pmc-13448782:
Hamed Al Ahbabi and colleagues report in 2026 a survey from the United Arab Emirates that ranks which childhood illnesses medical students must see during their pediatrics rotation. Students who had finished the rotation and doctors who teach it rated 81 illnesses grouped under common presenting complaints. Each illness was scored on a five-point scale, from must see to must not see.

Forty-nine usable replies came back, 39 from students and 10 from faculty or physicians. Asthma, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, gastroenteritis, iron deficiency anemia, febrile seizure, and heart murmur topped the shared list. Student and teacher rankings agreed closely, with a correlation of 0.863 across illnesses. A reliability analysis found that just ten student raters would suffice to keep such curriculum monitoring dependable over time.
pmc-13449782:
Hong-Yu Wu and colleagues test in 2026 whether the well-known Alzheimer gene APOE changes how strongly high blood pressure predicts the disease. Their data come from 318,923 UK Biobank participants free of dementia at entry, followed a median of thirteen years, with blood protein profiles for 34,141 of them across 2,790 proteins. Models accounted for the competing risk of death.

Hypertension interacted significantly with the APOE ε4 variant, yet the surprise lay in the ordering. The blood pressure association ran strongest in carriers of the normally protective ε2 form, at a hazard ratio of 1.570, then ε33 carriers at 1.213, then ε4 carriers at 1.129. In the ε2 group, two proteins, prosaposin and a ganglioside activator, statistically carried about ten and three percent of the link, both tied to fat metabolism in lysosomes. The authors call the protein clues exploratory.
pmc-13450482:
Batenkova and colleagues showed in 2026 how to coat surfaces with copper oxide nanoparticles, tiny grains used in sensors and catalysts, without any soap-like stabilizers. Electrophoretic deposition, which uses an electric field to pull charged particles onto a surface, is cheap and fast, but dirty particle surfaces make coatings uneven. The team cleaned the grains with mild washing and heating in oxygen or ozone gas.

Two lab methods, one using X-rays and one using antimatter particles that reveal missing atoms, confirmed the cleaning cut surface defects such as single missing atoms and small clusters of them. Cleaner grains carried a far stronger electric charge in ethanol, past the level that keeps suspensions stable, so they moved fast and packed evenly even at high loading. The result was uniform porous coatings free of organic residue, a greener route that works whatever the powder's past handling.
pmc-13450582:
Sakshi Chopra and co-authors tell in 2026 of a cancer drug side effect that looked like a severe drug allergy. The drug, blinatumomab, links immune killer cells to leukemia cells and is used for a blood cancer of B cells. That strong immune wake-up can flood the body with signals that cause fever, rash, and organ strain.

Their patient, a woman aged 65 with the leukemia, grew a syndrome of swelling, rash, and high counts of a white cell type tied to allergy. Those signs match a named allergy pattern called DRESS, yet here the cause was the immune flood itself. Oral steroids settled the episode fast, and the case urges care teams to sort look-alike reactions before changing cancer care.
pmc-13451082:
Katarzyna Nowak, Ashley Elliott, and Michelle McHenry report in 2026 on a plan to steady ultrasound training for joint-care trainees in Northern Ireland. Joint ultrasound is now a daily tool, yet no shared national training path exists in the United Kingdom. Their team first surveyed local trainees on practice, oversight, record keeping, and paths to formal proof of skill.

Most trainees scanned a few times a week, yet oversight varied and only one kept a planned logbook. The team built a logbook tied to European skill levels and launched it at a teaching day, with a bingo game to spur interest. The pack aims to give each trainee a clear road to formal qualification.
pmc-13451282:
Kardelen Akar and co-authors find in 2026 that a no-cost balance test spots early nerve decline in multiple sclerosis better than a timed walk. Strong new drugs leave many patients with low disability scores, so clinics need sharper tools for faint loss. The team ran ten balance tasks with motion sensors on 71 patients and 45 matched healthy peers.

Standing on one leg with eyes shut split early-stage patients from healthy peers, while the timed walk did not. Only a fifth of early patients held the pose for thirty seconds, versus over two thirds of healthy peers. A combined score with two standard hand and walk tests did even better, and a fresh group confirmed the result.
pmc-13451382:
Elbashir and Nour surveyed 261 children aged 5 to 16 in a canal-watered village of Gezira State, Sudan. They checked for urogenital schistosomiasis, the worm infection spread through contact with worm-bearing canal water. Urine was spun down and checked under the microscope for Schistosoma haematobium eggs in this one-time survey.

The overall share reached 44 percent, with 115 of 261 children infected at the time of the survey in the village. Most infections, 102 of the 115, were light by egg-count class used. The sex split was extreme. Boys made up 96.5 percent of infections and girls only 3.5 percent among positive cases found. Frequent canal contact for swimming, bathing, washing, and watering animals was strongly linked with infection. Tap water supplied drinking needs. The authors call for ongoing treatment rounds, health teaching, and sanitation upgrades.
pmc-13451582:
Michelangelo Sartori and co-authors pilot in 2026 a home pump for a blood-flow drug in patients with limbs at risk and no path to vessel repair. The drug, iloprost, ran slowly through a small squeeze pump at home for a year, and its record was set against a hospital group that got faster drips. Side effects were the main score, with death and major limb loss tracked over three years.

Side effects hit about a seventh of the home group, versus near a third of the hospital group. Deaths and major limb losses also ran lower at home, though the groups differed in age and were not a clean match. The authors call the home route better tolerated and ask for firmer trials.
pmc-13451782:
Lu and Chong pilot a mind and behavior program for the persistent tiredness that follows colorectal cancer treatment, known as cancer related fatigue. Their 2026 trial assigned 50 patients who had finished treatment to six weeks of the program or to usual care. The team tracked whether a full trial could run well, checking sign up, attendance, and drop out rates, plus patient satisfaction through surveys and interviews.

The pilot hit its targets: most patients stayed, attendance was solid, and satisfaction ran high. Against usual care, the program group showed a clear drop in fatigue by the week after the program ended. Patients also moved more, ate better, and slept with fewer problems. Mood outcomes were weaker: anxiety and low mood trended down but did not reach clear gains. The authors call for a larger, longer trial to confirm the effects.
pmc-13451882:
Vitor Nascimento Vidal and co-authors review in 2026 how a family of cell gates and body fats team up to drive swelling. The gates, P2X receptors, open when ATP spills from stressed cells, a spill that swelling itself triggers. Fats freed early in swelling can wake cells to spill more ATP, which keeps the loop turning.

One gate sparks pain paths, while another fires a danger assembly that frees a key swelling signal. Other fats, the resolving kind, cool the loop by cutting ATP spill and gate counts. Still others, such as cholesterol, sit in the gate's frame and shape its work. The review maps these ties as leads for pain and swelling drugs.
pmc-13452182:
Evan Kransdorf and Luke Masha reflect in 2026 on gene testing for heart muscle disease, under a title borrowed from a rock song. A firm share of cases in both kinds of heart muscle disease carry a gene cause. Yields run near a fifth to a third in one kind and near half in the other, in clinic cohorts. Sicker patients, those bound for pumps or transplants, test positive more often.

Finding a variant in one patient opens cascade testing for the whole family and can start guard care early. The piece argues that set subgroups also clear the path for gene-tied drugs that change the disease, not just its symptoms. Its core claim: the song of testing stays worth singing.
pmc-13452282:
Sugihara and colleagues reported in 2026 how a steerable microcatheter sealed a giant false aneurysm at the fork of the thigh artery. A false aneurysm is a leaking pocket of blood outside a vessel wall, here left by a long access sheath. The patient had septic shock and poor clotting, ruling out easy surgery.

The leak sat where the thigh artery splits into two branches, and its entry tract was narrow and crooked. Two operators working together bent the steerable tip through the tract under live X-ray guidance. They then injected a small amount of medical glue mixed with contrast oil into the inflow, sealing the pocket. Leg blood flow stayed intact, and the authors present the method as a safe option for fragile patients.
pmc-13453482:
Wu and colleagues pooled randomized trials in 2026 to ask whether immune checkpoint inhibitors, cancer drugs that release the immune system, raise infection risk in patients with solid tumors. Their systematic review and meta-analysis covered 141 trials with 87,484 participants, counting both all infections and severe ones.

When all reported infections during treatment were counted, checkpoint drugs raised any-grade infection risk by about a quarter and severe infection risk by about a third. The increase was clearest in fair head-to-head comparisons against placebo or against chemotherapy alone. When only infections judged treatment-related were counted, no overall increase appeared, though the same fair comparisons still showed one. The authors urge weighing this modest risk against survival benefit for each patient.
pmc-13454282:
Xi Chen and seven co-authors report a 2026 test of a soil cleaner made by loading humic acid onto tiny iron particles. The material targets soils polluted with both chromium and cadmium, two toxic metals that can move into food and water. The team ran soil incubation tests to see how much metal the material could lock in place.

After treatment, the share of chromium that plants could take up fell by about 58 percent, and the cadmium share fell by about 36 percent. By day 50, more metal sat in stable soil forms that move less. Soil microbes grew more diverse, and soil fertility improved. The authors credit chemical reduction, surface binding, ion exchange, and microbe help for the cleanup.
pmc-13455482:
Susanne Friis Søndergaard, Marie Dahl, and Annette Høgh evaluate, in a 2026 study, a telemedicine link used across hospitals and home care for diabetic foot ulcers. Photo sharing suits wound care well, yet tools often stall at organizational borders. The team observed professionals for 68 hours across Danish hospital and primary care settings during 2023 and 2024.

Three themes organize what they saw. Time came first: tight schedules squeezed the person-centered care the tool promised. Technology hurdles followed, as staff wrestled with devices and differing habits. Relationships proved decisive: where trust between sectors ran strong, the shared platform sped timely action and kept use alive. The authors' refined theory says the tool works when managers fix time and tech friction and when teams know each other well enough to collaborate across the boundary.
pmc-13456882:
Ramos Silva and colleagues review efforts to help primary care patients with long term non cancer pain cut back on opioids, pain drugs that carry real risks with long use. Their 2026 systematic review searched three databases for psychosocial programs, meaning support that targets habits and behavior, tested against a control group in primary care. The team also mapped which behavior change techniques each program used, to see what the working ones shared.

Thirteen studies with 3,130 patients qualified, but most were rated weak in quality, with only one rated strong. Eight programs succeeded in tapering opioid doses in primary care. One technique appeared in every effective program: behavior substitution, which means swapping the drug routine for a safer action or habit. The authors offer that map as a design guide, while warning that mixed study designs and patchy reporting limit firm claims.
pmc-13459282:
Hongfei Lu and co-authors tested how a critically endangered Chinese fir tree copes with the warmer, drier conditions climate change is bringing to its mountain home. Abies beshanzuensis survives only in cool, high-elevation forests, so the team grew seedlings along an elevation gradient from 500 to 1,200 meters, using lower altitude as a stand-in for future warming. In their 2026 study, they measured growth, photosynthesis, protective chemicals, and gene activity across the gradient to find where the tree thrives and where it fails.

Seedlings grew best at 1,000 to 1,200 meters, while those at 500 meters showed clear stress. Down low, photosynthetic efficiency and protective heat-dissipation collapsed, chlorophyll and biomass fell sharply from their 1,000-meter peaks, and cell-damage markers rose despite strong chemical adjustments by the leaves. Gene activity shifted too, with heat-shock and defense pathways switched on and photosynthesis genes suppressed. Warming clearly overwhelms this relic species.
pmc-13459682:
Sae H. Han and Nicholas D. Soulakis tested in 2026 whether Google search interest could help Chicago's health department predict COVID-19 vaccination demand. Using the search company's vaccination search insights alongside the city's own dose records, they modeled weekly doses across 2021 for neighborhoods grouped by social need. Time-series models with and without the search data were compared on prediction error.

Adding search frequencies, lagged by roughly a week and a half, sharpened in-sample accuracy most clearly in highly vulnerable neighborhoods, where forecast error fell dramatically. Outside those areas, forecasts with search data sometimes did worse. Prediction intervals narrowed everywhere, suggesting greater model confidence. The authors frame search data as an extra planning tool, strongest where need is greatest.
pmc-13463582:
Quehui Tang and eight co-authors present the full mitochondrial genome of Acartiella sinensis, a small estuary copepod. Copepods are tiny crustaceans that anchor food webs where rivers meet the sea. Their genome is the first of its kind for the whole family Acartiidae.

The genome runs 14,368 bases long, with adenine and thymine making up nearly four fifths of its letters. All of its genes sit on one strand, and two genes have swapped places compared with kin species. Family trees built from the data place this species next to Labidocera rotunda and Eurytemora affinis. Readers gain a firm gene record for tracing how estuary copepods split and spread.
pmc-13464082:
Yi Peng and ten co-authors review hypoxia-inducible factors, the protein switches that help tumors thrive in low oxygen. Solid tumors often outgrow their blood supply, and these switches reroute growth, fuel use, and vessel sprouting to fit the shortage. Three main forms exist, each with its own control path.

Genes that never code for protein, cell fuel byproducts, and chemical tags all bend switch activity in tumors. The switched-on program feeds spread and drug resistance across many cancer types. Proof for the third form still runs thin and needs animal checks, the authors note. Blocker drugs against the switches close the review as a hopeful route to cut tumor survival.
pmc-13464782:
Bahar Uslu Bayhan and four co-authors check whether day-one blood tests after weight-loss surgery flag patients headed for trouble. The team reviewed 260 adults who had elective bariatric surgery at one center. A combined bad-outcome count covered intensive care stays, infections, leaks, and readmission within a month.

About one in five patients met the combined outcome. Longer operations, higher AST liver enzyme levels, and a higher lactate-to-albumin ratio each tied to trouble on their own strength. AST sorted patients best, though only moderately well. The lactate ratio alone sorted poorly despite its link. Since many intensive care moves came before the blood draw, the authors frame the links as warning signs, not forecasts.
pmc-13464982:
Juan Carlos Solomando and six co-authors test a pocket near-infrared scanner for judging berry quality without cutting fruit. One hundred forty-five lots of aronia, haskap, and goji berries, across harvest years and ripeness stages, were scanned and lab-tested. Models tied light patterns to sugar, moisture, acidity, and health compounds.

Cross-checks scored the models strongly, and fresh-lot validation held up well for most traits. Sugar content forecast best of all, while total phenolics proved hardest to pin down. Error ratios supported rough quantity grading fit for field sorting. Growers and buyers gain a fast, fruit-sparing check that can run at harvest, in storage, or at the packing line.
pmc-13465482:
Trude and colleagues present a 2026 participatory design study of AgriShare NYC, a digital platform documenting urban food production across New York City. Top-down farm apps often fail with underserved growers through low digital literacy, mistrust, or poor fit. The team instead ran four design phases with growers: seventeen in-depth interviews and three workshops with twenty-one participants.

Growers' limits shaped the product: labor, time, digital skills, and organizational capacity constrained how much data anyone could monitor or enter. Simplicity became the platform's guiding principle, and design criteria came from growers' stated priorities rather than developer assumptions. The shift shows in what the platform asks of users and what it gives back.
pmc-13465782:
Kübler and co-authors studied a 2026 mouse model asking whether B cells, the antibody making immune cells, are needed for collateral artery growth. When a main artery blocks, nearby collateral vessels can enlarge to bypass it, a process called arteriogenesis guided by immune cells. B cell roles in that growth were poorly understood.

Mice genetically lacking B cells recovered blood flow significantly worse three and seven days after a thigh artery was tied off. Their collateral arteries grew less in diameter and their vessel cells divided less, Kübler found. Early on, platelet and neutrophil clusters and mast cell activation ran higher around vessels in deficient mice. By day seven, helpful M2-like macrophages were selectively reduced, and T cell subsets failed to shift from inflammatory to calming forms.
pmc-13466282:
Rui Ma and a large team tackle weld cracking in a nickel superalloy printed layer by layer for aircraft engine parts, in a 2026 engineering study. Printed parts weld worse than cast or forged ones, and this alloy family is especially prone to cracks. Laser welding trials on the printed Haynes 230 alloy let them dissect why cracks form.

Crack zones held brittle phases rich in tungsten and silicon that gather near boron-rich areas and bond poorly with the surrounding metal. Melt pool flow also set cooling speed and shrinkage stress in the danger zone. Lowering tungsten and silicon content in the alloy shrank the conditions that breed those phases, improving weldability in follow-up tests.
pmc-13466382:
Shang Wu and colleagues study how crystal regrowth inside notched aluminum burst vents changes the pressure at which they blow open, in a 2026 study. These vents protect equipment by rupturing at a set pressure, so drift in that setting matters. Samples of the AA8014 alloy were heated across a wide range for times from seconds to two hours.

A standard kinetic model produced numbers describing how fast new crystals form and grow, driven by stored energy from earlier working. A key window between three hundred and three hundred fifty degrees emerged; above it, regrowth and burst pressure stopped caring much about process variation. A simple linear formula tied regrown fraction to burst pressure with errors under about four percent.
pmc-13466482:
Adogaye Hamid Ben Bechir, Tong Li, and Ying-De Wang follow Crohn's disease patients on the biologic drug ustekinumab over the long term, in a 2026 review of one Chinese center's records. The drug blocks two interleukin signals and is approved for moderate to severe disease. Ninety-five patients who started it between 2020 and 2025 were included, most never having used a biologic before.

Clinical remission at six months reached a high share of the group, and most of those still followed at two years held their remission. Adding a common companion drug made no clear difference. Absence of disease around the anus was among the traits tied to better outcomes in the authors' modeling.
pmc-13466682:
Justyna Wrona and colleagues test two variants in a collagen-cutting enzyme gene for ties to coronary artery disease and long-term survival, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, MMP-8, comes from neutrophils and can weaken artery plaques by digesting their collagen cap. The group held 259 patients with the disease and 239 healthy blood donors for comparison.

Neither variant linked to disease risk, severity, or survival at five or ten years. The authors note the two variants sit in one inherited block, and their commonly paired forms may push enzyme function in opposite directions, cancelling out. The result argues against using these particular variants to judge heart risk or outlook.
pmc-13466882:
Teona Carciumaru and colleagues test whether three trusted scoring tools for microsurgery actually measure the same skill, in a 2026 study. Forty-five participants from twenty-six institutions in fourteen countries each sewed an eight-stitch join between vessel ends on a chicken leg model. Two trained graders scored every performance with all three instruments.

The tools split by philosophy: some grade the finished join, others grade the technique while it happens. Agreement between graders was high for all three, and rankings of performers lined up closely. Yet the authors conclude the instruments are reliable without being interchangeable, since each captures a different slice of competence. Swapping one for another would quietly change what a training program rewards.
pmc-13467082:
Rosario Mare and colleagues test whether blueberry compounds can shield gut lining cells from a heat-born contaminant found in baked foods, in a 2026 study. The contaminant, 5-HMF, forms during high-heat processing and stresses the intestine through oxidation and inflammation. The team first measured it in commercial bakery goods with two methods, finding the simple color test overstates levels that precise chromatography pins down.

In gut cells grown in dishes, the contaminant raised reactive oxygen, fat buildup, and inflammatory gene activity, and switched on two stress pathways. Blueberry juice added alongside cut the oxygen radicals and fats, strengthened a master antioxidant pathway, and damped the inflammatory signals. The pairing models a dietary counterweight to a processing byproduct.
pmc-13467482:
Gulzhanat Aitmurzinova and co-authors report a 2026 prospective study from Astana, Kazakhstan, on depressive symptoms after birth among women who had high anxiety during pregnancy. Of 1,232 women screened, 234 with elevated anxiety joined the PRISM prenatal education program, and 226 completed the follow-up check after delivery. Symptoms were measured with a short standard screening scale for postpartum depression.

The average score on the screening scale was 20.65 points across the group. The authors also tested whether age, number of prior births, and the timing of the follow-up check tracked with symptom scores. Because every woman received routine care and the program, with no comparison group, the study describes the burden of symptoms rather than proving the program worked. It still gives Kazakhstan rare local numbers for planning perinatal mental health care.
pmc-13468582:
Fronk and colleagues in Poland reviewed in 2026 all trials of fish oil fats given to women through breast cancer drug care. The fats, named EPA and DHA, are pitched to calm swelling and ease drug harm. Trials blend them in wild ways, with side adds like a bone vitamin. The review split the finds by mix and by goal.

Ten trials fed the pool, and no trial used one of the fats alone. One trial cut nerve harm from a key drug, but its twin found no gain on pain or nerve signs. Marks for swelling, food state, and life grade swung both ways. No mix showed a firm lift in tumor kill or life span. Proof strength was graded low to very low.
pmc-13468782:
Andreas Larsson published this 2026 report evaluating the Swedish version of the Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire-7. That is a seven-item scale measuring cognitive fusion, the tendency to treat thoughts as literal facts that must govern behaviour. The concept is central to acceptance and commitment therapy, and Swedish researchers needed evidence the translated scale measures it soundly. Larsson examined the questionnaire's structure and reliability in a sample using factor analysis and Rasch-family modelling.

The Swedish version performed strongly on most counts: high consistency, little missing data, full use of the response scale, and items that all loaded on one factor. Parallel analysis supported one dimension, and several fit indices excelled. The picture was not perfectly clean, though: one fit index ran high and stricter cut-offs withheld endorsement, hinting at complexity among items with similar content. Larsson concludes the scale is unidimensional and reliable for research scoring in Swedish adults.
pmc-13469082:
Molnar and colleagues test a finer ruler for transplant immune risk. Their 2026 single-centre study covers 493 adult kidney transplant recipients from 2021 to 2024. Donor-recipient pairs were classed by eplet mismatch, the count of mismatched antibody target patches. The ambiguous medium group was further split by PIRCHE scores. Those scores predict how the recipient's immune system will indirectly recognise donor tissue.

Medium mismatch carried more than double the adjusted hazard of early graft injury within a year compared with low-risk pairs, and high mismatch about five times. About twenty percent of the medium group were reclassified downward by PIRCHE. That subgroup's risk was not significantly above the low-risk group's. The confidence intervals were wide enough to hide a real increase, though. The authors present PIRCHE as a practical reclassification tool for the medium band, pending larger confirmation.
pmc-13469882:
Han Zhong Pei and a large group of co-authors show in 2026 that a protein released outside cells speeds the growth of B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. This aggressive blood cancer grows fast and often returns after treatment. The protein, extracellular cyclophilin A, was elevated in patients through release by the cancer cells themselves and by surrounding tissue.

In mice, giving the protein made the leukemia advance faster. It binds a hormone receptor on the cancer cells and switches on a signaling chain that raises movement proteins, helping cells cross vessel walls, and raises survival proteins that block cell death. Antibodies against the protein modestly lowered leukemia burden and slowed disease in two mouse models. Single cell analysis suggested treated cancers held fewer stem like cells. The team names the protein a possible treatment target.
pmc-13471382:
Barnard and co-authors asked whether high blood pressure, and whether it is treated, changes survival after breast cancer among Black women in the United States. Their 2026 analysis drew on 2,474 participants in the Black Women's Health Study who developed invasive breast cancer.

Overall, untreated hypertension showed no clear survival link, but treated hypertension came with a hazard ratio of 0.81 against no hypertension, hinting at lower breast cancer death risk. The split by tumor type was sharper: among estrogen-receptor-positive cases, treated hypertension carried a hazard ratio of 0.53 for breast cancer death. Among receptor-negative cases, untreated hypertension instead doubled the risk, with a hazard ratio of 2.19 recorded. The authors stress that trials are needed to prove the treatment itself causes the benefit.
pmc-13471482:
Deer and co-authors present the protocol for a randomized trial of an injectable disc supplement for chronic low-back pain from worn spinal discs. Their 2026 study plan enrolls adults aged 22 to 85 with MRI-confirmed degenerative disc disease, at least six months of back pain, and disability that conservative care failed to fix.

Participants are randomized in a 2:1 ratio to one injection of nucleus pulposus allograft, donor tissue meant to refill the disc's soft core, or to a sham procedure. Neither patients nor assessors are told which. The main test is whether at least 30% pain reduction at 12 months occurs more often with active treatment. Sham patients still symptomatic at one year may cross over to the real injection.
pmc-13471582:
Dong and Zhang investigated how a prized ornamental orchid wakes its flower buds from winter dormancy, suspecting the swollen storage stem, the pseudobulb, acts as a hormone depot. Their 2026 study paired hormone measurements with gene-expression profiling in buds and pseudobulbs of Pleione bulbocodioides across the release period.

Dormancy broke fast, within about one week, and the chemistry flipped in step: abscisic acid, the dormancy keeper, fell sharply while gibberellin, the growth promoter, and the ratio between them climbed. Both hormones sat at significantly higher levels in pseudobulbs than in the buds themselves, and their swings were bigger there too. Gene patterns separated the final release stage cleanly, with the first principal component explaining 55.4% of expression variance.
pmc-13472182:
Tadanori Koga and colleagues survey in 2026 how scattering methods reveal motion inside polymer nanocomposites at many scales at once. Adding nanoparticles to polymers toughens materials from tires onward, improving wear, grip, and fatigue life. Reinforcement grows out of structures and movements nested across lengths and times, which is why single scale measurements keep missing the mechanism.

Two techniques anchor the perspective. Neutron spin echo, paired with isotope labeling, follows chain segments from sub nanometer to tens of nanometers over lightning fast times. X-ray photon correlation watches whole nanoparticle networks and cross linked meshes move collectively at slower scales. Recent results on bound polymer layers, particle networks, and cross linked systems are woven together. The authors call for integrated measurement, analysis, and prediction to finally pin reinforcement down.
pmc-13472682:
Shibei Ni and Xiaorui Cheng examine in 2026 how money sources and family structure shape the care choices of older adults in China's southwest. Rapid aging is straining the tradition that children house and care for their parents. Their data came from a 2023 regional social survey covering 1,812 adults over fifty who had children, sorted into four preferred arrangements from self care at home to child provided care.

Financial reliance patterns predicted preferences strongly. Older adults who depended on children for money were more likely to prefer child provided care, and the pull ran stronger among women than men. The gender mix of a persons children, long assumed decisive, showed no significant link. Having four or more children shifted preferences toward mixed family care shared at home. The authors urge stronger pensions so preference can follow choice rather than need.
pmc-13472782:
Zhao and colleagues studied in 2026 how heritage tourism links to well-being in indigenous communities of Southwest China. They surveyed 180 people from the Miao, Dong, and Naxi groups with standard psychological scales. The mixed-methods design let numbers and lived experience check each other.

Taking part in heritage tourism linked with higher scores on every measured good: well-being, resilience, social support, and cultural identity. The links were moderate, in the range of roughly three to four tenths. Interview themes included taking part in culture building resilience, traditional healing supporting wellness, and social cohesion. The authors conclude tourism that keeps culture alive can support mental health, not only income. They caution the design shows a link, not proof of cause. The study offers local evidence for tourism planners weighing culture against commerce.
pmc-13474382:
Xiaolin Lu and co-authors share a cell-level data set in 2026 on tobacco stems hit by black shank disease. Black shank, caused by a water mold, is a major threat to tobacco crops. Two tobacco lines were compared: one that falls sick easily and a near-twin line bred to resist. Stem tissue near the infection site was taken two days after exposure.

Because plant tissue resists being split into whole cells, the team read gene activity from single nuclei instead. The data set holds gene profiles from both lines at the same early stage. Other groups can reuse it to name cell types, hunt defense markers, or merge with later studies. Open data of this kind speeds the search for hardier crops.
pmc-13474782:
Shiqiang Zhao and co-authors assemble the full mitochondrial genome of hexaploid oat in 2026, a first for this crop. Oats carry six gene sets, which makes their cell power plant genome hard to piece together. The genome came out as two circles totaling more than six hundred thirty thousand letters. It holds seventy-eight genes plus two broken gene copies.

Many repeat stretches were found, which can shuffle the genome over time. Code word use leaned strongly toward two of the four DNA letters. Most core energy genes showed signs of purifying selection across history. Links to the wild diploid oat relative were close, and gene flow from the green solar genome was frequent.
pmc-13474882:
Moselmani and colleagues reviewed animal and lab evidence in 2026 on resveratrol, a plant compound in grape skins, as a treatment for traumatic spinal cord injury. No drug yet reliably protects the cord after a crash or fall, and damage keeps spreading for days through inflammation and cell death. The team searched four databases for studies from 2015 to 2025 that tested resveratrol after cord injury.

The search found 456 candidate studies, and only eight met the review's standards for close reading and quality checks. Across those eight, resveratrol consistently improved movement recovery in injured animals, preserved more motor neurons, and boosted autophagy, the cell's recycling system, after injury. It also dampened cell suicide, inflammation, oxidative stress, and an iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis, so the authors call for stronger animal work and early human trials next.
pmc-13474982:
Yang and co-authors traced how influenza returned to Hong Kong after COVID-19 crushed flu seasons worldwide, using weekly laboratory surveillance data from 2014 to 2024. Their 2026 analysis separated influenza A from influenza B and broke each down further by subtype and lineage. A statistical method called interrupted time-series measured how the trend bent when the pandemic began in early 2020.

Both flu types collapsed in early 2020, with influenza B falling further than A in the Hong Kong data analyzed. Influenza A then climbed back over later years with returning seasonal peaks, alternating between its H1 and H3 subtypes from season to season. Influenza B stayed low through most of the post-2020 period, and among its characterized viruses nearly all belonged to the Victoria lineage, while Yamagata was not found at all in later data.
pmc-13475182:
Nitchanun Jinpisoot and colleagues judge success rates in 2026 for a pacing method that taps the heart natural wiring. Lead placement near the left bundle branch aims to keep heartbeats in sync. Records covered 407 adults implanted from 2019 to 2025. Success was judged by strict consensus rules from a European rhythm society, not loose local habit.

True bundle capture was reached in about eighty-six percent of cases. A shape shift during threshold testing confirmed most successes. Signal timing ran shorter in the success group, and lead measures stayed steady over time. Harm rates stayed low across the cohort. Standard rules let centers compare results on equal footing.
pmc-13476582:
Iftime Holst and colleagues report a 2026 study of motion correction during radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Daily cone-beam scans and couch shifts set the patient up, but people still move during treatment. The team reviewed 669 sessions from 20 patients where a surface-guided system watched movement live and an X-ray system, ExacTrac Dynamic, applied further corrections.

Tilt errors of the head, pitch and roll, came with sideways misalignments up to three millimeters, large in this precise field. The surface system triggered repositioning in about fifteen percent of sessions, though nearly half of those alerts were false positives. Even with false alarms, the authors judge surface watching a valuable, non-invasive second pair of eyes. Catching mid-session drift protects the tumor dose and spares nearby glands and the spinal cord.
pmc-13477282:
Utibe R. Essien and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of whether neighborhood racial segregation relates to new cases of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat. The work draws on the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, which enrolled adults in 2000 to 2002. Segregation was measured by comparing each census tract with its surrounding area for the resident's own racial or ethnic group.

The cohort held 5,375 Black, Hispanic or Latino, and White participants followed for a median of about 17 years. About one in five developed atrial fibrillation during follow-up. After accounting for personal, neighborhood, and health factors, segregation showed no clear link with new cases in any group. The authors say more work is needed on how personal and structural factors combine to shape risk.
pmc-13477382:
Young-Hae Go and coauthors published a 2026 Korean nationwide study on mental health after young adults receive an implanted heart device. The analysis used national health insurance data for adults aged 20 to 39 who had health checkups in 2009 to 2012. Device recipients were matched with five similar adults who received no device.

The study covered 569 device recipients and 2,821 matched controls, followed for a median of about five years. Both pacemaker and defibrillator recipients developed mood, anxiety, and stress-related disorders more often than controls. Risk was nearly double in the first two years and stayed higher afterward. Defibrillator and pacemaker groups did not differ clearly from each other. The authors recommend early mental health screening and continuing psychological support for young device patients.
pmc-13478582:
Paolo Armanetti and colleagues present a 2026 study of how lung tumors with EGFR mutations adapt to the targeted drug osimertinib. Such tumors first shrink on the drug, yet resistance always emerges, often through flexible non-genetic changes. Resistant H1975 cells in the lab grew more migratory and aggressive than their parent cells.

Forcing BMI1 up in parent cells recreated both resistance and migration, marking it as a central driver. The authors frame resistance itself as a source of drug targets.
pmc-13479382:
Jenna K. Honan and colleagues report a 2026 exposure study of PFAS, the long-lasting industrial chemicals, in pregnant women across Suriname in South America. These compounds enter bodies mainly through food and water and are linked to health harms, with fetal development a sensitive window. Participants identified as Indigenous or Tribal Peoples and lived in urban, rural, or remote rainforest areas.

Blood samples were profiled for a panel of PFAS compounds, and the team compared patterns by region. The study design tests a counterintuitive possibility: remote communities far from industry may carry higher levels than city residents, through diet and environmental pathways. Results are framed to guide local monitoring and advice for pregnant women, in a region where exposure data have been almost entirely missing.
pmc-13479582:
Xue Dong and colleagues report a 2026 feasibility study of a tiered training curriculum for gynecological keyhole surgery in southwestern China. Laparoscopy skills are essential yet training is patchy, leaving young surgeons to learn unevenly on patients. The program ran from September 2022 to December 2025 in three phases.

Phase one built the curriculum from needs assessment, task breakdown, and expert consensus. Phase two surveyed 112 trainees across junior, intermediate, and senior levels on satisfaction and perceived benefit. Phase three tested thirty-seven trainees before and after on pattern cutting and suturing tasks. The authors report whether staged difficulty, matched to experience level, produces measurable skill gains alongside happy trainees.
pmc-13480182:
Cheng and colleagues built a machine learning model in 2026 to predict kidney injury after heart bypass surgery, then stress-tested it at a second hospital to see if it travels. Training used 6,347 bypass patients from the MIMIC intensive care database, and nine algorithms competed before random forest won. The finished model was then run, unchanged, on 534 real surgical patients from a university hospital in Xuzhou, China.

At home the model looked strong, scoring 0.888 on the precision-recall curve and 0.709 on the standard accuracy curve in held-out tests. Abroad it collapsed, falling to 0.309 and 0.548 on the same measures, barely better than chance for the new population of surgical patients. Body weight, blood phosphate, and red cell width spread were its leading predictors, and the authors warn that models need local recalibration before clinical use elsewhere.
pmc-13480282:
Evandro Martins Filho and co-authors present a 2026 case of opening a blocked heart artery in a teen with a rare vessel-hardening disease. A 14-year-old girl had chest pain on effort since age eight. Her mother spotted the skin signs with an AI tool, and testing confirmed pseudoxanthoma elasticum, a gene condition that stiffens elastic tissue with mineral deposits.

Imaging showed a fully blocked main heart artery. Ultrasound from inside the vessel showed mineral in the elastic layer rather than the fatty plaques of adult disease. The team crossed the block and used a drug-coated balloon with no metal stent, keeping the vessel free to grow. Ten months later she stayed free of pain and the artery stayed open on a planned check. The authors claim a first for this guided approach in a child with the condition.
pmc-13480482:
Feng-Yuan Wang and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study on building large ring molecules without the wasteful trick of extreme dilution. Rings with two ester links, called macrodiolides, appear in prized natural products, yet chemists usually make them in vast solvent volumes to stop chains from linking wrongly. The team instead ran the reaction inside a molecular capsule built from six bowl-shaped units that hold and fold the chain ends.

Inside the capsule, simple chain alcohols and acid chlorides closed into rings of eighteen to thirty-two atoms at normal strength, with no slow drip feeding. The same pot also yielded larger four-ester rings that defeat standard methods. Against the usual metal-based ring closing, the capsule route ran shorter and reached tighter, more strained rings. Green chemistry gains follow from far less solvent per gram of product.
pmc-13480782:
Paull and colleagues used continuous glucose monitor data in 2026 to compare school hours with holidays for primary school children with type 1 diabetes in Western Australia. The population study covered 235 children, averaging nine and a half years old and about four years since diagnosis, over one 12-week stretch spanning a school term and the following holidays. School routine, staff support, and fixed meal times were the suspected drivers.

Children spent 58.0 percent of school hours in the target glucose range, clearly better than the 53.5 percent logged in the same hours during holidays. Weekends during term sat between the two at 56.6 percent, also below the school figure in the paired comparisons made by the team. Low glucose time stayed under 4 percent in every period, and the authors read the pattern as evidence that structured school days steady control rather than endangering it.
pmc-13482582:
Yang and colleagues test in 2026 which peritoneal dialysis patients with failing fluid removal can still benefit from icodextrin, a sugar polymer solution that pulls water across the belly membrane. The drug was designed for fast-transport membranes, called type 1 failure, but four failure types exist and responses vary. The exploratory study enrolled 19 patients with ultrafiltration failure and 24 dialysis controls without it, running a battery of membrane tests on everyone.

Icodextrin pulled the most fluid in type 1 and type 2 failure, while free water transport looked lower in type 2 patients in the test results. In types 3 and 4 the drug appeared less effective, which the authors read as a limit on its use across all failure patterns. Net fluid removal tracked with sodium sieving measures and small-pore water flow, leading them to suggest one membrane measure could predict who will respond before prescribing.
pmc-13483582:
Olufemi Erinoso and co-authors chart dental care use and tooth loss among adults in Nevada from 2018 to 2024. The share reporting a dental visit in the past year fell from 67.1 percent in 2018 to 63.5 percent in 2024, with no full rebound after pandemic disruption. Adults with disabilities used care less in every wave, and adults with diabetes started lower before the gap narrowed. Permanent tooth loss rose over the period and stayed higher for people with diabetes, disability, or rural residence. Persistent gaps point to access problems that coverage alone has not solved.
pmc-13485082:
Phuljhele wrote a 2026 editorial opening a special issue on neuro-ophthalmology. The field links eye signs to brain and body disease in daily practice. New scans of the retina now double as gauges of nerve health. Layer thickness in the eye mirrors disease load in several brain disorders. Those include multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, and Alzheimer disease in the text. Imaging can now name some optic disc lumps that once hid from view. Careful history taking still anchors the field, Phuljhele stresses throughout. Listening well and looking closely remain the specialty's twin skills.
pmc-13486882:
Vilakazi and co-authors turned human urine into a dry fertilizer by soaking it into pine bark products, then grew spinach with the result. Urine is rich in nitrogen, but storing and hauling liquid is impractical for small farms, so drying it onto bark, biochar, or ash could make it portable. Their 2026 glasshouse trial applied products dried at two temperatures to pots of spinach at the recommended nitrogen rate and grew the plants for 84 days.

Spinach fed the urine products grew as well as plants given commercial ammonium nitrate fertilizer in the pot comparisons. Nitrogen uptake and dry matter both rose clearly over unfertilized controls. Plant micronutrient levels stayed within safe limits overall, though manganese ran high with some bark products and sodium rose in tissues. Soil acidity eased and available phosphorus increased after application. Vilakazi recommends the fertilizer for salt-tolerant crops with monitoring.
pmc-13486982:
Steven Harris and Alain Michon argue in a 2026 critical review that the word lift, the most common promise in filler marketing and research, lacks any agreed meaning or measurement. Their structured critique covers hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, and several other filler families in facial rejuvenation. Millimeter-sized claimed effects often match or fall below the noise of the measurement itself. Dose studies show no tidy more-product-more-lift relationship, and less independent raters tend to report bigger gains. No study states tool accuracy beside effect size or sets a meaningful threshold beforehand. A proposed framework aims to give the field honest yardsticks.
pmc-13487182:
Prieto-González and team built a performance index just for center forwards in England's Premier League, arguing generic ratings miss what strikers are actually for. The hybrid index, weighted seventy percent toward market value, explained about 68 percent of the variation in player valuation in their fitting. Expected goals per ninety minutes, shots, and key passes per ninety were the strongest ingredients of a forward's score. Goal threat dominated, but creative passing contributed independently rather than riding on goals alone. Prieto-González notes the twenty-match minimum for inclusion may bias the index toward established starters over emerging players.
pmc-13487982:
Jie Liu and co-authors test utidelone in advanced soft tissue sarcoma in a 2026 single-arm phase II trial. Participants had cancers that kept growing despite anthracycline chemotherapy and antiangiogenic drugs, which cut off tumor blood supply. Twenty-seven patients received the drug by infusion on five days of each three-week cycle, continuing until the disease advanced or side effects became unacceptable.

Two patients had partial tumor shrinkage, and the middle time before progression was a little under five months in this heavily treated group. Most side effects were mild, though nerve damage was the most common severe problem. Survival data were still early. The authors judge the activity promising enough to explore drug combinations.
pmc-13489182:

A single catalyst built from four aluminum centers handled both monomers. It let the team assemble layered block structures by adding monomers in sequence. It also let them mix both at once and steer the outcome with heat.

At lower temperature, mixed chains formed with nearly even, near-random incorporation and short runs of each unit. At higher temperature, a swapping reaction called transesterification stretched runs of like units and created a gradual drift along each chain, called a gradient structure. The authors frame one catalyst as a dial for microstructure.
pmc-13490382:
Panahi and colleagues catalogued the BAG gene family in barley for the first time, hunting genes that help crops survive stress. The seven genes spread across the barley genome with distinct protein traits, one settling mainly in the nucleus and another in the mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Segmental duplications grew the family over evolution, while purifying selection kept their sequences conservative. Heat stress switched the genes on or off differently by tissue, fitting stress-response roles. Panahi offers the catalogue as a foundation for breeding hardier barley.
pmc-13491682:
Qiongyu He and four colleagues probe in 2026 why inbreeding shrinks stature in Brown Swiss cattle, measuring height at the sacral bone in 15,306 cows. Long, medium, and short identical stretches all contributed, so both old and new inbreeding matter. pmc-13495182:
Xuemei Bi and a large team pool, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, trials of dexmedetomidine given during shoulder arthroscopy, a keyhole surgery on the shoulder joint. Eighteen trials with 1,203 patients qualified. Pain scores at six and twelve hours after surgery ran lower with the drug, and nausea and vomiting after surgery fell as well. The drug also raised the risk of slow heart rate and low blood pressure, side effects the trials defined loosely. The pain gain was real but modest. The authors back the drug as one part of a mixed pain plan, with close watching of heart rate and blood pressure.
pmc-13495282:
Zirong Wang and a large team search, in a 2026 study, for shared gene signatures linking acid reflux disease and major depression. The two conditions often travel together, yet their shared molecular roots stayed unclear. The team mined gene activity data from five public sets covering both diseases and hunted for genes that shift in reflux and sit in depression-linked gene groups.

A three-gene signature emerged. The team tested seventy-one learning models, and a ridge regression model sorted depression best, holding up in an outside test set. In a clinic group of seventy reflux patients, the three genes' activity split clearly by depression severity, and worse depression went with worse reflux scores. The authors offer the trio as a lead for understanding how gut and mood illness intertwine, while noting the work rests on data sets rather than a designed trial.
pmc-13495382:
Ali Ceylan and colleagues test, in a 2026 study from Istanbul, whether gene screening of children with early cataracts can catch a rare treatable disease in time. Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis stems from faults in the CYP27A1 gene and slowly damages nerves, yet a replacement treatment exists if started early. Cloudy lenses in youth can be its first sign, years before body symptoms.

The team sequenced the gene in 128 patients aged six months to twenty-one years whose paired cataracts had no known cause. Two children carried a new harmful variant in both gene copies, and three carried a single copy of an unclear variant. Both fully affected children came from related-parent families and had blue-tinted cataracts. The authors back adding the gene test to the workup of paired youth cataracts, above all where cousin marriage is common.
pmc-13495482:
Yixin Zhu, Xin Zhang, and Ying Jin compare, in a 2026 study from Suzhou, children whose Mycoplasma pneumonia came with a virus against those whose came with a bacterium. Telling the two mixes apart early guides treatment, yet their signs overlap. The team reviewed 392 children with the base infection, split between the two co-infection kinds.

The virus group ran older and peaked in spring, with more crackly breathing sounds. The bacteria group peaked in summer and autumn, with more vomiting and a stronger bacterial blood marker. The virus group instead showed higher clotting and tissue stress markers. Rhinovirus led the viruses, and a pneumococcus led the bacteria, fully resistant to one common antibiotic yet sensitive to two others. The authors warn that single markers separate the groups weakly and urge joined reading with local germ patterns.
pmc-13499082:
Balthazar and colleagues cooked pork burgers with ohmic heating, which passes electric current through the food, and compared the results with conventional grilling, in a 2026 food processing study. Three electric field strengths were tested against grilling for microbe killing, energy use, texture, nutrient retention, and laboratory measures of bioactivity.

Balthazar found grilling reached the target temperature in seven minutes while ohmic heating took far longer, up to eighty-two minutes at the weakest field. The strongest ohmic setting, however, cut energy use by a marked forty percent and reduced bacteria far more than grilling. A bacterial family was undetectable in all heated samples. Ohmic burgers were firmer and held less water, macronutrients stayed unchanged, and vitamin B12 retention was better. Measured antioxidant-type activity rose but remained too low to support health claims. Modeling suggests industrial high-power equipment could erase the time penalty, making the trade-off attractive.
pmc-13499382:
Rocha and colleagues published a 2026 study on drug-resistant gut bacteria in trafficked parrots. Seven parrots seized from the illegal wildlife trade entered a rehab center in Brazil. Gene sequencing of their gut bacteria found a worrisome E. coli strain, ST162. Such strains infect both birds and people, raising shared-health concern.

Three of the seven bird isolates resisted many frontline antibiotics tested. The bird strains clustered with human strains in the family tree. That kinship suggests the germ passes between people and birds somewhere. Timing patterns hinted the strain also spread within the center itself. The authors call for routine gene checks in wildlife rehab centers. The first strain appeared in one bird early in its stay.
pmc-13500682:
Lin Ye leads a 2026 multicentre study asking whether muscle wasting changes who benefits from an aggressive triple therapy for inoperable liver cancer in older patients. The triple approach adds vessel-blocking chemoembolisation, targeted pills, and immune checkpoint drugs together, powerful but demanding for frail bodies. Records covered 231 patients aged 65 and over at seven Chinese centres between 2019 and 2023. Muscle mass was measured from scans at the third lumbar vertebra, and statistics were weighted to balance the groups.

After weighting, triple therapy extended median survival by roughly three months over vessel-blocking treatment alone in the reported analysis. Muscle wasting, present in over two-fifths of patients, significantly modified that benefit. Patients with preserved muscle gained a large survival advantage from triple therapy, while wasted patients gained none that reached significance, and severe side effects stayed comparable. A quick muscle check could help decide who should endure the triple regimen.
pmc-13501682:
Yiqing Meng leads an eleven-author team with a 2026 genetics study of drought tolerance in Brassica juncea, a vegetable and oil crop suited to dry regions. The team grew diverse accessions under drought and ran a genome-wide association study to find the genes responsible. One candidate stood out: BjuB.HAM1, a plant-specific GRAS-family transcription factor. Two variations inside the gene clearly impaired drought tolerance, marking the gene as a negative regulator, a brake on the plant's drought defences.

To test how the brake works, the researchers expressed the gene in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The factor bound elements in the promoter of AtUGT76C2, a cytokinin-modifying enzyme, and shut its expression down, reducing drought tolerance in the plants. The authors present the HAM1 and UGT76C2 module as a fresh piece of the drought resistance machinery and a target for breeding hardier Brassica juncea lines.
pmc-13501782:
Xuanyin Ding leads a ten-author team with a 2026 review of neurotransmitters as players in cancer growth and immune escape. The messengers fall into four families: cholinergic agents, monoamines such as serotonin and dopamine, amino acids such as glutamate and GABA, and peptides. Tumours and nearby nerves release them, and cancer or immune cells answer through surface receptors and internal signalling. Two unusual chemical changes get special attention: serotonylation and dopaminylation, where the messengers are attached directly onto proteins.

The effects cut both ways. Serotonin can fuel the energy metabolism of killer T cells and strengthen antitumour attacks, while GABA building up inside tumours helps them hide from immunity. The review surveys drugs that block synthesis, release, or receptor signalling, including pairings with checkpoint inhibitors that improved outcomes, plus vaccines built around these pathways. The authors frame neuroimmune crosstalk as a precision therapy frontier.
pmc-13501882:
Bielas and colleagues heated a polypeptide, poly-l-lysine hydrobromide, and watched its chain folding shift with effects for stiffness and conduction, in a 2026 study. The polymer starts as a mixture of helical, sheet-like, and turn structures. Using methods, infrared spectroscopy, X-ray scattering, calorimetry, and dielectric testing, the team tracked what heat does to structure.

Bielas found drying followed by heating driving a shift toward sheet-rich structures. The shift needed motion of hydrogen-bonded chains and an activation energy around sixty-four kilojoules per mole. Oddly, the more ordered sheet state softened the polymer, dropping its glass transition temperature rather than raising it. Electric conductivity fell even though the sheet state's hydrogen bonds are stronger. The authors infer that charge moves better through the helical state's looser electric setting, making this polymer a model for how folding governs a polymer's mobility and transport.
pmc-13502482:
Davidson Shandilya leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 MRI study of rotator cuff tears caused by injury rather than wear. Fifty patients with shoulder trauma had their shoulder scanned. The team recorded how each injury happened: falls onto an outstretched hand, direct blows, traction, lifting or loading, and high-energy trauma. Scans were graded for which tendons tore, whether tears were partial or full thickness, retraction, marrow swelling, fluid, and bursitis, using grading systems.

The supraspinatus tendon was involved in every case, alone or within multi-tendon patterns, and partial-thickness tears were commonest. Injury mechanism tracked with tear type, full-thickness tear size, and bone marrow swelling. High-energy trauma produced full-thickness components, larger tears, and marrow oedema, while gentler mechanisms gave partial tears.
