Retraction and grading within partial tears showed no mechanism link. The authors say matching scan patterns to the accident story sharpens confidence.
pmc-13503682:
Runhua Li presents a 2026 deep learning system that reads the mood of a song from sound, words, and track data joined as one input. Older tools often fail on new music styles and miss long patterns in a track. The design aims to fix both faults.

Two parts do the heavy lifting. A dual-path encoder pairs fine sound detail with a broad view of long-range links in the music, and it stresses the tone bands that carry mood. A training plan then pulls like passages close and pushes unlike ones apart at three levels. Tests on two public sets beat strong older models on accuracy scores, and part-by-part checks show each piece adds value.
pmc-13503782:
Geon Gug Yang and six colleagues build a security label that cannot be copied, in a 2026 paper. Such labels, called physical unclonable functions, rely on random patterns that form by chance during making. Checking the fine pattern is often slow and costly, which limits use.

Their label forms when tiny spheres settle into a patchwork of crystal grains. Each patch has both a place and a crystal direction, so the pattern holds two kinds of data at once. Light checks read both the reflected colour pattern and the scattered light pattern, each in visible light. The two reads must agree, which makes fakes hard. The label is thin, can bend, and can be remade, which suits tags on goods.
pmc-13503882:
Tang, Kang, and Kroemer argue in 2026 that ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation, does not always stop at the cell where it starts. Their perspective piece gathers evidence that the death can spread.

The authors describe three routes of spread that can act together. Waves of reactive oxygen can trigger neighbors, membranes that touch can transfer material directly, and parcels called extracellular vesicles carry signals between cells. They propose one framework in which these routes work at different distances, from adjacent cells to whole tissue regions. How far the damage runs depends on chemistry inside cells, membrane physics, and tissue layout. The idea matters for organ injury that keeps growing, for tissue shaping during development, and for cancer treatments that aim to trigger this death.
pmc-13504782:
Ling Ren leads a team testing whether a simple blood index forecasts major heart and brain events in heart failure patients, in a 2026 study. The index joins blood fat and sugar values and stands in for insulin resistance. Cheap markers that sharpen risk calls would help clinics sort care.

The cohort held 927 patients at one center, grouped by index quarters. Only 80 patients suffered a major event during follow-up. Each step up in the index raised event risk, and the top quarter faced about three and a half times the risk of the bottom quarter. The link was stronger in women and in patients over 75. On its own the index predicted only modestly, so the authors offer it as a supplement to standard risk factors.
pmc-13506582:
Hang Tian and colleagues report a 2026 survey of a gut parasite in Siberian tigers in Northeast China. The parasite, Enterocytozoon bieneusi, can infect people as well as animals. The team tested fecal samples from 97 captive tigers and 5 wild tigers with a DNA test that also identifies parasite types.

About four in ten captive tigers tested positive, with no clear gap between sites. Three types appeared, and all belong to a group known to infect people. Type D dominated, and the team found it in a wild tiger for the first time. Shared feed, such as chicken meat, may explain spread, so tighter hygiene and watch programs are urged.
pmc-13507082:
Huibin He and colleagues report 2026 work on a scalable way to build colloidal molecules, tiny particle clusters shaped like real molecules. Gold particles coated with polymers join in water when long-range electric pull and short-range hydrogen bonds act together. A dialysis step, which slowly changes the fluid, controls how fast clusters form.

Yields reached up to 95 percent, at particle levels about a thousand times higher than earlier methods. Cluster size stayed self-limited, with one central particle holding up to six partners. The clusters then served as blocks for arrays and open-pore layered structures. Large-batch cluster making could support new optics, sensing, and medical imaging materials.
pmc-13507182:
S P Sundar Singh Sivam, Stalin Kesavan, and A Johnson Santhosh optimize milling of nickel and stainless steel parts in 2026 work. The parts were built by wire arc additive manufacturing, a welding-based form of 3D printing. Seventeen milling trials varied cutting speed, feed, cut depth, and tool flute count. Outcomes tracked surface roughness, removal rate, power use, and cutting force.

A three-step method modeled the trials, weighted goals under uncertainty, and ranked settings. The best run used top speed, light feed, deep cut, and four flutes, giving a smooth finish and fast removal. The worst run sat mid-range on most settings. Speed and depth drove finish and removal most, while feed and flutes shaped power and force.
pmc-13508282:
Ting Hu leads an eleven-author team pairing light-based therapy with immune therapy against a stubborn form of bowel cancer, in 2026 work. Most bowel cancers of the microsatellite-stable type shrug off PD-1 immune drugs because few immune cells enter the tumors. The team built a light-activated drug that homes to a surface protein called integrin α6 on cancer cells. In the dark the compound did little harm, yet under light it killed cells strongly and damaged their outer walls. It also wrecked cell power stations and triggered a form of cell death that alerts the immune system.

In mice with bowel tumors, the compound gathered in tumors and stayed longer than a standard comparison drug. Light treatment alone shrank tumors and reshaped the immune mix inside them. Adding a PD-1 drug boosted the effect further, with more killer T cells and fewer suppressive cells present.
pmc-13509182:
Derya Gursel Surmelioglu and four co-authors test whether a shell-based disinfectant strengthens the glue bond between fillings and tooth dentin, in 2026 lab work. Cavity disinfectants can protect the bond, and chitosan, made from crustacean shells, may stabilize the collagen in dentin. The team used forty-eight sound human molars, split into shallow and deep dentin groups. Each group got no treatment, a standard chlorhexidine rinse, or a chitosan rinse before a two-step self-etch glue and composite were applied. After aging cycles, tiny beams were pulled apart to measure bond strength.

Chitosan gave higher bond strength than no treatment in both shallow and deep dentin, a statistical gap. Chlorhexidine landed in between, without a consistent edge over chitosan. The authors back chitosan as a bond-friendly disinfectant for this glue system. They caution that dish results on pulled teeth must still be proven in living mouths.
pmc-13509682:
Palak Grover, Rahul Jain, Gurleen Kaur, and Bipneet Singh chart deaths from a set of scarring lung diseases in the United States from 1999 to 2024, in 2026 work. The group used national death records covering the underlying cause of death, then adjusted rates for age so years could be compared fairly. Trends were split by sex and by race across the full period.

Yearly deaths roughly doubled over the period, rising from about eleven thousand to nearly twenty-three thousand, while the age-adjusted rate climbed more slowly. Men accounted for just over half of deaths throughout, and the share rose slightly by the end. The gap between white and Black rates widened over the first two decades. No drop in population deaths lined up with the arrival of anti-scarring drugs in 2014. The authors note this kind of data cannot judge how well the drugs work in treated patients.
pmc-13511082:
Xiaobo Zhang, Zhiming Li, Ruoxin Lin, Suping Yang, Xiaohui Sun, and Shicheng Chen study genes tied to a tagging process called SUMOylation in kidney cancer, in 2026 work. In this process, small tags attach to proteins and change their behavior. Kidney cancers vary widely at the molecular level, yet care guidance leans on one subtype and leaves others less served. The team hunted for tag-linked genes whose activity differs in tumors.

They found 298 such genes, with 151 tied to kidney cancer itself rather than to subtype quirks. Ten core genes stood out, and one of them separated tumor from normal tissue while also telling the main subtype apart from two rarer ones, a possible second-step marker. A six-gene risk model predicted survival well inside single subtypes, though pooling subtypes weakened its accuracy. The authors say subtype variety itself limits shared prediction tools.
pmc-13511882:
Bruno and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how faults in RNA splicing may help drive Parkinson's disease, a brain disorder that slowly kills the nerve cells that control movement. Splicing is the editing step that cuts and rejoins RNA copies of genes before they are used. Changed editing has been found in several genes tied to the disease.

The review covers splicing shifts in genes such as SNCA, LRRK2, MAPT, PRKN, and BIN1, and traces how those shifts disturb cell skeleton upkeep, energy production, and signal passing between nerve cells. It also looks at the RNA-binding proteins that run the editing, since their faults may spread the problem across many genes at once. The authors close with new lab models, among them tiny lab-grown brain-like organoids, that let researchers watch splicing go wrong in human-like tissue.
pmc-13512182:
Vítor Costa proposes a new form of the second law of thermodynamics translated into economics, in a 2026 theoretical work. The first law version sets conservation rules, yet it cannot capture one-way change or measure imperfection. The author builds the second law from watching an isolated economic system drift toward a balance point for traded goods, named merchandise economic thermal equilibrium.

That drift demands a new property, merchandise economic entropy, and an absolute temperature scale for goods defined at the point of greatest entropy. Temperature change and change in traded units run in the same direction under this scheme. Each economic system gains its own built-in demand curve, and a third law follows from the shape of the entropy function. A differential equation and a generation term complete the frame, with generation offered as the best gauge of how imperfect, or irreversible, an economic process runs.
pmc-13512382:
Lucas Murrins Marques proposes a mapping framework that pinpoints where city dwellers face the highest climate-related mental strain. The framework, Eco-Affective Health Mapping, joins environmental exposure, landscape shape, and emotional response data on one map.

City stressors such as heat, noise, pollution, and lost nature fall unevenly across neighbourhoods, and so do feelings like eco-anxiety and grief. By layering these signals, planners could spot vulnerability hotspots and aim mental health support where strain runs highest. The tool is built to work in data-poor settings too, including cities across the Global South. It treats climate emotions as public health signals that can be measured and mapped. Marques stresses the framework is a proposal awaiting real-world tests before it guides surveillance.
pmc-13514482:
Yuanchao Liu and ten colleagues present, in a 2026 study, a wild mushroom strain collected in Tibet and identified as Flammulina yunnanensis, a relative of the familiar enoki mushroom. The strain, labelled Z68, stood out for unusually high iron in its fruiting bodies. The team pinned down its preferred growing conditions, measured its protein and amino acid content, and sequenced its whole genome to hunt for the source of the extra iron.

Z68 grew best on maltose with yeast extract at mild temperatures and near-neutral acidity, and its mushrooms carried more iron, potassium, and zinc than two comparison species. Genome comparisons showed most iron-handling gene families conserved, yet one iron-uptake gene, FTR1, appeared doubled. Two changes in that gene's protein were predicted to make iron transport more efficient, suggesting a two-part explanation of expansion plus fine-tuning.
pmc-13515582:
Fei Teng leads a twelve-author team testing an engineered probiotic against pullorum disease in chicks, in a 2026 animal study. The disease, caused by Salmonella pullorum, kills many young chicks and costs poultry farms heavily. The team fitted a friendly bacterium, Bacillus subtilis, to deliver two gut-repair factors made by chickens themselves. Chicks received the strains by mouth before infection, alone or combined.

In dish tests, one factor sped cell growth and both helped gut cells migrate to close gaps. In infected chicks, death rates fell from about three-quarters in untreated birds to one-quarter in the combined group. Salmonella levels in the gut dropped sharply, growth and immune organ measures improved, and inflammation markers calmed. Gut lining grew taller and healthier, with milder damage in liver and intestine. Teng's team presents the approach as a promising alternative to antibiotics for chick protection.
pmc-13515882:
Abdelrahman and colleagues present a 2026 magnetic milligripper, a tiny untethered gripping tool meant for grasping and moving objects inside tight spaces in the body. Their design folds a titanium structure and adds two tilted permanent magnets, avoiding the hinges and multi-part builds that make similar tools hard to fabricate.

A three-axis coil system steers the gripper, controls its direction and position, and opens and closes it reversibly. A joystick lets one operator drive it in real time. The team checked the design three ways, with a math model of the magnetic forces, computer simulations, and bench experiments, and all three agreed closely. Operation stayed fully elastic across the tested range, supporting the design as a sturdy proof of concept.
pmc-13518882:
Denis Awany and a large team compare blood signals in 2026 between tuberculosis patients with symptoms and those found by community screening who feel well. More than half of TB cases in prevalence surveys report no classic symptoms, yet such silent disease may still spread. Whether its biology differs from symptomatic TB was unknown.

Gene and protein profiles from South African cohorts showed both forms share core patterns: innate, interferon, and inflammation pathways switched up, while T and B cell pathways switched down. Silent cases split into two clusters differing in bacterial burden and chest imaging. Marker tests performed worse for silent disease, so the authors warn against reusing symptom-based diagnostics for community screening without rework.
pmc-13518982:
Miit Daga and four colleagues build a 2026 hybrid quantum-classical system that picks its own quantum kernel for spotting Parkinson's disease, breast cancer, and diabetes on today's noisy quantum hardware. Quantum feature maps can sort tangled biomarkers, yet each map suits other data, and sloppy checking leaks details between training and testing.

Their setup routes data through three quantum encodings and two quantum scorers, then lets a logistic regression meta-learner, trained strictly on out-of-fold predictions, decide which kernel to trust per dataset. Parkinson's specificity jumped from 0.585 to 0.813 while recall stayed above 0.95, and diabetes recall rose too. A lone variational classifier failed at every task, matching known training plateaus.
pmc-13520182:
Demeke Geremew, Joanne T M Tan, Peter J Psaltis, and Christina A Bursill review in 2026 the widening roles of ASGR1. This liver receptor was long known for clearing worn-out sugar-coated proteins from blood. New evidence ties circulating ASGR1 to higher coronary artery disease risk, and blocking it in animals reduced atherosclerosis, the artery-clogging process behind heart attacks.

The receptor also sets platelet lifespan and behavior, shaping clotting and thrombosis. Some bacteria and viruses exploit it as a doorway into cells, with immune side effects. In cancer it plays both sides, promoting some tumors and suppressing others. Geremew and colleagues survey the mechanisms and the state of ASGR1-targeted therapy development.
pmc-13520382:
María Isabel Gaviña-Barroso and colleagues adapt in 2026 a swimming ability scale for Spanish-speaking professionals who teach or treat children in the water. No validated Spanish tool existed for judging functional performance in aquatic settings across typical and atypical development.

Adaptation followed six standard phases, with two translators, two back-translators and a five-member expert panel. After two review rounds, most items counted as fully equivalent and agreement indices reached perfect scores. Pilot testing with 20 professionals supported clarity and relevance. The Spanish version now allows consistent aquatic assessment for programme planning, pending fuller reliability testing in larger groups.
pmc-13520982:
Matteo Di Minno and Flora Peyvandi present a commentary, published in 2026. It covers the market withdrawal of Roctavian. The withdrawal was voluntary. Roctavian was the first gene therapy for severe haemophilia A. The failure was structural, not scientific, they argue. The one-time treatment was not pulled for safety problems. Its effect was not the issue either. Costs, weak uptake, and system readiness made it unsustainable.

The authors review the trial evidence. How long the inserted gene keeps working is still unsure. This complicates patient care. It also complicates value sums for payers. Roctavian sits in a wider pattern. Other gene therapies were withdrawn or restricted too. Payment models must be sustainable, the authors say. Delivery systems should be built alongside the science.
pmc-13521082:
Nicholas F. Aloi and colleagues compare in 2026 three surgical constructs for repairing sudden triceps tendon ruptures at the elbow, an injury from forceful straightening against resistance. Bone tunnels, suture anchors and a combined construct were weighed on complications and function.

Charts from one centre for 2014 to 2024 covered acute cases only, excluding chronic tears, revisions and graft reconstructions. Data included scan reports, surgical time, blood loss, strength before and after surgery, plus return trips to theatre. Adjusted models accounted for tear type and tendon retraction. Full comparative rates follow in the results, guiding technique choice for a rare injury.
pmc-13521482:
Diego de Silva and Achille Peiris review in 2026 how to stop type 2 diabetes in people with kidney disease and prediabetes. The frame is joint heart and kidney care. High blood sugar feeds paths that harm both organs at once. Prediabetes is both a warning sign and a chance to act.

Lifestyle change stays the base of care. Trial proof spans decades, adapted here for kidney diets and low stamina. Real-world follow-through lags trial levels. Metformin suits picked patients as an add-on drug. Newer heart-kidney drug classes get careful treatment. Direct proof in this exact group is still inferred, not trialled. Risk spotting gets equal space.
pmc-13522582:
Ran Zhang, Cancan Wang, Xiaomei Ma, and Xinxia Li hunt for cells behind lung cancer resistance to immunotherapy in a 2026 study. Records from one hundred ninety-seven patients with lung adenocarcinoma treated with checkpoint drugs were reviewed, separating responders from resistant cases. Fresh tumor tissue from a few patients in each group underwent single-cell sequencing, with spatial mapping in selected specimens.

A distinct myeloid cell group marked by the protein SPP1 was enriched in resistant tumors and sat close to tumor nests. Protein staining confirmed these cells were tumor-associated macrophages, a type of immune cell that can suppress attack. Their gene networks suggested immune suppression. The authors propose the cell group as a possible predictor of treatment outcome and a target for further study.
pmc-13523482:
Lujie Dong and others report a 2026 first study on using ultrasound thickness readings to spot peritonitis in children on peritoneal dialysis. Peritonitis is a serious risk of this dialysis method. The peritoneum often grows thicker in long-term patients, yet ultrasound data on the mesentery and bowel wall in children were scarce.

The study set 40 children with peritonitis against 42 without it, using belly ultrasound to measure peritoneal, mesenteric, and intestinal wall thickness. All four measures were thicker in the peritonitis group, and blood markers also differed. A joint model using time on dialysis, two thickness readings, and a blood ratio reached strong accuracy at telling the groups apart and beat single readings. The authors built a scoring chart that matched real cases well and argue ultrasound can help doctors find it sooner.
pmc-13525782:
Fernandes and colleagues published a 2026 case report on chemotherapy exposing a hidden nerve disease. Their patient, a 68-year-old woman, received breast cancer chemotherapy with nerve-toxic drugs. Her numbness grew so severe that treatment stopped after nine of twelve rounds. Unlike typical drug effects, her weakness kept worsening after the drugs stopped.

Nerve tests showed a myelin-stripping pattern, not the fiber damage taxanes usually cause. Steroids and immune treatments failed to help her walking or strength. Gene testing found a doubled gene that causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A. The inborn condition had stayed silent until chemotherapy stressed her nerves. Atypical nerve damage deserves a fresh diagnosis hunt, they stress. Serial nerve checks during treatment can flag such cases early.
pmc-13527082:
Rami Alfattani and Majed M. Hotami propose, in a 2026 engineering study, a digital twin system that predicts defects during metal additive manufacturing in real time. Their model links melt-pool physics, thermal fields, and part deformation through physics-informed neural network surrogates, fed by live thermal, acoustic, and optical sensors arranged across edge, fog, and cloud computing tiers.

Validation used a public benchmark dataset for laser powder bed fusion with two aerospace alloys. A hybrid convolutional and memory network classified six defect types, including porosity, cracking, and keyholing, with a macro F1 score near 0.984. Overall defect detection reached 98.72 percent with inference near eleven milliseconds per frame on edge hardware, beating seven baselines. Simulated production suggested scrap could fall by about a third, although directed energy deposition use remains unvalidated experimentally.
pmc-13527982:
Li Xueyi and four colleagues compare breathing muscle training methods for intensive care patients in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Weakness gained in intensive care, including weak inspiratory muscles, slows recovery and weaning from ventilators. The team gathered randomized trials of adults in intensive care. They tested training approaches alone and combined with wider rehab programs.

Twenty-three trials covering eleven strategies entered the analysis. Outcomes included muscle strength scores, inspiratory pressure, days on a ventilator, weakness rates, and weaning success. A component analysis tried to separate the effect of each part of mixed programs. Bias and evidence quality were graded with standard tools. The authors aim to show which training mix adds most. Full effect sizes sit in the paper's tables for clinicians planning rehab.
pmc-13528082:
Wei Chen and Bo Qin report a 2026 case where vision loss revealed chronic myeloid leukemia. A 38-year-old man lost sight badly in one eye. Exams found bleeding inside both retinas, twisted vessels, cotton-wool spots, and a swollen optic disc. Scans showed the left eye was in fact more infiltrated. The right eye simply saw worse.

Blood tests then found extreme white cell counts and an enlarged spleen. The Philadelphia chromosome confirmed the leukemia. Treatment with hydroxyurea and nilotinib normalized counts quickly. The cancer reached a deep molecular response. Vision fully returned, and the retinas and optic nerve looked normal again. The authors say eye signs can flag deadly blood disease early. They also propose eye checks as a handy way to track treatment response.
pmc-13529182:
Wen and colleagues tested whether a simple nutrition score predicts death among people with rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic autoimmune disease that inflames joints. Their 2026 study used United States national health survey data collected from 2007 to 2018. The score, called the geriatric nutritional risk index, combines blood albumin, a liver-made protein, with body weight relative to ideal weight.

Wen found that participants with rheumatoid arthritis scored lower on the nutrition index and died more often than those without the disease. Each one-point rise in the score came with a modestly lower risk of death from any cause after full adjustment. Patients below the risk cutoff faced roughly eighty percent higher death risk than those above it. No clear link appeared for cardiovascular death specifically, so the authors position the score as a general risk flag needing prospective confirmation.
pmc-13529782:
Sinan Vicil, Riza Serttas, and Suat Erdogan wrap a plant compound in nanoparticles to strengthen its hit on prostate cancer cells in a 2026 study. The compound is apigenin, found in many foods. The carrier is a selenium particle coated with hyaluronic acid. Tests ran in LNCaP cells, which answer to male hormones. A low working dose was picked from early screening.

The wrapped form cut the androgen receptor message to about a quarter of normal. Its partner signal, PSA, fell in step, and PSA protein dropped to a tenth. Cell death reached about forty-four percent, beating the drug enzalutamide's ten percent here. Growth and stem-like markers eased while death genes rose. Lumps of cells in 3D dishes also shrank. The authors call the carrier a booster worth animal testing.
pmc-13530182:
Ayaz Ahmad and co-authors outline a 2026 scheme for storing popular videos inside open radio access networks before users ask for them. Early caching cuts delay and eases traffic on core links. Open network design spreads storage across radio, distributed, and central units, which complicates placement choices.

Video features get compressed by a three-dimensional network, grouped into classes, and scored for likely popularity by a classifier. Even unseen videos receive a popularity guess from their features. Copies then fill storage from the network edge inward by rank. Simulations beat older methods on hit rate, delay, and core traffic.
pmc-13532282:
Amy L Leber and co-authors alert in 2026 that variant gene cassettes let some MRSA staph strains slip past a leading rapid nose test. Two surgical patients screened before operations were told they carried ordinary staph, yet cultures grew the resistant form. Extra testing backed the cultures in both cases.

Genome reading showed each strain carried a cassette variant the test cannot see, since the assay needs two resistance signals to declare MRSA. Overall miss risk stays low, the authors note, yet high-risk patients may warrant backup culture while local strain surveillance continues.
pmc-13534482:
Matthew D Mellow and colleagues pool in 2026 genome scans to find inherited variants that raise risk of uveal melanoma, a cancer inside the eye. Nine studies held 5,839 people with the cancer and about 350,000 healthy controls. Five new scans joined four published ones in a combined analysis.

Nine separate risk regions passed the strict threshold, three of them new. Follow-up gene analysis pointed to five candidate target genes, several already tied to other cancers. Risk also shared genetic roots with skin melanoma, hinting at shared biology that may guide future drug targets.
pmc-13534682:
Marta Kowal and colleagues test in 2026 whether changing hormonal contraceptive use after meeting a partner lowers love and relationship quality. Samples from 51 countries held 10,482 people, with analysis focused on 2,224 partnered women aged 45 or younger who reported use at both time points. Three parts of love were rated separately.

No robust support appeared for the matching hypothesis overall. In one weighted model, women who changed their use pattern reported slightly lower passion than steady users or steady non-users. The authors offer broad reassurance while noting very small effects could still matter personally.
pmc-13535882:
S Habte and colleagues report in 2026 an improved open-source autofocus module for light microscopes that uses an LED instead of a costlier diode source. Keeping samples in focus during long imaging runs is vital, and drift blurs fine detail. A new scoring method based on bead image patterns measures focus stability on its own.

The LED system held axial stability within ten nanometres for at least 45 minutes from a cold start, even as lamp power varied during warm-up. The scoring method corrects for power drift, making fair comparisons easier for labs building low-cost setups.
pmc-13536182:
Norris and colleagues interview the clinicians who shepherd surgical patients with metabolic syndrome. The syndrome is the cluster of obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, and abnormal cholesterol that blights a third of humanity and worsens surgical outcomes. No programme exists around surgery for these patients. Their 2026 qualitative study used a behaviour science framework to structure interviews about what blocks and what enables good care before, during, and after operations.

Clinicians named resource constraints, fragmented pathways where nobody owns the whole journey, and blurry team roles as the barriers. On the enabling side sat peer validation, teamwork, and decision-support tools that make risk handling uniform. Emotions and motivation mattered more than the authors expected: engagement rose or fell with whether clinicians felt the work was valued and feasible. The team's output is an intervention framework arguing for defined roles, streamlined workflows, and training, theory-informed from the start.
pmc-13536582:
Poonam Joshi and colleagues evaluate in 2026 simulation-based training to cut needlestick injuries among nursing students in eastern India. Such injuries expose trainees to infection risk, and hands-on drills may teach safer habits. Over 200 students joined a two-day blended course with scenario drills and guided review.

Satisfaction was high, and knowledge, reported practice, and attitudes all improved and held at three months. Reported injuries fell sharply after training, though recall periods differed and no control group was used. The authors see promise but call for larger controlled trials before firm claims.
pmc-13538582:
Mohammad Mouner Ahmad Alsayegh, Ekbal Ahmad Fadel, and Flora Yahya Mayhoub measure prenatal pollutant exposure in first newborn stool across Syria in a 2026 study. First stool captures late-pregnancy exposure as metals and pesticides cross the placenta. Samples came from 123 full-term newborns in Damascus and Latakia during late summer 2025, tested for eleven metals and five pesticides with sex-split adjusted models.

Every target pollutant appeared in the samples, showing widespread exposure with wide personal variation. Among boys, mercury tied to lower birth weight while nickel tied higher, and one pesticide tied to smaller head size. Among girls, lead, thallium, and a banned pesticide metabolite tied to birth weight, with length links for two pesticides. The authors urge caution given the one-time design and call for follow-up studies.
pmc-13539982:
Bahejianati Nuerbolati and colleagues report a 2026 study of HIV care in China. The setting was the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps. The team asked why some people on treatment still had unsuppressed virus. Viral suppression is the goal of antiretroviral therapy and of global targets.

Among 369 people, about fifteen percent had unsuppressed virus. Shorter time on treatment played a part. So did lower immune cell counts, drinking, and stigma. Weak confidence in self-care also mattered. Support from others and self-belief lowered risk. They did so mainly by helping people take their medicine regularly.
pmc-13540882:
Donald E Warden and colleagues set out an asthma study protocol in 2026. The cohort will follow children in Corpus Christi, Texas. That city has a majority-Hispanic population. Petrochemical plants ring the area. Asthma rates there exceed state and national levels.

About two hundred children under ten will join. All of them have asthma already. Parents will answer a monthly questionnaire for up to eighteen months. The questions cover home exposures, attacks, and wheezing. Medical records will check the answers. Daily pollution readings from official monitors will link to home addresses. Models will hunt exposure patterns and wheeze paths over time.
pmc-13543382:
Beatriz Carmona's team published a 2026 study of what drives burnout and quitting intentions among early childhood educators in New York. The workforce is stressed and unstable, and the StayWell ECE project surveyed licensed educators twice: a large health behaviours survey with 1,423 respondents, and a smaller social environment survey with 263. Path analysis tested how stress, workplace support and strain, health habits, and burnout feed into plans to leave.

Higher burnout came with poorer diet, less physical activity, and worse sleep, while weak workplace support also tracked with worse diet and sleep. In the path model, stress eroded support, raised strain, and fed burnout, and the burnout dimensions in turn raised turnover intentions. Personal accomplishment, one burnout facet, was protected by support. The authors argue that retaining educators means treating stress and workplace relationships as health issues, not only staffing issues.
pmc-13544382:
Sundeep Srivastava and colleagues report the safety of iliac vein stenting performed in an office-based laboratory rather than a hospital. Their 2026 analysis covers nonthrombotic iliac vein lesions, narrowings not caused by blood clots, in patients with chronic venous insufficiency.

The team reviewed 4,312 procedures in 2,642 patients treated from 2012 to 2024, all assessed with ultrasound imaging inside the vein. Patients received clopidogrel daily afterward, with no heparin during the procedure. Clotting inside the stent within 30 days was rare in every age group, from patients in their thirties to those over ninety, and did not vary meaningfully by age or disease class. Most early clots were partial rather than complete blockages. The authors present the record as evidence that office-based stenting can be done safely.
pmc-13547382:
Raiyan Gani and co-authors built in 2026 a lightweight model that diagnoses cucumber leaf diseases from photographs by reasoning about both texture and the spatial layout of sick spots. Most image models treat leaf patches independently and demand heavy computing. Their design pairs a phone-friendly feature extractor with a graph network that links neighboring feature regions, letting distant symptoms inform each other.

On a public set of 4,000 leaf images in five classes, the model scored accuracy near 99.8 percent, beating several much larger networks while using a fraction of the computation. Two explanation tools confirmed it attends to the actual lesions. A prototype phone app shows live diagnosis is feasible, which the authors pitch for field monitoring by growers.
pmc-13548582:
Antoine Muchir, Antonio Musaro, and Jeffrey Chamberlain review Duchenne muscular dystrophy from its gene defect to the newest genetic treatments, in a 2026 article. The disorder, passed on the X chromosome, removes the protein dystrophin, so muscles break down through childhood toward loss of walking, breathing failure, heart disease, and early death. Supportive care has improved, yet no cure exists, and its single-gene cause makes it a prime target for precision therapy.

The review explains the disease's mechanisms and natural course. It then walks through treatments that skip faulty gene sections, read through stop signals, or edit the genome directly. A further family delivers a shortened dystrophin gene by virus. Each approach faces limits, from working only for certain mutations to immune reactions and unknown durability. The authors see combination treatments and better delivery as the road ahead.
pmc-13550282:
Selahattin Çelik and colleagues ask whether a patient's vitamin D level before treatment forecasts how long a breast cancer drug holds the disease back, in a 2026 single-center analysis. Eighty-nine women with hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer received ribociclib plus hormone therapy between 2018 and 2023. The team split them by whether their starting vitamin D counted as deficient or sufficient and compared time without progression.

The gap was stark: women with sufficient vitamin D had not reached their median progression-free point, while deficient women progressed at a median of fourteen months. At two years, every sufficient patient remained progression-free against under a quarter of the deficient group. Statistical adjustment kept the association, though with very wide uncertainty because few sufficient-group events occurred. The authors label the finding exploratory and demand larger prospective tests.
pmc-13550482:
Nicolas Prieur-Blanc and colleagues check whether a new instrumented figure-of-eight walking test gives the same answers on repeat visits, in a 2026 methodology study. Turning makes up a large share of daily walking, yet nobody agrees how to measure curved gait or even when a turn starts. Fourteen healthy volunteers walked the figure eight barefoot and shod, at easy and fast paces, across three sessions, wearing knee sensors and a body motion unit while radar tracked speed.

The team defined five landmarks of a turn, from slowing down to speeding back up. The main timing intervals varied by under ten percent between repeats, with low measurement error throughout, though the window for detecting small true changes exceeded the natural spread. The authors say the setup is repeatable, and a simpler version could bring curved walking assessment into clinics.
pmc-13550582:
Zuwu Hu, Hongjuan Li, and Ling Liu published a 2026 survey study on why memorable trips leave people feeling better. Drawing on broaden-and-build theory, which links good experiences to lasting gains, they asked 665 university teachers about travel memories, positive emotions, resilience, and overall well-being. Standard scales measured each factor, and a statistical model tested how they connect.

Memorable experiences correlated strongly with well-being, and positive emotions carried much of that link. Resilience changed the second step: teachers with higher resilience held on to trip-related good feelings more effectively and reported stronger well-being. The authors suggest the results can guide care programs for university staff, while noting the design shows associations rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13551682:
Si-Wen Wang, with four colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a leaking replacement mitral valve fixed by re-tensioning. A frail 75-year-old woman with severe mitral regurgitation and repeated heart failure received a transcatheter valve held by an apical fixation design. She later returned with worsening heart failure, leakage around the valve, and hemolysis, the breakdown of red blood cells, after the valve slipped late.

Surgeons reopened the earlier chest incision and re-tensioned the device, which resolved the leak and relieved the hemolysis. Imaging by transesophageal echocardiography, an ultrasound probe passed into the gullet, guided the diagnosis. The authors stress that even mature fixation designs can dislodge, and that prompt re-tensioning can rescue the repair.
pmc-13551782:
Mohamad Reza Kordasti, Masoud Sheidai, and Fahimeh Koohdar published a 2026 study of a hardy shrub across dry parts of Iran. The shrub, Calotropis procera, thrives in arid land. Its leaf form may track local climate. The team sampled twelve wild groups. They measured leaf shape and inner structure, then modeled how traits map to place and weather.

Leaf traits differed clearly among groups and shifted within groups too. Spatial tests tied trait patterns to climate and geography. Map methods flagged some groups as strong reservoirs of adaptive traits. Other groups looked at risk. The team offers the frame for guarding dryland shrubs as the climate warms. Field teams can use the maps to pick which groups to protect first.
pmc-13551982:
Xin Xiao, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 two-year study of drinking and cyberbullying among school teens in Ningbo, China. Baseline data came from 1,902 students with a mean age near twelve. The survey covered drinking, lifestyle, and feelings. Cyberbullying harm was measured two years later. The team tested whether loneliness, sadness, or nervousness carried the link.

About forty percent of students reported drinking at the start. Roughly one in nine reported cyberbullying harm at follow-up. Drinking predicted higher odds of later harm after adjustments. The link ran strongest in boys and in frequent drinkers. Loneliness and nervousness each carried part of the effect. Sadness did not, the team reports.
pmc-13552582:
Roosa Moilanen leads a five-author team behind a 2026 Finnish cohort study on early life and eczema. The group asks whether age at birth, type of delivery, or birth weight shape later risk of atopic dermatitis, a common itchy skin disease. Their data come from a northern Finland birth group followed since 1986. In all, 8,993 people were split by whether they had the disease or not.

About one person in four had eczema at some point. Neither early birth nor surgical delivery changed the odds in this group. Low birth weight did lower risk, though only among men, whose rate fell by close to half. No such link appeared among women, which hints that early risk factors may differ by sex.
pmc-13555882:
Kaijing Zhong leads a seven-author team studying dry mouth and oral quality of life in older Chinese adults in a 2026 survey. Their group held 583 community residents aged sixty and up in Jingzhou, Hubei. Dryness was rated by a standard inventory, and life quality by an elder oral health index. Dentists also examined decay, fillings, missing teeth, gum disease, and dentures.

Most cases of dryness were mild, with very few severe. Losing more than ten teeth nearly doubled the odds of dry mouth compared with keeping all teeth. Tooth loss and dryness each independently dragged life quality scores down. A combined model sorted dry from non-dry participants with acceptable accuracy. The authors link dry mouth care with tooth preservation in elder services.
pmc-13555982:
Takeru Nara and eight colleagues reported in 2026 on walking problems in people with POEMS syndrome, a rare disorder that damages peripheral nerves. Their first study covered 60 patients and rated walking ability with a standard functional scale. A second, retrospective part followed 27 patients after treatment and split them into groups whose walking improved or stayed the same.

Walking difficulty tracked closely with strength in the hip, thigh, and shin muscles, and with position sense in the big toe, while nerve conduction test results showed no such link. Strength in those same muscles improved in the group whose walking got better after treatment. The findings point clinicians toward muscle strength and joint sense, rather than nerve test values, when judging recovery.
pmc-13556082:
Jacqueline L Tilley and seven colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for testing whether one focused consultation can draw people with both chronic physical illness and mental health problems into treatment. Such patients carry heavy costs and poor outcomes, yet past attempts to raise engagement with mental health services have largely failed. The planned work runs in a community health setting in Singapore in two phases.

Phase one surveys outpatients about their health, service use, hope, and readiness to change. Phase two randomly assigns up to 60 people with raised depression or anxiety scores to either a solution-focused single-session consultation or a single supportive therapy session. The pilot trial will judge feasibility and acceptability first, with early signs of benefit second. Results would show whether a brief, structured conversation deserves a full-scale trial.
pmc-13558582:
Aliaa M. Alabdali and Esam A. A. Hagras proposed in 2026 an image encryption scheme that builds its keys with a deep learning chaotic generator and newly designed elliptic curves. Image security needs unpredictable substitution tables and shuffling patterns, and static designs can be reverse-engineered. Their method feeds a cascaded two-dimensional sine-cosine chaotic map into several parts of the system at once.

A convolutional network produces the key stream, while the chaotic map sets the parameters of multi-prime elliptic curves whose points generate fresh substitution boxes and permutation tables for each use. Because the tables are dynamic and key-dependent, the cipher can be rekeyed by changing the shared curve. The paper walks through the construction and the security reasoning behind it. The authors position the design for cybersecurity settings where images must travel over open channels.
pmc-13558682:
Weijie Liu and Yanyan Fan proposed in 2026 a lean framework for recognising acoustic scenes, the task of labelling a recording as a park, a station, or a street. Models must run on small devices and cope with microphones unlike those used in training. Their design first splits sound into harmonic and percussive parts, then models each stream with asymmetric convolutions shaped differently along time and frequency, joining the streams with a dual attention fusion.

Validation on two standard scene datasets showed a much smaller, faster model that kept competitive accuracy. Against transformer systems, it proved sturdier when the test recordings came from different devices, and it held together when clips were shortened. The authors frame the work as structure-aware design: using what is physically known about sound to buy efficiency and interpretability at once.
pmc-13560482:
Alina Salganicoff, Ivette Gomez, and Usha Ranji examine how state policy choices shape access to sexual and reproductive health care across the United States. Their 2026 perspective argues that states, through Medicaid design, payment levels, licensing, and rules, decide whether services broaden or narrow. The 2022 Dobbs ruling, which returned abortion policy to the states, grew that role.

Cost, supply, and coverage still block care in much of the country. Some states on purpose restrict abortion, while built-in problems also squeeze contraception and maternity services. Recent state moves include telehealth abortion supply, drug-counter prescribing rights, and mother-care quality programs. The authors stress that funding rules treat contraception, abortion, and maternity care as apart, yet women seek them from the same doctors across one linked life course. Low-income women bear the sharpest costs of tight choices.
pmc-13562482:
Datta and colleagues use single-cell sequencing to learn why blocking a protein called Axl helps some cancers but disappoints in trials, in 2026 cancer immunology research. Axl sits on myeloid cells, immune cells inside tumors that can suppress anti-cancer responses. The team grew human melanoma cells with macrophages from four healthy donors, in pairs and in three-way cultures adding dendritic cells. They then measured how each cell type's gene activity and cell-to-cell signaling changed under Axl inhibition.

Communication-mapping tools showed the drug's effects depended on which cells were present. Prior treatment of the tumor cells reshaped how myeloid cells answered Axl blockade, altering the inferred signaling patterns between cell types. Datta argues these context effects help explain the translation gap between tidy mouse experiments and mixed human trial results. Understanding myeloid responses in realistic mixtures, the authors say, should guide combination therapies built around Axl.
pmc-13563882:
Maaz Khan and eight colleagues fine-tune iron and phosphorus feeding for mung bean grown in chalky soils, where nutrients lock away out of roots' reach. Their 2026 report describes a two-year field trial, 2022 to 2023, in randomised blocks. Iron went on as a leaf spray at four strengths up to 0.6 percent, crossed with phosphorus fertiliser at four rates to 90 kilograms per hectare. Growth, yield, seed quality, nutrient uptake, and the money return were tracked across the combinations.

A mid-strength recipe won. Spraying 0.4 percent iron lifted seed yield to 790 kilograms per hectare, 23.44 percent above untreated plots, while 60 kilograms of phosphorus gave 796 kilograms and the trial's best chlorophyll and growth rates. The strongest sprays maximised nitrogen and iron inside the seed. Efficiency peaked at low phosphorus rates. Combining 0.4 percent iron with 60 kilograms of phosphorus produced the best value for money, the recipe the authors recommend to farmers.
pmc-13568982:
Kylie J. Yineman and co-authors run, in a 2026 randomized trial, a comparison of dressings for the roof-of-mouth wound left when gum graft tissue is taken from the palate. Patients received either an amnion-chorion membrane, a birth-tissue dressing with healing properties, or a standard clot-promoting agent, then were scored weekly for a month and rated their pain for three days.

Healing scores improved in both groups and ran clearly higher with the membrane across all four weeks. Pain ratings and painkiller use did not differ between groups. Older patients healed with higher scores regardless of dressing. Gum surgeons get evidence that the membrane speeds visible healing even though comfort gains were not shown.
pmc-13571782:
Jade Ramini and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, three Xhosa South African fetuses carrying the same two-copy faulty variant in the CHAT gene. That gene makes an enzyme essential for producing the nerve signal chemical acetylcholine. Faults in this gene were known for a muscle weakness syndrome appearing after birth, not for lethal disease before birth.

All three pregnancies showed reduced fetal movement. Ultrasound found small jaw, neck swelling, narrow chest, and joints fixed in bent positions across the body, the pattern of fetal akinesia, meaning failure to move. The shared variant ties this gene to a lethal multiple pterygium syndrome, and the authors argue it belongs on fetal akinesia testing panels.
pmc-13573382:
Merve Dilek Karataş reports a 2026 study of how tomato plants answer salt stress over time. Salt in soil and water cuts tomato yields worldwide by harming growth, body function, and chemistry. Plants were raised under four salt levels, from none to the strongest dose, and sampled at day 15 and day 45 of exposure.

The cultivar under test was H2274. Measures spanned leaf green pigment and colour, defence chemistry tied to oxidation, and fat damage in cell walls. Gene activity reads joined the body and chemistry measures at both time points. That spread lets the team see which defences switch on early and which fade or grow by day 45. Dose and time together shape the picture, since a mild short dose can prime a plant while a strong long dose overwhelms it. The results feed breeding for salt-tough tomatoes.
pmc-13573482:
Matthieu Dagenais, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 pilot trial of yoga classes designed to build a positive body image in adults. Past yoga studies centred on young women, so this pilot widened the lens to men and women across adult life. The main question was plain feasibility: could such a program recruit, run, and hold people?

Adults who did no yoga and scored low on body appreciation were assigned at random to ten weeks of classes or a waitlist. Fifty-seven people entered, with a mean age of 52, and ratings for the yoga arm ran high on feasibility and fit, near the top of a five-point scale. Class attendance averaged 79 percent. Gains in valuing body function favoured the yoga group. The authors say a full trial can work, with better outreach to men and the young.
pmc-13574882:
Madline Yacoub-Kenyi Leju and Amsalu Degu report a 2026 study from Kenyatta National Hospital in Kenya. They looked at how well hydroxyurea, a drug used for sickle cell anaemia, worked in real care for children and teens. Records covered care given from January 2020 through December 2023.

The team reviewed charts for 54 patients aged 16 or younger who took the drug for at least six months. Pain crises, hospital stays, transfusions, and blood tests were tracked for up to two years. Mean haemoglobin rose from 7.8 to 10.5 grams per decilitre by month 24, while crises and admissions fell. The authors link the drug to steady gains, though the study had no comparison group.
pmc-13575682:
Kan and co-authors, in a 2026 letter, map the next steps for prediction models in combined heart, kidney, and metabolic care. They respond to a study by Patel and colleagues. That study built machine learning models from electronic health records. The models forecast worsening heart failure and death in people with mild-to-moderate kidney disease. They reached strong discrimination, around 0.88 on the standard accuracy curve.

The letter argues the real work starts after prediction. Static risk scores should become live decision support inside medical records, flagging high-risk patients and suggesting specific guideline-directed treatment upgrades for their condition mix. That closes the loop between spotting risk and acting on it. The authors also float digital twins, virtual patient models that update over time, as a route to simulating treatment choices before applying them to the person.
pmc-13576282:
Junhong Yang leads a 2026 community study of liver scarring and fat in Gansu Province, northwest China. Liver disease in China is shifting from viral causes toward metabolic ones, yet population data from the northwest are scarce. The survey enrolled 5,043 adults across three counties during 2025, with body measures, blood tests, and a stiffness scan of the liver.

Significant scarring appeared in 5.18 percent of participants, and advanced scarring or cirrhosis in 1.67 percent. Fatty liver was far more common, at 50.45 percent for any grade. Hepatitis B infection, obesity, diabetes, a raised liver enzyme, and low platelet counts each tied independently to advanced scarring. Obesity carried the strongest tie to severe fatty change, at more than seventeen times the odds. The authors frame the results as a regional baseline.
pmc-13577082:
Rose M Lee, Keun Pil Kim, and Jeong H Joo study a DNA-guarding protein during meiosis in yeast, in a 2026 paper. Meiosis is the cell division that makes sex cells, and it starts with deliberate DNA breaks that must be repaired into crossovers between partner chromosomes. Replication protein A coats the exposed single strands, yet its exact meiotic jobs were unclear.

The team switched the protein's large subunit off on demand using a degron tag. Without it, break processing faltered, chromosome axes assembled badly, and the zipper-like structure that pairs chromosomes formed poorly. Crossovers that depend on the ZMM protein family failed. Shutting down a checkpoint kinase that normally pauses the process did not rescue the damage. The authors cast the protein as a stabiliser that ties repair steps to pairing and crossover formation.
pmc-13579182:
Wenjiang Han and colleagues report a wearable sensor study, published in 2026. They built electronic skin that senses pressure, odour, and humidity at once. It needs no battery or wires. The device is an array of tiny resonant circuits. Each circuit is tuned to its own frequency. A layered gel with a micro-pyramid surface handles touch sensing.

The pressure channel answered in about five milliseconds. Its sensitivity was high. The chemical channels detected odour traces down to two hundred parts per billion. Each stimulus shifts a different circuit's frequency. The system can thus separate overlapping signals. The authors demonstrate a step toward skin-like sensing for health monitoring and robotics.
pmc-13582782:
Abbas Dehghanian leads a 2026 computer study that looks for new cancer-fighting peptides inside proteins of the parasite Leishmania major. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, and some can kill cancer cells while sparing healthy ones. The team worked from two parasite proteins, named KMP11 and GP63, and cut them in silico into short pieces between 5 and 25 units long.

Software tools first scored each piece for likely action against cancer, then checked the best ones for safety risks such as poison effects or allergy triggers. A ranking method picked ten lead candidates for closer study with models of cell membranes and cancer-linked receptors. None has yet been tested in living cells, so the work is a shortlist for lab follow-up rather than proof of a drug.
pmc-13583382:
Irene Uski and colleagues count teeth in Finland's adult population in this 2026 report from the Healthy Finland 2023 study. Tooth count is a classic sign of oral health, yet the team also counted meeting pairs of back teeth, which matter for chewing. Trained dentists examined 1,798 adults aged 20 and over and linked the counts to age, income, schooling, and place of residence.

Adults held an average of close to 25 teeth, and only a small share had lost all their teeth. Younger adults kept nearly full sets. Older age, low schooling, and low income each went with fewer teeth and fewer chewing pairs, with schooling showing the strongest tie. Gaps also appeared for widowed and unmarried people and for some regions.
pmc-13584282:
Qiqi Lv and colleagues chart how daily skills, thinking, and mood move together in older adults in China, and how those paths relate to falls. Falls are a leading cause of injury death in old age. Their 2026 study drew on five rounds of a national ageing survey from 2011 to 2020, covering 2,938 people aged 60 and over.

A modelling method sorted people into five paths, from a large group that stayed normal to groups with steady decline in one or more areas. Every decline group faced a higher risk of falling between 2018 and 2020 than the normal group. The risk was greatest where daily skills fell steeply alongside weak thinking and low mood, at close to triple the normal rate. The authors call for fall prevention that covers body, mind, and mood at once.
pmc-13584582:
Chidinma Ejike-Okongwu and colleagues hunt for Salmonella in live bird markets in Plateau State, Nigeria, in this 2026 study. Salmonella is a germ that spreads through food and causes much illness where market hygiene is weak. The team collected 1,120 samples across eight markets, from bird droppings and soil to rinse water, table swabs, and organs, in both dry and wet seasons.

The germ turned up in about one sample in nine. Wet season samples ran dirtier than dry season ones, and one market, Chobe, showed the highest rate. Swabs from slaughtering tables were the most contaminated of all sample kinds, marking them as a key spread point. The authors say their map of hot spots can guide clean-up efforts and safer poultry handling across the state.
pmc-13585082:
Sahana Mitra and colleagues work with fruit flies to pin down a partner protein in the cell stress response. Cells under strain switch on a shared rescue program called the integrated stress response. In flies, a factor named crc, kin to human ATF4, helps run that program, yet which partners it needs inside living tissue was unclear.

The team found that a protein named Irbp18 is that essential partner. Without it, stress target genes in the eye failed to switch on in a fly model of retinitis pigmentosa, a blinding disease, and crc could no longer grip its target DNA. Losing Irbp18 also sped eye decay in that model and quieted stress signaling in a fly model of Parkinson's disease. The work names a concrete cog in a pathway tied to many degenerative diseases.
pmc-13585882:
Juliana Sasaki Ijiri and colleagues try a paired-measurement control chart on routine lab data in this 2026 study. Labs often track two linked readings at once, such as two drug levels in one sample, and watching each alone can miss a joint drift. Their chart uses the squared Mahalanobis distance, a measure that weighs how far a pair sits from its usual center while allowing for how the two readings move together.

Four small datasets from fuel and drug labs were charted, mostly showing steady processes with no alarms. One drug pair did cross the action line, showing how the joint view can flag what single charts miss. Repeat shuffling of the data showed the warning lines themselves wobble when history is short. The authors back the chart as a clear, spreadsheet-friendly extra tool, not a proven fault finder yet.
pmc-13589182:
Rika Möller and colleagues put a small knee tendon under a sodium-sensitive MRI scan. Sodium levels in tendon mirror its sugar-protein content, which rises early in tendinopathy before structure visibly changes, offering a possible early warning. Achilles tendons had been measured this way, but the thinner patellar tendon invites measurement blur. The team scanned seven patients with patellar tendinopathy and twenty healthy controls on a standard clinical scanner, applying a custom correction for that blur.

Sodium concentration in patients ran far above controls, and a comparison measure of structural alteration was also roughly doubled; both gaps were statistically solid. The team first measured the tendon's sodium relaxation times to anchor the numbers. Because the method runs on ordinary hospital equipment, the authors argue it could flag tendon trouble while it is still chemical, not yet structural.
pmc-13589382:
Na Guo and six colleagues trace metformin's benefit in polycystic ovary syndrome up into the brain's hormone control center. The syndrome involves overactive release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, and metformin helps many patients, but its brain-side action was murky. Working in 2026, the team treated rats with a drug-induced version of the syndrome, profiled hypothalamus proteins, and probed a hormone-producing cell line made insulin resistant.

Metformin eased the rats' insulin resistance, hormone overshoot, broken cycles, and ovary changes. Protein maps pointed at insulin and cAMP signaling, and in the cells, metformin restored a protein called Epac2 and its downstream AKT signal while calming hormone overproduction. Silencing Epac2 in the mouse hypothalamus reproduced insulin resistance and hormone excess. The authors conclude the Epac2 pathway helps carry metformin's central benefit, with more work needed on the balance between brain and body effects.
pmc-13592482:
Toro-Perez and colleagues dissect a seizure pattern in children whose epilepsy is classed as generalized, meaning seizures start across the whole brain at once. Some children begin with an absence, a blank stare spell, that then turns one sided before erupting into a full convulsion. Their 2026 review of a monitoring unit cohort uses EEG, computer analysis of brain wave recordings, to trace that path in children with brain scans.

Seven of 66 children with generalized epilepsy, all girls, showed the pattern, across eight recorded seizures. Wave analysis showed the slow spike wave rhythm of absence first. A focal buildup followed over the side frontal and back regions, stronger on the right, before the convulsion spread to both sides. The syndromes behind the cases were absence and myoclonic epilepsies of youth. The team proposes a relay through the thalamus, the brain's switchboard, and calls for cohorts to confirm the route.
pmc-13592682:
Adi Shuchami and six colleagues ask how often children's emergency departments repeat blood tests that community clinics just ran. Repeats within hours rarely change care, yet they cost money, time, and sore arms. Their dataset covered a nationwide health plan's records for children aged three months to eighteen years. Repeat rates for blood counts, electrolytes, and an inflammation marker were judged against preset need criteria, then a learning model tried to predict which repeats were truly needed.

Only about thirteen to nineteen percent of repeats proved justified, depending on the test. A standard boosted tree model predicted need with up to ninety two percent accuracy, and stayed useful when tuned to miss no needed repeat for two of the three tests. Shuchami and the team say live practice studies come next.
pmc-13593682:
Musab Işık and colleagues tested whether fluoxetine, a widely used antidepressant, can shield the liver from the damage that follows when blood flow is cut off and then restored. In their 2026 rat study, the injury was created by clamping the main abdominal artery for an hour and then releasing it, with one group pretreated with fluoxetine for three days.

Untreated animals showed heavy oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death signals, and visible tissue damage, along with weakened antioxidant defenses. Fluoxetine pretreatment largely reversed that pattern, restoring antioxidant capacity and improving the tissue picture under the microscope. The authors read the protection as working through three routes at once: fighting oxidation, calming inflammation, and limiting programmed cell death. They propose the drug as a possible candidate for liver surgery and transplant settings where this injury is common.
pmc-13596782:
The PLOS One editors retracted a multilevel study of early marriage among women in Bangladesh. Concerns had been raised that its design could not support its stated aims. The notice sets out the dispute in detail. The central problem was definition: the article measured early marriage as the share of ever-married women aged eighteen to forty-nine who wed before eighteen, which departs from the international standard.

That standard counts all women aged twenty to twenty-four, married or not. Excluding unmarried women skewed the pool and made the reported figures incomparable with official survey and development goal indicators. The author defended the broader age range as support for the modeling method. Two editorial board members advised that determinants analysis may fairly use married women. Prevalence language, they warned, misleads under this design. The editors concluded the reporting could not stand, and the article was withdrawn.
pmc-13599882:
Elīza Ance Beņislavska and three colleagues use Swedish health registers to ask whether being active before a mini-stroke protects against a later stroke. A transient ischaemic attack briefly blocks blood flow to the brain and warns of higher stroke risk ahead. The study covered 1,610 adults treated at stroke units in Gothenburg between late 2014 and the end of 2019, most of them reporting only light activity before their attack.

In simple comparisons, people with moderate or vigorous activity beforehand had much lower rates of later stroke. Once age and sex were taken into account, those gaps shrank and no longer reached statistical significance. Adding clinical, social, and treatment factors changed little. The authors suggest earlier activity may mostly reflect general health, not protection on its own. They note the numbers still leave room for a real benefit that larger studies could settle.
pmc-13599982:
Andreza Parreiras-Gonçalves and colleagues review forecasts of how yellow fever may spread as the climate warms and habits change. Yellow fever is a serious viral disease carried by mosquitoes, now centered in Africa and Latin America but capable of large epidemics. The scoping review screened 1,243 studies and kept 42 using original data to project future trends in the disease or its carriers.

Most were computer models projecting that warming would expand the range and numbers of the main carrier, Aedes aegypti, with temperature and rainfall the top drivers. City and population growth also raised human exposure in many models. Far fewer studies tied the projections directly to future yellow fever transmission, and results there varied. Gaps included other mosquito types, future trends inside Africa, and forest transmission cycles. Shifting climate and land use, they conclude, will likely widen the zone where yellow fever can take hold.
pmc-13601582:
Sizhe Ma and three colleagues release Rail-VIVID in 2026, a paired dataset meant to push railway track monitoring forward. Trains can inspect track as they run, using vibration sensors that feel hidden defects but cannot locate them, or cameras that show surface damage but miss what lies beneath. The two approaches grew up apart, partly because no public dataset paired both signals for direct comparison.

Rail-VIVID records synchronized vibration and video from repeated runs over one track segment with documented faults. Researchers can use it to study how each kind of fault signs itself in each signal, and to benchmark detection algorithms on the same material. It also supports building fusion methods that combine both streams for sturdier detection. The authors frame the dataset as groundwork for predictive maintenance, where catching faults early from ordinary train runs could replace some manual inspection.
pmc-13602082:
Danielle L. Orrell and five colleagues follow one flapper skate through two catches in 2026, using tag data to watch its behavior after each release. Flapper skates are critically endangered, and catch-and-release anglers may hook the same resident fish repeatedly. Off Ireland's southwest coast, a tagged skate was caught, released, and recaptured six days later. Its tag popped off on schedule a day after the second capture, while acoustic receivers tracked it for 212 more days.

After each release, the skate moved far more than usual, with rapid vertical excursions. Models confirmed depth and mobility changes, with settling at 9 hours after the first release and 10 hours after the second. Vertical movement before settling ran 441 percent above the normal hourly rate. Even so, the skate stayed near the capture area both times. The authors offer rare two-event evidence for judging catch-and-release welfare in a threatened species.
pmc-13602582:
Sevilay Aydın Çelik and three colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial in Istanbul asking what a single climate lesson does to pregnant women's minds. Pregnant women are especially exposed to climate harms, and learning about them could raise worry or, handled well, hope. The trial enrolled 154 women at a public hospital, assigning 77 to a 60-minute face-to-face session on climate change and pregnancy and 77 to no training. Scales measured worry, awareness, and hope before and four weeks after.

The trained group rose significantly on all three measures, with large effect sizes. The control group drifted the other way on anxiety and hope, gaining only slightly in awareness. Statistical tests confirmed the groups changed differently over time. Structured climate education, the authors conclude, can raise awareness while feeding hope rather than despair. They suggest antenatal programs use such teaching for awareness and psychological support alike.
pmc-13606082:
Yunxiu Wu leads a seven-author team testing a simple artery measure as a kidney warning sign across two countries. Estimated pulse wave velocity, from age and blood pressure, reflects arterial stiffness without special equipment. The team linked it to chronic kidney disease in US NHANES surveys, representing about 100.9 million adults, and in China's CHARLS cohort of 21,853 people. Machine learning models were trained in one population and checked in the other.

Higher estimated velocity meant higher kidney disease odds in both cohorts, with odds ratios near 1.5 per extra meter per second. The association ran stronger in men and in obese and diabetic subgroups. Machine learning discrimination was moderate, the best model scoring about 0.80, and velocity ranked as the top feature, ahead of uric acid and diabetes history. Cutoffs sat near 10.2 and 10.6 meters per second. No calculated number replaces direct kidney tests, the authors caution.
pmc-13612182:
Mincheng Zou and six colleagues build a decision model for one of children's spine surgery's judgment calls. Children born with a hemivertebra, half a vertebra, develop scoliosis, and removing the malformed bone plus fusing segments is the standard fix. How many segments to fuse trades correction against preserving motion and growth, and choices have rested on surgeon feel. The team studied 36 patients who had posterior resection and fusion, mining imaging for predictors separating short from long fusions.

Screening by effect size surfaced three measurements: lumbar lordosis, thoracolumbar kyphosis, and pelvic tilt. A decision tree built on pre-surgery imaging, stratified by hemivertebra position, classified the needed strategy with 93.5 percent accuracy and an area under the curve of 0.982. The core predictors held across subgroups. The authors offer the tree as a neutral aid for balancing correction against function, noting the modest cohort behind it.
pmc-13616282:
Dong Cheng and colleagues present DUET-seq, an open-source droplet platform that reads both open chromatin and active genes from the same single cell nucleus. Linking the two views shows which control switches drive which genes, yet current tools miss many paired reads, cost a lot, or stay locked behind company systems. Their rig uses dissolving gel beads with two-part tags and a one-step reaction inside each droplet to label both kinds of molecule together.

Library building finishes within twelve hours. Careful tuning, including shutting off a leftover enzyme, yielded about 3,200 genes per test cell while keeping the chromatin picture sharp. Full plans for parts and reagents are published, so any lab can build it. Cheaper, open paired profiling could spread a powerful method beyond wealthy centres.
pmc-13616382:
Yan Zhang and colleagues find, by screening a library of compounds, that an antibiotic called danofloxacin helps mouse embryonic stem cells keep their all-purpose state. Growing such stem cells from many animal species in the lab stays stubbornly hard, and richer culture recipes are needed. Cells treated with the drug formed more undifferentiated colonies and contributed better to chimeric mice, the standard test of true stemness.

The drug lowers the amount and action of HDAC1, an enzyme that strips chemical tags from DNA packaging. With stripping reduced, activating tags rose at two key genes, Tert and Prdm10, which then switched on more strongly. Mimicking the drug by boosting either gene worked, and silencing either broke the effect. A farm antibiotic, oddly, may help labs found stem cell lines for species that have resisted for decades.
pmc-13616582:
J. Tyler Bruce, Tobias Z. Donlon, John L. Bass, and Juan C. Samayoa report a 2026 case series on narrowing at the mouth of the left atrial appendage. The appendage is a small pouch of the heart. The condition is so rare that only 28 adult and two child cases appear in past reports. Most were found by chance, and what the narrowing does over time is unknown. The series adds three patients of their own.

Two were infants born with a membrane narrowing the pouch entrance, one a four-month-old found during a work-up for a heart murmur that proved innocent. The third case appeared after a mechanical mitral valve was placed above its usual ring. With follow-up this scarce, each carefully described case helps cardiologists judge whether a silent narrowing needs watching, treatment, or neither.
pmc-13617682:
Karen Vinall-Collier and eight colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of oral care in British care homes, where older residents often depend on staff for daily mouth care. The team ran focus groups in 2022 with fifty people: residents, relatives, frontline care workers, managers, and outside dental professionals. Views were mapped onto the COM-B model, which sorts behavior into capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Opportunity dominated the findings, especially the physical environment, context, and resources available to staff. Capability issues centered on skills and self-regulation, while motivation turned on beliefs about consequences and drive. Access to outside dental professionals, training fitted to specific conditions, and strong backing were all judged pivotal. Staff warned that small fixes fail against structural barriers such as scarce dental access and heavy workloads, and relatives asked for clearer guidance to help their loved ones.
pmc-13617882:
Justin Aunger and ten colleagues argue that research governance in England can accidentally break the privacy promises that sensitive health workforce research depends on. Studies of bullying, speaking up, or patient safety need staff and hospitals to trust that taking part will stay hidden, since identifying a site can expose the individuals inside it. Standard steps such as site forms, local investigator rules, research passports, and portfolio reporting can leak that participation before recruitment even begins.

Reforms from the Health Research Authority starting March 2026 streamline set-up for staff-only studies, hide sites, and relax local investigator and passport demands for remote work. The authors say more is needed: special pathways for sensitive team research, restricted-access portfolio reporting, and more centralized governance forms. They recommend co-designing the next changes with researchers and hospital research departments so accountability survives while privacy becomes credible.
pmc-13618382:
Getachew Tadesse Siyoum, writing alone, reports surgical repair of an umbilical hernia in a ram at a veterinary teaching hospital in Ethiopia. The one-year-old ram arrived at Addis Ababa University's hospital with a progressively enlarging swelling at the navel. Examination confirmed a large umbilical hernia, where abdominal contents push through an unclosed ring in the wall, and the animal was admitted for herniorrhaphy.

Under locally infiltrated lidocaine, the surgeon opened the hernia sac, returned the protruding omentum and intestine to the abdomen. The ring was closed with a cruciate, cross-stitch, suture pattern using size two silk. Antibiotics and an anti-inflammatory followed for three days. Healing was uneventful and complete, and at sixty days the ram was healthy and gaining weight. Siyoum concludes the cruciate silk technique is a practical option for hernias of similar size when paired with timely surgery and careful aftercare.
pmc-13621582:
Jesse Johnson, Lynn Griffin, Kathryn Vickery, and Elissa Randall asked whether PET scan numbers can reveal lymphoma hiding in a dog's spleen without a needle. Staging canine lymphoma normally leans on sampling organs directly, yet spleen sampling carries risk and effort. The team followed dogs through chemotherapy with repeated FDG PET/CT scans, outlining the spleen each time and comparing three metabolic measures against the organ's actual cell samples.

Seven dogs contributed seventeen spleen samples. Spleens harboring lymphoma showed clearly higher uptake and tumor-volume measures than spleens with benign findings.
